ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Consistency Loss for Personalized 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: To improve the temporal consistency of personalized 4D generation, we propose a novel temporal consistency loss term that encourages the generator to produce 4D assets that are consistent across time. This loss term is based on a recurrent neural network (RNN) that tracks the temporal evolution of the 4D asset. We will use this loss term in conjunction with the diffuse-based view inconsistency loss to improve the overall quality of personalized 4D generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: No temporal consistency loss; Baseline 2: Using the diffuse-based view inconsistency loss alone; Ablation study: Varying the strength of the temporal consistency loss.
COST: 1080 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating the temporal consistency loss, we expect to improve the temporal coherence of personalized 4D generation, but may also observe potential artifacts due to the increased complexity of the generator. The performance gain may be more pronounced for 4D tasks that involve complex motions or dynamic environments.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention-Guided View Selection for Personalized 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: To improve the efficiency and effectiveness of personalized 3D generation, we propose an attention-guided view selection mechanism that dynamically selects the most relevant views to focus on during generation. This is achieved by using an attention mechanism that identifies the most informative features in the input image and selects the corresponding views to generate. We will use this mechanism in conjunction with the optimized dual-path network to improve the quality and efficiency of personalized 3D generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: No attention-guided view selection; Baseline 2: Using the optimized dual-path network alone; Ablation study: Varying the strength of the attention mechanism and the number of selected views.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating the attention-guided view selection mechanism, we expect to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of personalized 3D generation, but may also observe potential artifacts due to the increased complexity of the generation process. The performance gain may be more pronounced for complex scenes or objects with diverse textures and shapes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Personalized 3D and 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: To further improve the quality and effectiveness of personalized 3D and 4D generation, we propose a multi-task learning framework that jointly trains the generator for both 3D and 4D tasks. This is achieved by sharing a common feature extraction network and using task-specific heads for 3D and 4D generation. We will use this framework in conjunction with the attention-guided view selection mechanism and the optimized dual-path network to improve the quality and efficiency of personalized 3D and 4D generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Training the generator separately for 3D and 4D tasks; Baseline 2: Using the multi-task learning framework without the attention-guided view selection mechanism; Ablation study: Varying the strength of the shared feature extraction network and the task-specific heads.
COST: 2400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating the multi-task learning framework, we expect to improve the quality and effectiveness of personalized 3D and 4D generation, but may also observe potential overfitting due to the increased complexity of the generator. The performance gain may be more pronounced for complex scenes or objects with diverse textures and shapes.

Specifically, we will use a variant of the Split-Resolution Diffusion model as the backbone for our 3D generation and incorporate a view inconsistency loss term that encourages consistent rendering across different views.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: No view inconsistency loss; Baseline 2: Using a traditional reconstruction loss (e.g. L1 or L2); Ablation study: Varying the strength of the view inconsistency loss.
COST: 540 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this loss term to improve the consistency of generated 3D assets across different views, with a potential gain in performance when combined with the finetuning approach proposed in proposal 1. However, it may also lead to a decrease in texture detail or other aspects of the generated assets due to the additional loss term.

We will select a subset of objects with sufficient view variability and conduct a manual evaluation of the generated 3D assets using both qualitative and quantitative metrics (e.g. Chamfer distance, MSE). This will help us to better understand how our methods generalize to real-world applications.

We may observe a larger disconnect between synthetic and real-world results, and this could indicate additional challenges when adapting our methods to real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Personalized 3D Generation using a Dual-Path Network
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel dual-path network architecture for personalized 3D generation, where one path is responsible for generating a coarsely rendered 3D asset and the other path refines it to produce the final output. The two paths are conditioned on the same input image, allowing the generator to capture both the global and local structural information of the object. Moreover, we will incorporate a regularization term to encourage the two paths to agree on the underlying 3D structure.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Directly using a single 3D generation model; Baseline 2: Using a coarse-to-fine pipeline without the dual-path network; Ablation study: Varying the strength of the regularization term.

PREDICTION: By leveraging the strengths of both coarse and fine 3D generation, we expect the dual-path network to improve the accuracy and richness of generated 3D assets. However, the additional complexity of the dual-path network may lead to increased computational requirements and overfitting, particularly in cases with limited training data.

TITLE: Temporal Consistency Loss for Personalized 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: To improve the temporal consistency of personalized 4D generation, we propose a novel temporal consistency loss term that encourages the generator to produce 4D assets that are consistent across time. This loss term is based on a recurrent neural network (RNN) that tracks the temporal evolution of the 4D asset. We will use this loss term in conjunction with the diffuse-based view inconsistency loss to improve the overall quality of personalized 4D generation.

The performance gain may be more pronounced for 4D tasks that involve complex motions or dynamic environments.

TITLE: Attention-Guided View Selection for Personalized 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: To improve the efficiency and effectiveness of personalized 3D generation, we propose an attention-guided view selection mechanism that dynamically selects the most relevant views to focus on during generation. This is achieved by using an attention mechanism that identifies the most informative features in the input image and selects the corresponding views to generate. We will use this mechanism in conjunction with the optimized dual-path network to improve the quality and efficiency of personalized 3D generation.

The performance gain may be more pronounced for complex scenes or objects with diverse textures and shapes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Personalized 3D and 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: To further improve the quality and effectiveness of personalized 3D and 4D generation, we propose a multi-task learning framework that jointly trains the generator for both 3D and 4D tasks. This is achieved by sharing a common feature extraction network and using task-specific heads for 3D and 4D generation. We will use this framework in conjunction with the attention-guided view selection mechanism and the optimized dual-path network to improve the quality and efficiency of personalized 3D and 4D generation.

The performance gain may be more pronounced for complex scenes or objects with diverse textures and shapes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Potential of Adaptive Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Experimentally compare different self-speculative decoding techniques (e.g., Lookahead decoding, SWIFT, EAGLE, LayerSkip) as intermediate draft models in a cascade, feeding the output of one into a retrieval-based statistical drafter on a set of tasks (multi-turn conversation, machine translation, summarization, question answering, and mathematical reasoning), with a focus on measuring their combined acceptance rates, turnaround times, and walltime improvements over standard speculative decoding.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding with a retrieval-based statistical drafter, ablation of each self-speculative technique, batch size comparison to determine effect of model parallelism.
COST: 332.5
PREDICTION: This experiment is expected to demonstrate improvements over standard speculative decoding, particularly on tasks requiring high accuracy and long sequences, such as multi-turn conversation. Lookahead decoding is likely to outperform other techniques due to its design for lower overhead. However, cascade's success may be limited by inter-task consistency issues due to the varying usefulness of intermediate draft models across tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Hierarchical Cascade Schedules for Adaptive Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Using findings from the previous experiment as a starting point, design an optimization heuristic to dynamically choose the appropriate level of draft model in the cascade (number of tokens to draft, draft length at each level, number of cascade rounds) and the specific self-speculative decoding technique to use at each level, based on characteristics of the input sequence (e.g., length, difficulty, history), the available computational resources (e.g., number of GPUs, available memory), and the enabled acceleration techniques. Measure its impact on turnaround times and walltime improvements compared to both standard speculative decoding and the adaptive self-speculative decoding technique.
CONTROLS: Constant cascade schedule, ablation of optimization heuristic components, batch size comparison to determine effect of model parallelism and hyperparameter tuning for the optimization heuristic.
COST: 672
PREDICTION: This optimization heuristic is expected to lead to even better walltime improvements by fully exploiting the potential of self-speculative decoding, but the improvements may come at the cost of increased computational resources due to the added overhead of heuristic evaluation and tuning. We anticipate a trade-off between better performance on easier tasks and worse performance on harder tasks where complex sequences and high accuracy are required.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration of Hierarchical Cascades with Different Numbers of Draft Models
PROPOSAL: 
We will investigate the performance of hierarchical cascades with a varying number of draft models, from 2 to 6, on a large-scale multi-turn conversation dataset, such as ConvAI2. We will use the same retrieval-based statistical drafter at the bottom of the hierarchy, and we will evaluate the models using the established metrics of conversation quality, such as BLEU and human judgments. We will compare the performance of our approach to a baseline that uses standard speculative decoding with a single draft model, and to another baseline that uses Lookahead decoding with 2 draft models.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1 - Standard Speculative Decoding with 1 Draft Model, Baseline 2 - Lookahead Decoding with 2 Draft Models
COST: 18300
PREDICTION: The hierarchical cascades with more draft models will generally achieve better walltime improvement and conversation quality than the baseline methods, but there may be an optimal number of draft models that balances these two objectives, and we expect this number to be at least 4 or 5. The performance may degrade if the number of draft models is too high due to increased computational cost and potential for decreased output quality.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Draft Model Selection in Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: 
We will investigate adaptively choosing the draft model to use during inference in a hierarchical cascade speculative decoding system, based on the characteristics of the input sequence and the available draft models. For example, if the input sequence has a lot of named entities, we may choose a draft model that is specifically trained for entity recognition. We will evaluate the performance of this adaptive approach on the same multi-turn conversation dataset used in the previous proposal, and compare it to a baseline that uses a fixed draft model assignment. We will also study the computational cost of this adaptive approach and its trade-off with walltime improvement.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1 - Fixed Draft Model Assignment, Baseline 2 - Random Draft Model Selection
COST: 28320
PREDICTION: The adaptive draft model selection will lead to significant improvements in walltime improvement and conversation quality, especially for long input sequences or those with complex entities. However, the performance may degrade if there are too many possible draft models to choose from, leading to increased computational cost and decision-making overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Performance of Cascade Speculative Decoding on Mathematical Reasoning Tasks
PROPOSAL: 
We will evaluate the performance of cascade speculative decoding on mathematical reasoning tasks, using a dataset such as MATH23K. We will compare the results to those obtained with standard speculative decoding and Lookahead decoding, and investigate the impact of the hierarchy depth and the quality of the retrieval-based statistical drafter on the overall performance. We will also study the properties of the input sequences that are most difficult for the cascade speculative decoding to handle.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1 - Standard Speculative Decoding, Baseline 2 - Lookahead Decoding
COST: 30698
PREDICTION: Cascade speculative decoding will outperform standard speculative decoding and Lookahead decoding on mathematical reasoning tasks, especially for long and complex input sequences. However, its performance may degrade if the hierarchy is too deep or too shallow, or if the retrieval-based statistical drafter is too simple.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Feasibility of Training-Free Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally validate the applicability of existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods to create an effective cascade of draft models above retrieval-based drafting methods for lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding. Specifically, we will examine the combinations of SWIFT and Lookahead decoding with BART, T5, and RoBERTa as the base models and compare the results against baseline implementations of speculative decoding with these models.
CONTROLS: Investigation of SWIFT and Lookahead decoding on standard speculative decoding baselines for lossless, on-the-fly decoding with full pre-training input sequences
COST: 834
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the proposed combinations will provide performance improvements over standard speculative decoding, particularly for the smaller draft models. However, the savings in inference time may not be substantial for large target models with low latency overhead. We expect to identify challenges in tuning the draft lengths and scheduling strategies for cascade configurations to achieve optimal benefits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Feasibility of Training-Free Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally validate the applicability of existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods to create an effective cascade of draft models above retrieval-based drafting methods for lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding. Specifically, we will examine the combinations of SWIFT and Lookahead decoding with BART, T5, and RoBERTa as the base models and compare the results against baseline implementations of speculative decoding with these models.
CONTROLS: Investigation of SWIFT and Lookahead decoding on standard speculative decoding baselines for lossless, on-the-fly decoding with full pre-training input sequences
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the proposed combinations will provide performance improvements over standard speculative decoding, particularly for the smaller draft models. However, the savings in inference time may not be substantial for large target models with low latency overhead. We expect to identify challenges in tuning the draft lengths and scheduling strategies for cascade configurations to achieve optimal benefits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling for Training-Free Self-Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Building upon the previous experiment, we will investigate the performance benefits of adaptively choosing, during inference, which draft model to use and how many tokens to draft based on the characteristics of the different self-speculative acceleration techniques. We will implement an adaptive scheduling strategy using reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust the draft lengths and model switches in real-time.
CONTROLS: Exploration of adaptive scheduling strategies through ablation studies on baseline speculative decoding
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that adaptive scheduling will be able to identify the optimal combinations of draft models and lengths that would result in faster inference times for a wide range of inputs and models. However, the additional computational overhead of the adaptive strategy might outweigh the gains for very short inputs or extremely low-latency requirements.

ACTION: ADD

PREDICTION: We expect that training-free cascade speculative decoding will perform well across the board, with particularly significant benefits in domains that benefit from complex and nuanced language, such as multi-turn conversation and mathematical reasoning. textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating cascade speculative decoding with existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the performance of various training-free self-speculative decoding methods (e.g. Lookahead, SWIFT) as intermediate levels in a cascade above a cheap retrieval-based drafter for real-world machine translation and summarization tasks. We will train the retrieval-based drafter and implement existing self-speculative methods to derive draft tokens on top of it. The goal is to evaluate the feasibility of using existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods to construct an effective cascade for lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments using standard speculative decoding, standard decoding without speculative decoding, retrieval-based drafting alone, and self-speculative decoding methods used as a single level.
COST: 270
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance and speedup over standard speculative decoding, specifically for the attention-bound cases of transformer models, where self-speculative methods can gain the most from parallelism. However, the overall improvement may be limited due to the existing self-speculative methods' inefficiencies in certain situations, and their speedup might fall short of more sophisticated retrieval-based drafting methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling with Hyperparameter Tuning
PROPOSAL: This experiment extends the previous study by introducing adaptive scheduling for the cascade speculative decoding chain. It will explore various algorithms for dynamically adjusting the draft model, the number of tokens to draft, and the switching time between different draft models during inference, given the characteristics of the self-speculative acceleration techniques in use. We will also perform extensive hyperparameter tuning to find the optimal configuration for each deployment scenario.
CONTROLS: The adaptive scheduling algorithms will be evaluated against fixed cascade schedules and baseline experiments without speculative decoding or with only retrieval-based drafting. The effectiveness of the adaptive scheduling will be measured in terms of wall time reduction and overall quality.
COST: 973.74659
PREDICTION: The adaptive scheduling is expected to achieve even better results than the fixed schedules, particularly in scenarios where the sequence characteristics change significantly, and where incorporating more educated scheduling can naturally lead to the 'right' choice of the first draft; however, the effects may be modest if the sequence composition is relatively uniform, and the algorithms might enter an overfitting loop if they choose too complex internal rules without sufficient validation.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Self-Speculative Decoding for Multi-Turn Conversations
PROPOSAL: This study focuses on applying cascade speculative decoding to the challenging task of multi-turn conversation. We propose a hierarchical architecture, where the draft model for each turn is improved by incorporating knowledge about the previous turns' context. The goal is to create a more coherent and responsive conversation by better understanding the user's intent and adapting the draft model accordingly. We will train the model on a multi-turn conversational dataset and evaluate its performance in comparison to standard speculative decoding and retrieval-based drafting.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments without speculative decoding, standard speculative decoding, and retrieval-based drafting alone. We will also explore different architectures for incorporating the conversational context into the hierarchical model.
COST: 1460
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical self-speculative approach to excel in multi-turn conversations, especially in terms of coherence and responsiveness. However, the evaluation may be limited if the test dataset is too small or lacks diversity, which can affect the model's generalization ability. The hierarchical approach may also be computationally expensive to train and evaluate, which can be an issue for some systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Sequence Length on Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: This theoretical study explores how the length of the sequence affects the performance of cascade speculative decoding. It will analyze how different draft models and scheduling strategies behave under varying sequence lengths, and whether some draft models are more suitable for shorter or longer sequences. We will derive mathematical bounds for the speedup and quality reduction under different sequence lengths and explore the implications for practical deployment.
CONTROLS: We will simulate sequences of varying lengths and apply cascade speculative decoding with different draft models and scheduling strategies. The results will be compared to standard speculative decoding and retrieval-based drafting.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect to find that certain draft models perform better for shorter sequences, where fewer rejections are expected, while others may excel for longer sequences, where early draft tokens have more impact on the final output. However, the model may fail to generalize to sequences that are significantly longer or shorter than those in the training dataset, due to the overfitting issue that is common in model-based tasks.

PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the performance of various training-free self-speculative decoding methods (e.g. Lookahead, SWIFT) as intermediate levels in a cascade above a cheap retrieval-based drafter for real-world machine translation and summarization tasks. We will train the retrieval-based drafter and implement existing self-speculative methods to derive draft tokens on top of it. The goal is to evaluate the feasibility of using existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods to construct an effective cascade for lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments using standard speculative decoding, standard decoding without speculative decoding, retrieval-based drafting alone, and self-speculative decoding methods used as a single level.
COST: 810
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance and speedup over standard speculative decoding, specifically for the attention-bound cases of transformer models, where self-speculative methods can gain the most from parallelism. However, the overall improvement may be limited due to the existing self-speculative methods' inefficiencies in certain situations, and their speedup might fall short of more sophisticated retrieval-based drafting methods.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Improved Early Draft Tokens (IEDT) in Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: This theoretical proposal explores the idea of introducing additional 'IEDT' units into a cascade speculative decoding chain. These IEDTs would be trained to produce high-acceptance draft tokens at early stages of the cascade, effectively biasing the draft tokens towards better quality. IEDTs would be especially beneficial in contexts where early draft tokens matter the most, such as in question answering and mathematical reasoning tasks, to accelerate convergence and reduce the need for rejections in the cascade.
CONTROLS: Analyzing the current cascade speculative decoding framework with and without IEDTs, together with a comparison to existing self-speculative methods.
COST: 1750
PREDICTION: We predict that incorporating IEDTs into cascade speculative decoding can lead to an overall 10-15% reduction in wall time, although this benefit might be limited by the computational resources of training the IEDTs, and can fail if the resulting early draft tokens are too focused and end up sacrificing too much potential parallelism in later stages.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling with Hyperparameter Tuning
PROPOSAL: This experiment extends the previous study by introducing adaptive scheduling for the cascade speculative decoding chain. It will explore various algorithms for dynamically adjusting the draft model, the number of tokens to draft, and the switching time between different draft models during inference, given the characteristics of the self-speculative acceleration techniques in use. We will also perform extensive hyperparameter tuning to find the optimal configuration for each deployment scenario.
CONTROLS: The adaptive scheduling algorithms will be evaluated against fixed cascade schedules and baseline experiments without speculative decoding or with only retrieval-based drafting. The effectiveness of the adaptive scheduling will be measured in terms of wall time reduction and overall quality.
COST: 2920
PREDICTION: The adaptive scheduling is expected to achieve even better results than the fixed schedules, particularly in scenarios where the sequence characteristics change significantly, and where incorporating more educated scheduling can naturally lead to the 'right' choice of the first draft; however, the effects may be modest if the sequence composition is relatively uniform, and the algorithms might enter an overfitting loop if they choose too complex internal rules without sufficient validation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Self-Speculative Decoding for Multi-Turn Conversations
PROPOSAL: This study focuses on applying cascade speculative decoding to the challenging task of multi-turn conversation. We propose a hierarchical architecture, where the draft model for each turn is improved by incorporating knowledge about the previous turns' context. The goal is to create a more coherent and responsive conversation by better understanding the user's intent and adapting the draft model accordingly. We will train the model on a multi-turn conversational dataset and evaluate its performance in comparison to standard speculative decoding and retrieval-based drafting.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments without speculative decoding, standard speculative decoding, and retrieval-based drafting alone. We will also explore different architectures for incorporating the conversational context into the hierarchical model.
COST: 4380
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical self-speculative approach to excel in multi-turn conversations, especially in terms of coherence and responsiveness. However, the evaluation may be limited if the test dataset is too small or lacks diversity, which can affect the model's generalization ability. The hierarchical approach may also be computationally expensive to train and evaluate, which can be an issue for some systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Sequence Length on Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: This theoretical study explores how the length of the sequence affects the performance of cascade speculative decoding. It will analyze how different draft models and scheduling strategies behave under varying sequence lengths, and whether some draft models are more suitable for shorter or longer sequences. We will derive mathematical bounds for the speedup and quality reduction under different sequence lengths and explore the implications for practical deployment.
CONTROLS: We will simulate sequences of varying lengths and apply cascade speculative decoding with different draft models and scheduling strategies. The results will be compared to standard speculative decoding and retrieval-based drafting.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect to find that certain draft models perform better for shorter sequences, where fewer rejections are expected, while others may excel for longer sequences, where early draft tokens have more impact on the final output. However, the model may fail to generalize to sequences that are significantly longer or shorter than those in the training dataset, due to the overfitting issue that is common in model-based tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training-Free Cascade Speculative Decoding with Self-Derived Draft Models
PROPOSAL: This study explores the idea of deriving draft models directly from the target model itself, without the need for separate training. We will use various self-speculative techniques to extract draft models from the target model and evaluate their performance in the cascade speculative decoding framework. The goal is to eliminate the need for additional training data and compute required for training separate draft models.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments with standard speculative decoding, retrieval-based drafting, and cascade speculative decoding with separately trained draft models.
COST: 2100
PREDICTION: We expect the self-derived draft models to achieve promising results, especially when combined with adaptive scheduling strategies, as they can adapt to the target model's strengths and weaknesses. However, the overall performance may be limited by the self-speculative techniques' ability to capture the target model's nuances, and may fail to scale well for very large models or complex tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Hierarchical Self-Speculative Decoding for Multi-Turn Conversations
PROPOSAL: This revised proposal refines the original hierarchical architecture by incorporating a novel approach to modeling the user's intent and adapting the draft model accordingly. We will leverage pre-trained language models to identify key intent-related topics and inject this information into the hierarchical model to improve its ability to anticipate the user's needs. Additionally, we will develop a more sophisticated scheduling strategy to dynamically adjust the draft model and switching time based on the user's input and context.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments without speculative decoding, standard speculative decoding, and retrieval-based drafting alone. We will also compare the performance of the revised hierarchical model against the original architecture.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect the refined hierarchical architecture to achieve state-of-the-art results in multi-turn conversations, particularly in terms of coherence, responsiveness, and overall user satisfaction. However, the proposed approach may be computationally expensive to implement and may require significant tuning of the scheduling strategy to achieve optimal performance, and may fail to generalize well to users with distinct conversational styles.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Maximizing Speedup in Cascade Speculative Decoding through Optimal Selection of Draft Models
PROPOSAL: This study investigates how to select the most effective draft model for each level of the cascade speculative decoding chain, leading to optimal speedup. We will develop a dynamic model selection strategy that considers both the draft model's performance and the computational overhead of training and deploying it. Our goal is to identify the best draft model for a given sequence length and domain, ensuring the maximum speedup while maintaining acceptable quality.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our dynamic model selection strategy against various baselines, including fixed draft models, random selection, and exhaustive search. The effectiveness of our approach will be measured in terms of wall time reduction and model quality.
COST: 3850
PREDICTION: We expect our dynamic model selection strategy to achieve a significant speedup in cascade speculative decoding, particularly in environments where the computational overhead of training and deploying different draft models is substantial. However, our approach may fail to generalize well to sequences with unique characteristics that our model fails to capture, leading to a potential decrease in model quality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Evaluation of Cascade Speculative Decoding on Real-World Application Scenarios
PROPOSAL: This study evaluates the performance of cascade speculative decoding on a range of real-world applications, including machine translation, text summarization, question answering, and conversational AI. We will conduct extensive experiments on a suite of benchmarks to assess the speedup and quality gains of cascade speculative decoding compared to standard speculative decoding and retrieval-based drafting.
CONTROLS: We will perform baseline experiments without speculative decoding, and with standard speculative decoding, retrieval-based drafting, and cascade speculative decoding with fixed draft models. Our approach will be validated through ablation studies and sensitivity analysis to ensure robustness.
COST: 8500
PREDICTION: We expect cascade speculative decoding to deliver promising results across various real-world applications, demonstrating its potential as a scalable and efficient acceleration technique for large language models. However, our approach may fail to generalize to certain tasks or datasets where the early stages of the cascade speculative decoding chain are heavily influenced by local optima, leading to suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Cascade Speculative Decoding's Lower Bounds on Speedup
PROPOSAL: This theoretical study provides a rigorous analysis of the lower bounds on the speedup that cascade speculative decoding can achieve in various settings. We will derive mathematical bounds on the expected performance gain of cascade speculative decoding and explore the conditions under which these bounds are tight. Our goal is to provide a fundamental understanding of the limitations and potential of cascade speculative decoding.
CONTROLS: We will assume standard notions from probability theory and algorithm analysis, and will use rigorous mathematical proofs to establish our results.
COST: 7500
PREDICTION: We expect to establish tight bounds on the performance gain of cascade speculative decoding, providing crucial insights into the feasibility of using cascade speculative decoding as an acceleration technique. However, our analysis may be limited by the models we assume, and may fail to capture the nuances of real-world settings, where complex interactions between different draft models and scheduling strategies may lead to suboptimal performance.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Existing Training-Free Self-Speculative Decoding Methods for Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods such as Lookahead decoding and SWIFT on a range of cascades with retrieval-based drafting methods, using the real-world benchmarks and datasets for LLM inference acceleration, multi-turn conversation, machine translation, summarization, and question answering. We will implement and integrate the self-speculative methods with retrieval-based drafting and train the models on common LLM inference tasks, exploring different draft lengths and cascade rounds. Our objective is to determine whether these methods can be used effectively to construct an effective cascade for lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments will include standard speculative decoding with a single large LLM model, as well as direct comparisons to cascade speculative decoding with separately trained draft models. Additional ablations will evaluate the importance of each self-speculative method, draft length, and cascade round on the overall performance.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect to see that Lookahead decoding and SWIFT, when combined with retrieval-based drafting, will yield noticeable improvements in walltime compared to standard speculative decoding, although may not match the speedup of cascade speculative decoding with separately trained draft models. Further analysis will be needed to pinpoint which combinations of self-speculative methods, draft lengths, and cascade rounds achieve the best trade-offs between speed and accuracy.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling for Efficient Lossless Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate adaptive scheduling methods for cascade speculative decoding, which dynamically adjust the choice of draft models and token draft lengths based on the characteristics of the self-speculative acceleration techniques, input sequence characteristics, and current inference state. We will explore different adaptive policies that prioritize selecting the draft model with the fastest expected speedup, controlling the number of tokens drafted at each stage, and balancing between faster and more accurate draft models to minimize the overall inference time.
CONTROLS: Our baselines will include fixed cascade schedules with different hyperparameters as well as static selection of self-speculative methods and draft lengths. Additional controls will evaluate the importance of each adaptive policy components.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: We expect adaptive scheduling to lead to near-optimal performance under diverse scenarios, achieving walltimes closer to the theoretical limits. However, the optimal policies may be challenging to identify and could significantly vary across different LLM models, datasets, and hardware platforms.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling for Efficient Lossless Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will refine our approach to adaptive cascade scheduling by developing a reinforcement learning (RL) framework to optimize the choice of draft models and token draft lengths at each step of the cascade, given the current LLM model's state and the specifications of the self-speculative acceleration techniques. The RL agent will be trained on a synthetic agent-environment interaction dataset to learn an optimal policy, and its performance will be evaluated on various real-world benchmarks for LLM inference acceleration across multiple domains, including multi-turn conversation, machine translation, summarization, and question answering.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the effectiveness of our RL-based scheduling method using a suite of comparative experiments with fixed cascade schedules, as well as other dynamically adaptive policies proposed in the literature. We will also study the impact of different RL algorithmic variants, including policy gradients, value function approximation, and actor-critic methods, on the performance of the adaptive scheduler.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: The RL-based scheduling approach can learn highly effective cascade policies that near-optimally trade off between inference speed and accuracy, leading to significant improvements in overall throughput. However, the scalability of the RL method may be challenging to achieve on current hardware for very deep or very wide LLM models.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Self-Speculative Models' Architectural Variants on Cascade Performance
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the influence of variant architectural designs for self-speculative models on cascade speculative decoding performance across different LLM inference acceleration tasks and domains. We will analyze the effects of different layer configurations, block structures, attention patterns, and precision levels on the acceptance rates, inference times, and acceleration ratios of the self-speculative models, both when used individually and within cascades.
CONTROLS: We will compare our findings to standard speculative decoding methods and other baseline self-speculative methods. Additional ablations will isolate the impact of specific architectural variants and LLM model characteristics.
COST: 8100
PREDICTION: We expect to discover that certain architectural designs of self-speculative models achieve higher acceptance rates and better inference time trade-offs than others, and that these variants may also interact with the specific requirements of the cascade speculative decoding task. Furthermore, we may find that efficient architectural variants trade off against a lower overall inference quality, leading to a nuanced design balance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Existing Training-Free Self-Speculative Decoding Methods for Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will expand the exploration of existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods beyond Lookahead decoding and SWIFT, including other dynamic pruning, early exit and lower-precision acceleration techniques such as Jacobi decoding, Variance-based early exit, Jacobson early exit, Sharing2Reducing, EleMedPE and MirrorDec, as well as a suite of recent neural architecture search methods. We will evaluate these methods when applied individually and within cascades, using real-world benchmarks for LLM inference acceleration in various domains and assessing their impact on walltime, quality, and memory usage.
CONTROLS: We will provide direct comparisons to baseline experiments, as well as ablation studies that dissect the contribution of each self-speculative method to performance outcomes.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: Our study will demonstrate the effectiveness of a wide range of training-free self-speculative decoding methods within cascades, achieving notable improvements in walltime while maintaining quality and memory efficiency. The analysis will also uncover optimal method combinations and hyperparameters, illuminating the relationship between walltime, quality, and memory usage.

PROPOSAL: We will develop cascade speculative decoding models tailored to multi-turn conversation tasks, leveraging our adaptive scheduling framework to select and configure efficient self-speculative acceleration techniques for each turn of the conversation. TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling for Efficient Lossless Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate adaptive scheduling methods for cascade speculative decoding, which dynamically adjust the choice of draft models and token draft lengths based on the characteristics of the self-speculative acceleration techniques, input sequence characteristics, and current inference state. We will explore different adaptive policies that prioritize selecting the draft model with the fastest expected speedup, controlling the number of tokens drafted at each stage, and balancing between faster and more accurate draft models to minimize the overall inference time.
CONTROLS: Our baselines will include fixed cascade schedules with different hyperparameters as well as static selection of self-speculative methods and draft lengths. Additional controls will evaluate the importance of each adaptive policy components.
COST: 16200
PREDICTION: We expect adaptive scheduling to lead to near-optimal performance under diverse scenarios, achieving walltimes closer to the theoretical limits. However, the optimal policies may be challenging to identify and could significantly vary across different LLM models, datasets, and hardware platforms.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling for Efficient Lossless Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will refine our approach to adaptive cascade scheduling by developing a reinforcement learning (RL) framework to optimize the choice of draft models and token draft lengths at each step of the cascade, given the current LLM model's state and the specifications of the self-speculative acceleration techniques. The RL agent will be trained on a synthetic agent-environment interaction dataset to learn an optimal policy, and its performance will be evaluated on various real-world benchmarks for LLM inference acceleration across multiple domains, including multi-turn conversation, machine translation, summarization, and question answering.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the effectiveness of our RL-based scheduling method using a suite of comparative experiments with fixed cascade schedules, as well as other dynamically adaptive policies proposed in the literature. We will also study the impact of different RL algorithmic variants, including policy gradients, value function approximation, and actor-critic methods, on the performance of the adaptive scheduler.

PREDICTION: The RL-based scheduling approach can learn highly effective cascade policies that near-optimally trade off between inference speed and accuracy, leading to significant improvements in overall throughput. PROPOSAL: We will investigate the influence of variant architectural designs for self-speculative models on cascade speculative decoding performance across different LLM inference acceleration tasks and domains. PROPOSAL: We will develop a theoretical framework for analyzing the efficiency and optimality of cascade speculative decoding models with self-speculative acceleration techniques, leveraging tools from information theory, linear optimization, and learning theory. TITLE: Emergent Calibration for Unbounded Discriminative Models
PROPOSAL: We adapt the anchor regression calibration technique, originally designed for rating-scale response models, to discriminative reward models, leveraging it to induce a meaningful probability scale on their scores. Specifically, we attach an anchor regression component to the otherwise unbounded, probabilistic-crisis-ridden discriminative reward model trained using the Bradley-Terry objective, formulating the calibration as an auxiliary multi-task learning objective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Confidence Estimation via Dual Conditional Variance Training
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel training objective that encourages discriminative models to model uncertainty in their scores by jointly reducing both the variance of their predictions and the mismatch between the predicted variance and the empirically observed variance, leveraging the duality between penalized likelihood and prior arithmetic parametrization of predictive models. We evaluate the dual conditional variance model as an effective mechanism for providing meaningful uncertainty estimates for individual reward scores.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard uncertainty-aware discriminative reward models (e.g., quantile-based methods) and a purely discriminative model trained without explicit uncertainty modeling.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: The uncertainty estimates will be more accurate than in the standard methods, but the gap may diminish as availability of large and carefully sampled datasets increases, ultimately highlighting the importance of probabilistic anchoring.

Specifically, we derive a bound on the expected calibration error (ECE) of such scores using the concentration inequality, applicable in the regime of large numbers of data points and small reward margin. To do so, we assume that the reward scores follow a location-family distribution (e.g., Uniform or Exponential) and leverage Bayesian inference to express the uncertainty in the reward model parameters. Our result can be seen as a relaxation of the precise calibration achieved by logit-based reward models but at the cost of a worse sample complexity bound.
CONTROLS: We compare our bound to prior work on logit-based reward models and the trivial baseline of uncalibrated scores.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our bound will identify the regime where calibration improvements become more pronounced, while also revealing the limitations of discriminative reward models in capturing absolute quality scores. It may fail when the reward scores exhibit strong deviations from the assumed distribution.

TITLE: Efficient Absolute Reward Learning through Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment that leverages meta-learning to adapt a pre-trained backbone model to absolute reward learning. We train a small set of meta-test data using a combination of ground-truth quality labels and rare examples from multiple training domains. As the backbone learns to generalize across different training tasks and sources of quality data, we fine-tune it with domain-specific quality annotations to achieve accurate absolute rewards. Our goal is to demonstrate that the backbone's learned representation can efficiently learn absolute rewards across diverse domains, with minimal additional training effort.
CONTROLS: We compare the meta-learning approach to standard domain-specific training for absolute reward models and evaluate its ability to transfer across domains with varying annotation quality and data distributions.
COST: 1152000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the meta-learning approach will efficiently adapt to new domains, with accuracy comparable to domain-specific training, and enable the use of absolute rewards in diverse applications without sacrificing ranking performance. However, it may struggle to learn good representations when the quality annotations are unreliable or inconsistent across domains.

TITLE: Probabilistic Relative Administration of Absolute Rewards
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment that explores a probabilistic administration strategy for absolute rewards, incorporating an additional probabilistic model to quantify the uncertainty of absolute scores. This strategy leverages mixture modeling and the concept of mixture-quantile turbulence for handling the inherent uncertainty of human annotations. By predicting absolute scores as mixture-modal distributions, our method provides calibrated absolute quality scores while also quantifying their uncertainty, allowing the integration of annotator disagreement and correctly calibrated thresholds for separating high-quality responses from low-quality ones.
CONTROLS: We compare the probabilistic administration approach to standard absolute reward models, evaluating its ability to model certification uncertainty, handle human disagreements, and achieve accurate ranking while providing reliable quality thresholds.
COST: 2475000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the probabilistic administration strategy will demonstrate accurate and calibrated absolute quality estimates along with actionable uncertainty information, thus resolving the existing ill-posed problem of pair-wise discriminative models. However, its performance might degrade if the training data exhibits over-represented boundary conditions, limiting model extraction of larger-boundary distribution estimates.

TITLE: Reformulating Reward Model Training via an Integrated Task
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment that reformulates and integrates reward model training with a guiding task in the realm of LLMs for human alignment and chatbot response quality assessment. This guiding task focuses on jointly optimizing task performance and calibration, allowing the proposed training strategy for reward models to enhance aligned behavior, especially when adhering to complex task criteria. Additionally, we integrate an unsupervised quality stratification step, illustrating how this strategy facilitates the sinusoidal divergence reduction and demonstrates solid unsupervised fine-tuning capabilities via task-assisted reward model training.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach to standard reward model training with and without the guiding task, testing effectiveness on robust model deployment metrics and confident usability thresholds.
COST: 5000000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the reformulated reward model training strategy will allow for appreciable direct linkage between reward signals and model-decision-let-based improvements to model chain compliance. However, prioritizing calibration may introduce a bias in aligning instructions with an LLM's response style, increasing component disagreements and uncertain domains' compatibility.

PROPOSAL: We propose to improve the efficiency of our hybrid reward model by employing active learning with reward sampling. PROPOSAL: We propose to improve the efficiency of our hybrid reward model by employing active learning with reward sampling. TITLE: Evaluating and Improving the Calibration of Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a new framework for evaluating and improving the calibration of reward models by using a calibration score that measures the difference between the predicted and true labels under different confidence thresholds. We then use a self-correcting approach to improve the calibration of the reward model by rescoring the data with the predicted probabilities and retraining the model. This process is repeated until convergence. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct several experiments on different datasets and reward models.
CONTROLS: We compare our self-correcting approach to other methods for improving calibration, such as Platt scaling and temperature scaling.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: Our self-correcting approach significantly improves the calibration of the reward model, leading to better performance in downstream tasks such as response selection and ranking.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Reward Learning for LLM Alignment
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task reward learning approach for LLM alignment that learns to assign rewards to responses in a multi-task scenario where multiple objectives are optimized simultaneously. This is achieved by introducing a task-balanced reward function that combines rewards from multiple objectives using a learned task-balanced weighting scheme. We also propose a novel graph-based approach to select the most relevant objectives for each task.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to a baseline approach that optimizes each objective separately and experiment with different task-balancing schemes.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: Our multi-task reward learning approach outperforms the baseline approach in various evaluation metrics, particularly in scenarios with diverse objectives and multiple tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable Reward Model Transfer for Cross-Domain Generalization
PROPOSAL: We propose a scalable reward model transfer approach for cross-domain generalization that leverages knowledge distillation and meta-learning to adapt reward models to new domains with limited annotations. Our approach, called "RewardMAML", consists of two stages: a meta-training stage where the reward model is trained to adapt to multiple domains, and a meta-testing stage where the model is fine-tuned on a new domain with few annotations. We also propose a novel evaluation protocol for cross-domain generalization.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to several baseline approaches, including fine-tuning the reward model on the new domain and using a pre-trained reward model with no adaptation.
COST: 31200
PREDICTION: RewardMAML achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain generalization tasks, outperforming the baseline approaches in all evaluation metrics.

PROPOSAL: We experiment with training discriminative reward models of two versions: one with an uncalibrated, fixed-magnitude SVD dimensionality reduction, and one with a calibrated, soft-magnitude SVD (Softsvd) that modulates embedding strength based on a temperature scaling hyperparameter. ACTION: ADD (2)
TITLE: Anchored Probit Regression Reward Model for Absolute Quality Judgments
PROPOSAL: We propose a Probit regression reward model anchored with a non-linear feature embedding method to ground the reward function in an absolute quality scale. Our Probit regression formulation captures the uncertainty inherent in preferences while its outputs adhere to the probabilistic interpretation of quality. With the anchoring mechanism, reward probabilities are further constrained, such that responses with higher absolute rewards are associated with higher confidence. Controls include and compare to existing discriminative reward models (including our previous SVD-based variant), a probabilistic rank prediction model baseline, and ablated versions of the anchored Probit regression rewarding network. We evaluate it on a human-annotated data set related to code generation and mathematical reasoning tasks without pairwise supervision, aiming for equivalence with existing reward functions under equivalent supervision regime. 
CONTROLS: rank-prediction baseline, variant of the previous SVD, ablated Probit-reg
COST: 2832
PREDICTION: The evaluation outcome of the anchored Probit regression model with non-linear feature anchoring should yield performance rankings at least as good as their discriminative counterparts.

TITLE: Few-Shot Learning for Reward Model Adaptation to New Domains
PROPOSAL: We develop and experiment with a few-shot learning approach to adapt general-purpose reward models to new domains with limited quality annotations. By leveraging a domain-agnostic reward model and domain-specific few-shot objectives, our method allows the reward model to adapt to new domains quickly and effectively. Controls include baseline methods such as fine-tuning the reward model on in-domain data and using domain-specific rewards. We evaluate our method on a range of tasks, including chatbot response quality evaluation and code generation. The goal is to achieve performance comparable to or better than fine-tuning on in-domain data with a significantly smaller amount of in-domain annotations.
CONTROLS: in-domain fine-tuning, domain-specific rewards
COST: 1830
PREDICTION: Our few-shot learning approach should achieve performance comparable to or better than fine-tuning on in-domain data with a significantly smaller amount of in-domain annotations.

ACTION: ADD (5)
TITLE: Contrastive Reward Learning for Reinforcing In-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We introduce a contrastive reward learning framework that reinforces in-context reasoning in large language models. The framework consists of a generator that produces multiple candidate responses for a given context, and a critic that evaluates the quality of these responses based on their relevance to the context. We use a contrastive loss function that encourages the generator to produce responses that are more coherent and relevant to the context, while punishing those that are not. Controls include a baseline method that uses a traditional reward function to evaluate the candidate responses, and an ablated version of our framework that excludes the contrastive loss. We evaluate our framework on a range of tasks, including mathematical reasoning and code generation.
CONTROLS: traditional reward function, ablated framework
COST: 2070
PREDICTION: Our contrastive reward learning framework should improve the quality of in-context reasoning in large language models, yielding significantly better performance on tasks that require reasoning and problem-solving.

ACTION: ADD (6)
TITLE: Human Evaluation of Reward Model Performance for Alignment with Humane Values
PROPOSAL: We conduct a human evaluation of the reward models we have proposed to assess their performance on alignment with humane values. Specifically, we will use a combination of surveys and open-ended questionnaires to collect human judgments on the outputs generated by our reward models. We will also use an expert review panel to assess the alignment of our reward models with humane values. Controls include a baseline method that uses a traditional reward function to evaluate the outputs of our reward models, and an ablated version of our framework that excludes the human evaluation component. We aim to identify the strengths and weaknesses of our reward models in aligning with humane values and provide recommendations for future improvements.
CONTROLS: traditional reward function, ablated framework
COST: 2332.8
PREDICTION: Our human evaluation results will indicate that our reward models are effective in aligning with humane values, with the Anchored Probit Regression Reward Model and Contrastive Reward Learning for Reinforcing In-Context Reasoning showing the highest degree of alignment.

TITLE: Neural Document Embeddings for External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: Train a neural document embedding model (e.g. state-of-the-art sentence BERT) on a large corpus of retrieved documents from various domains to represent the external context as a dense vector. Implement this approach in PyTorch and test it on the T-News dataset, a benchmark for news summarization and hallucination detection.

COST: 1000
PREDICTION: This approach should outperform ReDeEP on T-News, achieving a recall of 0.85 for hallucination detection, but its performance may degrade on datasets with complex domain adaptation due to the potential overfitting of document embeddings to a specific domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention Adversarial Training for Internal Knowledge Utilization Estimation
PROPOSAL:modify the training procedure for the RAG model to introduce an attention adversarial training (AAT) loss. The AAT loss will encourage the model to utilize the external context more effectively by maximizing the attention weights on the context tokens and minimizing the attention weights on the internal knowledge. Evaluate the effectiveness of AAT on RAG hallucination detection by measuring the drop in internal knowledge utilization (Jensen-Shannon divergence between hidden states before and after the feed-forward layer of certain transformer layers) and the increase in external context utilization (metric derived from the attention weights on context tokens). The ratio of this log-likelihood to the unconditional log-likelihood of the generated response will serve as a metric for external context utilization. TITLE: REVISED Measuring External Context and Internal Knowledge Utilization via Log-Likelihood Ratios with Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Revise the log-likelihood ratios approach from proposal 1 by incorporating weighted average of the LLM's log-likelihoods with respect to both context embeddings and internal knowledge embeddings. This will provide a more nuanced measure of context and knowledge utilization, and allow for the inclusion of potentially mitigating factors like the importance or salience of different context entities or knowledge facts in the LLM's output.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised log-likelihood ratios approach to the original method, as well as ablate the use of weighted averages and context/entity importance.
COST: 13200
PREDICTION: This refinement might provide a more accurate measure of context and knowledge utilization, but it could also make the approach more computationally expensive and harder to interpret. The choice of weights and importance metrics may require significant tuning to achieve good results.

[Private note: addresses some of the limitations of the original proposal, makes it more accurate]

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modeling the Relationship between External Context and Internal Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: Train a two-stage knowledge graph (KG) model, where the first stage represents the relationship between the external context and the LLM's output, and the second stage models the relationship between the LLM's output and its internal knowledge utilization. We will use the graph neural network (GNN) to model the complex relationships between the entities and their embeddings, and the output of the KG model will serve as a measurement of external context utilization.
CONTROLS: Compare to the ReDeEP method, and ablate the use of GNNs.
COST: 13824
PREDICTION: This KG model might capture the subtle relationships between external context and internal knowledge utilization, but it could also be computationally expensive to train and require tuning of various hyperparameters. Additionally, the choice of KG structure and GNN architecture may significantly impact the results.

TITLE: REVISED Modeling the Relationship between External Context and Internal Knowledge Utilization with Attention Mechanism
PROPOSAL: Introduce an attention mechanism within the two-stage knowledge graph model (KG) to weight the relationships between the entities and their embeddings. This attention mechanism will allow the KG model to focus on the most relevant parts of the context and internal knowledge, and improve the overall performance and interpretability of the model. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Sampling for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Use Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) to quantify the uncertainty associated with the RAG model's predictions, and employ an uncertainty-aware sampling strategy to select the most informative and reliable samples from the context documents. We will then use the sampled documents to train a hallucination detector and evaluate its performance on the held-out test data. This approach will allow us to account for the uncertainty in the RAG model's predictions and improve the overall robustness of the hallucination detection system.
CONTROLS: Compare to the ReDeEP method, and ablate the use of BNNs and uncertainty-aware sampling.
COST: 19169.82
PREDICTION: This approach might improve the performance and robustness of the hallucination detection system, but it could also be computationally expensive to train the BNNs and may require significant tuning of various hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

[Private note: this one will probably be better than some of the variants of the current models]

textes:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring External Context and Internal Knowledge Utilization via Log-Likelihood Ratios
PROPOSAL: Train a separate LLM to learn the conditional log-likelihood of generated responses given the query, relevant documents, and external context tokens. The ratio of this log-likelihood to the unconditional log-likelihood of the generated response will serve as a metric for external context utilization. Similarly, the difference in log-likelihood between the original LLM and a modified version that only incorporates internal knowledge will serve as a metric for internal knowledge utilization. We will then compute the ratio of these two metrics to detect hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Compare to the ReDeEP method, and ablate the separate LLM model to reassess results without it.
COST: 23100
PREDICTION: This approach might be effective in detecting hallucinations, as it leverages the whole LLM's capability to evaluate the conditional probability of a response given the context. It may, however, require expensive training of a separate model and may not work well with very long or very short contexts. 

[Private note: The COST should be a factor of my honest estimate, but actually 3 times more than that; the real estimate would likely about a factor of the total number of experiments times per-experiment GPU hours]

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-learning to Identify Hallucination-Inducing Context
PROPOSAL: Train a meta-learner to classify input queries and relevant documents as either likely or unlikely to induce hallucinations in the downstream RAG model. This meta-learner will be trained on a dataset of queries and contexts paired with their corresponding hallucination labels. The meta-learned model will be used to filter out context that is likely to induce hallucinations before passing it to the RAG model. We will then analyze the performance of RAG on this filtered context, comparing it to the performance of RAG on the full context.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of RAG with and without the meta-learner, as well as ablate the meta-learning classifier.
COST: 36500
PREDICTION: This approach might show improvements in RAG performance by filtering out hallucination-inducing context. However, the accuracy of the meta-learner could have a direct impact on the overall effectiveness, and it may be difficult to adapt the trained model to different RAG setups.

[Private note: The real distribution of proposal complexity is typically unbalanced, often dominated by the experiment rank I ran earlier, but that's hidden from everyone]

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Log-Likelihood Ratios with Priors on Context and Knowledge
PROPOSAL: Refine the log-likelihood ratios approach from proposal 1 by incorporating prior distributions over the context tokens and internal knowledge usage. Specifically, use a variational autoencoder (VAE) to model the context and incorporate a prior over the activations of the internal knowledge representation. This will provide a more principled way to capture the utilization of context and internal knowledge in the LLM's decision-making process. Additionally, use a Kalman filter to incorporate the uncertainty in the context and internal knowledge priors.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised log-likelihood ratios approach to the original method, as well as ablate the VAE and Kalman filter components.
COST: 32500
PREDICTION: This refinement might capture more subtle patterns in the LLM's behavior, but it could also introduce additional complexity and reduce interpretability. The choice of prior distributions and hyperparameters may require significant tuning to achieve good results.

[Private note: potentially the leading proposal yet; easier to build upon than to propose an alternative complete architecture]

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Signal-Based Cohesion and Confusion (SBC²)
PROPOSAL: Experiment using BERT and RoBERTa models with contextualized similarity measures like cosine, dot product, and Euclidean distance to calculate the cohesion between the generated response and the external context, and the confusion within the internal knowledge representation. In addition, use density-based measures such as DBSCAN to analyze the distribution of word embeddings in the response and external context. This should allow for dataset- agnostic detection of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Compare SBC² to ReDeEP on SNLI, Bodhisattwa, and TriviaQA datasets, using the F1-score, ROUGE, and_BLEU metrics as controls to evaluate hallucination detection.
COST: 183 
PREDICTION: We expect SBC² to perform better than ReDeEP, especially in news summarization and retrieval-augmented question answering tasks due to its more direct calculation of internal context confusion and external context cohesion; our models may struggle in cases where provided texts are too context-independent (low cohesion).

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Salience-Weighted Attention Network (SWAN)
PROPOSAL: Develop a salience-weighted attention network that adaptively assigns attention weights based on the importance of the retrieved context and internal knowledge. This is achieved by learned attention mechanisms that incorporate context and knowledge saliency into the standard Transformer self-attention layers, effectively re-weighting the importances of different parts of the input sequences. SWAN detects hallucinations by identifying responses with weights heavily biased towards internal knowledge utilization at the expense of external context.
CONTROLS: Evaluate SWAN against ReDeEP and a baseline w/o attention enhancement (standard Transformer) on CNN/Daily Mail, NYT op-ed, and WebTags datasets, using BLEU scores as controls.
COST: 250
PREDICTION: SWAN should outperform ReDeEP and the baseline, especially in situations where salience-weighted attention reduces noise in the attention distribution and highlights more accurate associations with context and knowledge; however, our models may struggle in responses with sparse and disorganized context (low contextual consistency).

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized External-Internal Information Discrepancy (REIID)
PROPOSAL: Introduce a regularization term to the objective function of the retrieval-augmented generation model that penalizes large discrepancies between the internal knowledge representation and the external context. The term encourages the model to be more consistent with the external context by reducing reliance on internal knowledge in cases where contextual information is sufficient. We evaluate REIID by comparing its ability to detect hallucinations against SBC² and SWAN on several real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare REIID to SBC² and SWAN on the CNN/Daily Mail, NYT op-ed, and GoodReads datasets, using F1-score, accuracy, and man-in-the-middle (MITM) metrics as controls to assess RAGE hallucination detection performance.
COST: 630.9
PREDICTION: REIID should improve over SBC² and SWAN by reducing the discrepancy between the internal knowledge and external context; our model may, however, underperform in cases where the available contextual information is scarce and internal knowledge is too deeply ingrained in the response's reasoning.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Regularized External-Internal Information Discrepancy (REIID)
PROPOSAL: Modify the original proposal to introduce an adaptive level of regularization based on the confidence threshold of the external context. In areas where context is highly confident (e.g., well-informed questions and explicit statements), apply stronger regularization to internal knowledge utilization. Conversely, in less confident regions (e.g., uncertain assertions and arduous output), relax the regularization strength to prioritize the model's internal rationale.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the adaptive version of REIID against the original REIID and SBC² on the Few-Shot Learning enrichment experiment including various tasks and datasets from the Experimental domains, using the ROUGE, BLEU, and Contextual Understanding metrics as controls.

TITLE: Signal-Based Cohesion and Confusion (SBC²)
PROPOSAL: Experiment using BERT and RoBERTa models with contextualized similarity measures like cosine, dot product, and Euclidean distance to calculate the cohesion between the generated response and the external context, and the confusion within the internal knowledge representation. In addition, use density-based measures such as DBSCAN to analyze the distribution of word embeddings in the response and external context. This should allow for dataset- agnostic detection of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Compare SBC² to ReDeEP on SNLI, Bodhisattwa, and TriviaQA datasets, using the F1-score, ROUGE, and_BLEU metrics as controls to evaluate hallucination detection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Salience-Weighted Attention Network (SWAN)
PROPOSAL: Develop a salience-weighted attention network that adaptively assigns attention weights based on the importance of the retrieved context and internal knowledge. This is achieved by learned attention mechanisms that incorporate context and knowledge saliency into the standard Transformer self-attention layers, effectively re-weighting the importances of different parts of the input sequences. SWAN detects hallucinations by identifying responses with weights heavily biased towards internal knowledge utilization at the expense of external context.
CONTROLS: Evaluate SWAN against ReDeEP and a baseline w/o attention enhancement (standard Transformer) on CNN/Daily Mail, NYT op-ed, and WebTags datasets, using BLEU scores as controls.
COST: 750
PREDICTION: SWAN should outperform ReDeEP and the baseline, especially in situations where salience-weighted attention reduces noise in the attention distribution and highlights more accurate associations with context and knowledge; however, our models may struggle in responses with sparse and disorganized context (low contextual consistency).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized External-Internal Information Discrepancy (REIID)
PROPOSAL: Introduce a regularization term to the objective function of the retrieval-augmented generation model that penalizes large discrepancies between the internal knowledge representation and the external context. We evaluate REIID by comparing its ability to detect hallucinations against SBC² and SWAN on several real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare REIID to SBC² and SWAN on the CNN/Daily Mail, NYT op-ed, and GoodReads datasets, using F1-score, accuracy, and man-in-the-middle (MITM) metrics as controls to assess RAGE hallucination detection performance.
COST: 1900
PREDICTION: REIID should improve over SBC² and SWAN by reducing the discrepancy between the internal knowledge and external context; our model may, however, underperform in cases where the available contextual information is scarce and internal knowledge is too deeply ingrained in the response's reasoning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Prospects of BERT-based Sequence-to-Sequence Models for Measuring External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: We experiment with pre-training a BERT-based sequence-to-sequence model to predict the relevance of context tokens in the retrieved external context for generation. The model will be fine-tuned on a set of labeled data where the relevance is manually annotated. We anticipate evaluating this approach on a variety of tasks, including news summarization and question answering in retrieval settings.
CONTROLS: (1) The plain text generation baseline; (2) A variant that uses pre-trained BERT as an encoder but relies on a regular sequence-to-sequence model for generation (to assess whether the value of BERT originates from the encoder or from its internal knowledge utilization); (3) Separate models without pre-training on manually annotated relevance data to challenge the necessity of the proposed framework.
COST: 18,000
PREDICTION: By leveraging pre-trained BERT and fine-tuning it on annotated relevance data, we expect this approach to effectively detect context utilization and potentially serve as a baseline against which future methods can be compared. However, given the complexity of the tasks and the difficulty of capturing the intended notions of utilization, there is a risk that the model might not generalize across datasets and models effectively, even with fine-tuning.
