ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Salinenet: Augmenting BERT with Attention-Supplied Contrastive Learning for Enhanced Context Utilization Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose to integrate a novel contrastive learning approach with BERT, designing a model that expands upon existing techniques by focusing on the relevance of context tokens in a retrieval-augmented generation process. The contrastive learning component will be optimized using a margin-based loss to push similar context tokens closer together and dissimilar ones further apart, aiding in the detection of genuine versus hallucinated generation. Such an augmented architecture, coined Salinenet, seeks to enhance context utilization detection.
CONTROLS: BERT-based sequence-to-sequence model with a weighted attention mechanism; Regular sequence-to-sequence model as a baseline; Contrastive learning component trained without the weighted attention mechanism to investigate its contribution.
COST: 27,000
PREDICTION: By leveraging the strengths of contrastive learning and carefully coupled attention mechanisms to pinpoint reliable and inaccurate context information, we expect Salinenet to yield a superior performance on various retrieval-augmented generation tasks and notably improve hallucination detection. However, potential complexity introduced by the novel contrastive learning method could lead to increased demands for computational resources and shorter experimentation.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Context Utilization Detectors using Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: We propose evaluating the robustness of the previously developed context utilization detectors against various types of adversarial attacks. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theory-based Evaluation of Context Utilization Detectors
PROPOSAL: We propose developing a theoretical framework to evaluate the performance of context utilization detectors. This framework will be based on a measure of internal knowledge utilization and external context utilization, allowing for a principled comparison of different approaches. We will derive a set of formal bounds and approximations that can be used to analyze the detectors' performance under different assumptions and constraints.
CONTROLS: None (theory-based evaluation)
COST: 37,800
PREDICTION: By providing a rigorous theoretical foundation for context utilization detection, we expect to identify important limitations and requirements for the designs of effective context utilization detectors. However, the theoretical analysis may not directly inform the design of practical detectors, and there may be a disconnect between theoretical optimality and real-world performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Combining Symbolic Reasoning with Deep Learning for Robust Context Utilization Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose combining the symbolic reasoning module from earlier with the Salinenet model to create a robust and principled framework for context utilization detection. The symbolic reasoning module will provide a deeper understanding of the context and generated response, while the Salinenet model will provide a more accurate and robust detection of context utilization. We expect this combination to lead to a significant improvement in the accuracy and robustness of context utilization detection.
CONTROLS: All previously proposed models and evaluations
COST: 48,200
PREDICTION: By combining the strengths of symbolic reasoning and deep learning, we expect to achieve a robust and principled framework for context utilization detection that outperforms existing approaches. However, the integration of these two methods may require significant tuning and optimization, and there may be challenges in reconciling the different levels of abstraction and expressiveness of the two methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Prospects of BERT-based Sequence-to-Sequence Models for Measuring External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: We experiment with pre-training a BERT-based sequence-to-sequence model to predict the relevance of context tokens in the retrieved external context for generation. The model will be fine-tuned on a set of labeled data where the relevance is manually annotated. We anticipate evaluating this approach on a variety of tasks, including news summarization and question answering in retrieval settings.
CONTROLS: (1) The plain text generation baseline; (2) A variant that uses pre-trained BERT as an encoder but relies on a regular sequence-to-sequence model for generation (to assess whether the value of BERT originates from the encoder or from its internal knowledge utilization); (3) Separate models without pre-training on manually annotated relevance data to challenge the necessity of the proposed framework.
COST: 54,000
PREDICTION: By leveraging pre-trained BERT and fine-tuning it on annotated relevance data, we expect this approach to effectively detect context utilization and potentially serve as a baseline against which future methods can be compared. However, given the complexity of the tasks and the difficulty of capturing the intended notions of utilization, there is a risk that the model might not generalize across datasets and models effectively, even with fine-tuning.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Prospects of BERT-based Sequence-to-Sequence Models for Measuring External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: We experiment with pre-training a BERT-based sequence-to-sequence model to predict the relevance of context tokens in the retrieved external context for generation. The model will be fine-tuned on a set of labeled data where the relevance is manually annotated, focusing on tasks in the news summarization and retrieval-augmented question answering domains. To further explore the potential of BERT-based models for measuring external context utilization, we will also investigate the use of a weighted attention mechanism to give more importance to context tokens deemed relevant by the pre-training data.
CONTROLS: (1) The plain text generation baseline; (2) A variant that uses pre-trained BERT as an encoder but relies on a regular sequence-to-sequence model for generation (to assess whether the value of BERT originates from the encoder or from its internal knowledge utilization); (3) Separate models without pre-training on manually annotated relevance data to challenge the necessity of the proposed framework.
COST: 54,000
PREDICTION: By incorporating a weighted attention mechanism into the BERT-based sequence-to-sequence model, we expect to improve the model's ability to detect context utilization and provide a more nuanced assessment of the relationship between the generated response and the external context. However, we also risk overfitting to the annotated data, especially given the limited number of expert-annotated instances, which might lead to decreased performance on unseen data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Salinenet: Augmenting BERT with Attention-Supplied Contrastive Learning for Enhanced Context Utilization Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose to integrate a novel contrastive learning approach with BERT, designing a model that expands upon existing techniques by focusing on the relevance of context tokens in a retrieval-augmented generation process. The contrastive learning component will be optimized using a margin-based loss to push similar context tokens closer together and dissimilar ones further apart, aiding in the detection of genuine versus hallucinated generation. Such an augmented architecture, coined Salinenet, seeks to enhance context utilization detection.
CONTROLS: BERT-based sequence-to-sequence model with a weighted attention mechanism; Regular sequence-to-sequence model as a baseline; Contrastive learning component trained without the weighted attention mechanism to investigate its contribution.
COST: 81,000
PREDICTION: By leveraging the strengths of contrastive learning and carefully coupled attention mechanisms to pinpoint reliable and inaccurate context information, we expect Salinenet to yield a superior performance on various retrieval-augmented generation tasks and notably improve hallucination detection. However, potential complexity introduced by the novel contrastive learning method could lead to increased demands for computational resources and shorter experimentation.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Context Utilization Detectors using Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: We propose refining the evaluation of the robustness of context utilization detectors by incorporating a Directional Adversarial Attack (DAA) that specifically targets the detectors' bias towards internal knowledge utilization. This attack will be designed to manipulate the attention mechanism and the context generator to produce responses that mimic internal knowledge utilization, while minimizing the incorporation of relevant external context information.
CONTROLS: (1) Original adversarial attacks; (2) A variant of the DAA attack that focuses on disrupting the weighted attention mechanism of BERT-based sequence-to-sequence models; (3) The Salinenet model without contrastive learning as a baseline for comparison.
COST: 99,000
PREDICTION: By introducing a DAA attack that specifically targets the bias towards internal knowledge utilization, we expect to identify more robust measures of context utilization and develop more effective defenses against adversarial attacks. However, the complexity of the attack may compromise the reliability of the detectors, particularly when used in real-world settings.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Objective Masking for Joint Encoder-Decoder Training
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-objective masking strategy for joint encoder-decoder training, where the encoder learns to reconstruct both masked and temporal-shifted versions of the input signal, while the decoder predicts future values. This approach encourages the model to capture both local and global temporal dependencies. We will investigate this method on the M4 dataset, which consists of real-world time-series datasets in various domains, including meteorology, electricity, and transportation.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline that employs a simple linear projection decoder and a channel-independent masking strategy, as well as an ablation where only one of the objectives is used for training.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that this approach will improve forecasting accuracy by 5-10% compared to the baseline, with potential caveats in extreme weather domains.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Channel-Dependent Transformers with Adaptive Attention
PROPOSAL: We design a channel-dependent Transformer variant that adaptively allocates attention between channels based on their interdependencies. This is achieved by dynamically learning parameterized attention weights for each channel, which are then combined using an attention switching mechanism. This architecture can effectively capture both local and global cross-channel interactions without incurring high computational costs. We will investigate this method on a range of datasets from the M4 repository, including the weather, electricity, and traffic flow forecasting datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to the Transformer model with a fixed channel-independent attention mechanism and a baseline channel-dependent encoder that uses a simple (frequency-domain) channel dependency model.
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: We expect that our adaptive attention mechanism will provide a 5-10% boost in forecasting accuracy compared to the channel-independent baseline, with smaller but still significant gains compared to the fixed channel-dependent encoder.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Nonlinear Decomposition for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical approach that decomposes the time-series data into multiple layers, each representing different frequency components and channel dependencies. By applying a nonlinear transformation to each layer, the model can capture local and global patterns in the data. We will investigate this approach using the stationary wavelet transform to decompose the time-series data into multiple layers.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline channel-independent encoder and a channel-dependent encoder with a simple (frequency-domain) channel dependency model, as well as an ablation where only one of the layers is used for decomposition.
COST: 13300
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the hierarchical approach will improve forecasting accuracy by 8-12% compared to the channel-independent baseline and 3-6% compared to the simple channel-dependent encoder, but may struggle with extreme weather events due to its reliance on frequency decomposition.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Neural-Augmented Gaussian Processes for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of neural networks and Gaussian processes to capture both local and global patterns in time-series data. By leveraging the expressive power of neural networks and the Bayesian inference capabilities of Gaussian processes, our model can accurately model complex dependencies between variables.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline Gaussian process model and a neural network model, as well as an ablation where our model is used without neural networks.
COST: 10700
PREDICTION: We expect that our approach will improve forecasting accuracy by 12-18% compared to the baseline Gaussian process model and 8-12% compared to the neural network model, while also providing uncertainty estimates that are more accurate than both baselines.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Data-Augmented Training for Few-Shot Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a data-augmentation technique specifically designed for time-series forecasting, which involves generating synthesized data by warping the original datasets using a learned temporal transformation. This allows our model to learn robust feature representations that generalize well to unseen data. We will evaluate this approach using a dataset with limited observed data and scarce examples.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline that trains the model on the original dataset only and an ablation where the model is trained using random data augmentation.
COST: 12300
PREDICTION: We anticipate that data-augmented training will improve forecasting accuracy by 15-20% compared to the baseline and 10-15% compared to the random data augmentation ablation, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for optimal results.

TITLE: Joint Channel and Temporal Clustering for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a clustering-based approach to simultaneously group channels and segments of the time-series data across different channels. This allows our model to learn channel- and segment-specific representations that capture complex dependencies between variables. We will evaluate this approach using datasets from the M4 repository, including the weather and electricity consumption forecasting datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline that clusters channels and segments separately and an ablation where our model is used without joint clustering.
COST: 16320
PREDICTION: We expect that joint channel and temporal clustering will improve forecasting accuracy by 10-15% compared to the baseline and 5-10% compared to the ablation, while also reducing computational costs.

TITLE: Automated Hyperparameter Tuning for Time-Series Forecasting Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a Bayesian optimization-based approach to automate the hyperparameter tuning process for time-series forecasting models. This allows our model to efficiently search for optimal hyperparameters across a wide range of possibilities. TITLE: Multi-Objective Masking for Joint Encoder-Decoder Training
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-objective masking strategy for joint encoder-decoder training, where the encoder learns to reconstruct both masked and temporal-shifted versions of the input signal, while the decoder predicts future values. This approach encourages the model to capture both local and global temporal dependencies. We will investigate this method on the M4 dataset, which consists of real-world time-series datasets in various domains, including meteorology, electricity, and transportation.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline that employs a simple linear projection decoder and a channel-independent masking strategy, as well as an ablation where only one of the objectives is used for training.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that this approach will improve forecasting accuracy by 5-10% compared to the baseline, with potential caveats in extreme weather domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Channel-Dependent Transformers with Adaptive Attention
PROPOSAL: We design a channel-dependent Transformer variant that adaptively allocates attention between channels based on their interdependencies. This is achieved by dynamically learning parameterized attention weights for each channel, which are then combined using an attention switching mechanism. This architecture can effectively capture both local and global cross-channel interactions without incurring high computational costs. We will investigate this method on a range of datasets from the M4 repository, including the weather, electricity, and traffic flow forecasting datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to the Transformer model with a fixed channel-independent attention mechanism and a baseline channel-dependent encoder that uses a simple (frequency-domain) channel dependency model.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: We expect that our adaptive attention mechanism will provide a 5-10% boost in forecasting accuracy compared to the channel-independent baseline, with smaller but still significant gains compared to the fixed channel-dependent encoder.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Nonlinear Decomposition for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical approach that decomposes the time-series data into multiple layers, each representing different frequency components and channel dependencies. By applying a nonlinear transformation to each layer, the model can capture local and global patterns in the data. We will investigate this approach using the stationary wavelet transform to decompose the time-series data into multiple layers.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline channel-independent encoder and a channel-dependent encoder with a simple (frequency-domain) channel dependency model, as well as an ablation where only one of the layers is used for decomposition.
COST: 40000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the hierarchical approach will improve forecasting accuracy by 8-12% compared to the channel-independent baseline and 3-6% compared to the simple channel-dependent encoder, but may struggle with extreme weather events due to its reliance on frequency decomposition.

PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of neural networks and Gaussian processes to capture both local and global patterns in time-series data. By leveraging the expressive power of neural networks and the Bayesian inference capabilities of Gaussian processes, our model can accurately model complex dependencies between variables.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline Gaussian process model and a neural network model, as well as an ablation where our model is used without neural networks.
COST: 32000
PREDICTION: We expect that our approach will improve forecasting accuracy by 12-18% compared to the baseline Gaussian process model and 8-12% compared to the neural network model, while also providing uncertainty estimates that are more accurate than both baselines.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Encoding and Decoding with Dual Attention Mechanism
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel multivariate time-series forecasting model that jointly considers encoding and decoding using a dual attention mechanism. The model has two main components: an encoder that utilizes self-attention with feedback connections to capture both temporal and channel dependencies; and a decoder that applies a dual attention mechanism to weigh the importance of different channels and time steps when generating predictions. We implement this model using a transformer-based architecture, with a combination of channel-wise residual blocks and transformer encoder-decoder modules.
CONTROLS: This proposal will be compared against channel-independent transformers with simple linear projection decoding, as well as state-of-the-art multivariate forecasting models such as AutoTEM and GRU-D.
COST: 14,400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this model to show improved forecasting accuracy compared to channel-independent baselines, especially when capturing complex channel-channel interactions, and potentially outperform existing channel-dependent models due to its efficient attention mechanism. However, it may struggle with high-dimensional input variables and large time-series lengths.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Stage Training for Efficient Channel-Dependent Modeling
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-stage training framework to efficiently model cross-channel dependencies in multivariate time-series forecasting. The framework consists of two stages: a pretraining stage where the model learns to reconstruct partial masks in the input data using a channel-dependent encoder, followed by a metastage where the model learns to predict the future time-series values using the preactivated encoders. This setup allows the model to learn both local and global temporal dependencies without the high computational cost.
CONTROLS: To evaluate the effectiveness of this framework, we compare it against the standard channel-dependent approach using a triplet learning strategy and against the channel-independent baseline using cross-validation and experiments on an ablated version of the channel-dependent model.
COST: 50,400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this framework to show significant improvement in forecasting accuracy over existing channel-dependent models, especially in scenarios with moderate to high dimensionality, and reduce the gap between channel-dependent and channel-independent models. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance and may underperform in regimes with strong channel-channel dependencies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Domain Adaptation for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We explore the effectiveness of domain adaptation techniques for multivariate time-series forecasting in the presence of limited labeled target data. We propose to leverage synthetic or simulated data generated using physically informed probabilistic models (PIPMs) as additional training data in source domain adaptation settings, focusing on regimes where limited target data drives underperformance of current methods. Experiments will be executed across the specified real-world domains.
CONTROLS: The baseline will include the Iterative Multiple Local Update (IMLU) plus simple affine transformations for pretraining; Use a Transformer trained on a robustly sourced variant of it with minimum viable masks.
COST: 25,760 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect domain adaptation using simulated data from PIPMs to significantly improve performance, especially in scenarios where real-world data is scarce or very large, and to fill in gaps in the existing prevailing literature on domain adaptation for time-series forecasting, which focuses on capturing more temporal dependencies, via unfolding additional improvements for simpler noise reduction using classical an-CNNs.

TITLE: Data Augmentation for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel data augmentation strategy specifically designed for multivariate time-series forecasting, which leverages both temporal and channel dependencies to generate augmented data. The approach involves modifying the original time-series data by applying random temporal masking, channel-wise noise injection, and time-channel perturbations, followed by a reinforcement learning-based method to evaluate the quality of the augmented data.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed data augmentation approach against state-of-the-art techniques, such as GRU and Variational Autoencoder, as well as a baseline that uses randomly generated noise.

PREDICTION: We expect our proposed data augmentation strategy to significantly improve the robustness and generalization of multivariate time-series forecasting models, especially when combined with other techniques, such as transfer learning and multi-task learning.

TITLE: Weighted Linear Decoding for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a weighted linear decoding method that improves upon the simple linear projection found in most prior works. Our method, named Weighted Linear Decoder (WLD), learns to assign different weights to each input feature, allowing it to capture complex temporal structures and better predict future values. WLD is designed to be flexible and easily integrated with various encoder architectures, making it a strong baseline for our C2AE model in experiment 1. We train WLD on four real-world datasets (weather, electricity, traffic, and solar) with MAPE as the evaluation metric.
CONTROLS: We evaluate WLD in combination with TimeNet, TFN, VAR, and C2AE (from experiment 1) as the encoder, comparing their performance using the same experimental setting.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: We anticipate WLD to achieve better forecasting accuracy than the simple linear decoder, especially when used in conjunction with C2AE, which effectively captures cross-channel dependencies. WLD might not perform significantly better when used with channel-independent encoders like TimeNet, however.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Improving Prediction Accuracy with Cross-Channel Attentive Encoders
PROPOSAL: We revise our original C2AE model (experiment 1) to include an interactive training scheme, where the encoder and decoder (WLD) are trained simultaneously. By alternating between data encoding and prediction tasks, C2AE learns the complex patterns in the data more effectively. The decoder's output helps guide the encoder to attend to the most relevant features, resulting in improved forecasting performance. Additionally, we add a novel objective function to the loss, focusing on the absolute differences between predicted and actual channel values to better capture temporal patterns.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised C2AE with the original model, as well as the channel-independent TimeNet and the weighted linear decoder WLD, using the same evaluation metric (MAPE) on five real-world datasets.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: With our revised training scheme, we expect C2AE to consistently surpass the performance of the original model and compare favorably to WLD across different datasets and forecasting tasks. However, the high dimensionality of the weather dataset might lead to reduced model performance in this domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Pretraining Strategies for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting Models
PROPOSAL: We compare the effectiveness of two pretraining strategies, BERT's masked-reconstruction task and a novel masked-AE task, in improving the generalizability of our C2AE model on five real-world forecasting datasets. The masked-AE task involves masking parts of the input sequences and asking the encoder to reconstruct the original sequence. We evaluate the impact of these pretraining tasks on both in-domain and out-of-domain forecasting performance, exploring whether they can improve model robustness and flexibility.
CONTROLS: We compare the proposed pretraining strategies with a baseline that uses random initializations for the C2AE encoder, training it from scratch on the target forecasting task.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: We predict that the proposed masked-AE pretraining task will consistently outperform the masked-reconstruction task, improving C2AE's performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain forecasting tasks. The model performance might degrade when working with high-dimensional input sequences, due to increased computational complexity and reduced control over the masked input.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Encoder-Decoder Asynchronous Training on Model Performance
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effect of asynchronous training between the encoder and decoder of the C2AE model, a technique that has shown promise in other sequence-to-sequence tasks. In particular, we examine how asynchronous training affects convergence rates and forecasting accuracy on four real-world datasets from various forecasting domains (weather, electricity, traffic, and solar). We also investigate the level of adaptability of our model when fine-tuning the encoder or decoder while keeping the other component fixed.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of C2AE models trained with synchronous and asynchronous encoders and decoders, using both the masked-AE pretraining task and a baseline that trains the C2AE encoder and decoder together from scratch.
COST: 16560
PREDICTION: We anticipate that asynchronous training will generally improve the convergence speed and forecasting accuracy of C2AE on the examined datasets, especially when combined with the masked-AE pretraining task. However, if the asynchronous training scheme is not properly adjusted, it may introduce instabilities during the training process and have a detrimental effect on the final model performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Multistage Tuning Approach for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel multistage tuning approach for optimizing the hyperparameters of our C2AE model and other BERT-inspired architectures for multivariate time-series forecasting. Our approach combines a series of local and global searches to tune the model's hyperparameters, factoring in the relationships among different variables in the dataset and exploring diverse combinations of hyperparameters that may not be feasible with traditional methods.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our multistage tuning approach to several baselines, including grid search, random search, and double-search for all possible models (TFN, TimeNet, VAR, and C2AE).
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: We expect the multistage tuning approach to identify optimal combinations of hyperparameters that significantly improve the forecasting performance of our C2AE model and other BERT-inspired architectures, particularly in complex forecasting domains such as traffic flow forecasting. However, the computational cost of the method might be prohibitively high for very large datasets or extensive hyperparameter search spaces.

TITLE: Real-World Transfer Learning for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We explore the potential of real-world transfer learning for multivariate time-series forecasting models, adapting the weights of our C2AE encoder and decoder from one domain (e.g., traffic flow forecasting) to another (e.g., electricity consumption forecasting). Our experiments focus on analyzing the transfer learning ability of the proposed C2AE models, as well as those of TFN and VAR, when learning to predict time-series data across multiple forecasting domains.
CONTROLS: We select four real-world datasets from various domains (traffic flow, electricity consumption, weather and solar) and evaluate transfer learning with different domain similarity metrics (e.g., distance metrics and correlation coefficients).
COST: 33250
PREDICTION: We anticipate that transfer learning using the proposed C2AE architecture will provide good performance and substantial improvements over non-transfer learning models, especially when dealing with similar domains or similar data characteristics. However, significant numerical errors may occur during transfer learning due to changes in domain distributions, and more systematic methods to mitigate such issues must be further explored.

PROPOSAL: We delve into the C2AE model's model convergence and hyperparameter sensitivity, analyzing both the effects of factors such as learning rate, batch size, and initial weight distribution on model performance. CONTROLS: We perform a thorough evaluation of our proposed C2AE architecture regarding its robustness to changes in hyperparameters, analyzing the separate effects that harmonic regression loss, learning rate, batch size, and initialization method impose on model convergence speed and forecasting accuracy.

PREDICTION: By examining the reasons behind the interactions between our encoder's weights and different data characteristics, we expect to identify optimal strategies to address convergence speed and sensitivity to hyperparameters, enabling more statistically reliable training and giving users finest tuning parameters especially in multivariate datasets with time series built in.

PROPOSAL: We propose a novel channel-dependent encoder architecture, called Cross-Channel Attentive Encoder (C2AE), which can selectively focus on cross-channel interactions without incurring a high computational cost. We evaluate C2AE on five real-world datasets from various forecasting domains, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow forecasting. Our baseline comparison includes three popular models: TimeNet, Temporal Fusion Network (TFN), and Vector Autoregression (VAR).

Additionally, we ablate C2AE to demonstrate the effect of different cross-attention mechanisms. Experiments are conducted on NVIDIA V100 GPUs, and the total compute cost is approximately 15000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect C2AE to outperform existing channel-independent encoders (TimeNet and VAR) and show comparable results to TFN, which is known for capturing cross-variable interactions. However, C2AE might struggle with very high dimensional inputs (e.g., over 10 variables) due to the limitations of the cross-attention mechanism.

TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Multiscale Encoding with Cross-Attention for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose to design a multivariate time-series forecasting model that incorporates a multiscale encoder, followed by a cross-attention mechanism, to effectively capture temporal and cross-channel dependencies. The encoder will utilize a variant of the Transformer architecture with multiple scale attention blocks, enabling it to process inputs at different scales and resolutions. The cross-attention mechanism will then enable the model to selectively attend to relevant channels across different scales, facilitating the extraction of meaningful channel dependencies.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed model with a baseline that employs a standard Transformer encoder with a linear decoder. Additionally, we will conduct ablation studies to evaluate the importance of the multiscale encoder and the cross-attention mechanism separately.

PREDICTION: We anticipate that our proposed model will significantly outperform the baseline and exhibit competitive results with state-of-the-art methods. TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Architectural Designs on Pretraining and Fine-Tuning Strategies for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate how the architectural design of the time-series forecasting model affects the choice of pretraining and fine-tuning strategies. Specifically, we will evaluate the performance of models with different encoder-decoder architectures (e.g., channel-independent vs. channel-dependent) when pretraining with masking-and-reconstruction tasks and fine-tuning with supervised learning. We will also examine the impact of different pretraining objectives (e.g., masked segments vs. future time steps) and fine-tuning objectives (e.g., mean squared error vs. cross-entropy loss).

PREDICTION: We expect that architectural design will have a significant impact on the choice of pretraining and fine-tuning strategies, with some designs performing better with masking-and-reconstruction pretraining and others benefiting from supervised fine-tuning. However, we also anticipate that achieving consistent improvements will be challenging, requiring careful tuning of hyperparameters and architectural design.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Channel Attention Mechanism for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We'll propose a novel channel attention mechanism that adaptively learns to weigh the importance of individual channels (variables) for the current forecast. This will be achieved by using an auxiliary neural network that takes the encoded representation of the input sequence and the forecast horizon as input. We'll implement and experiment with this mechanism in the context of a Transformer-based multivariate time-series forecasting model. To test its effectiveness, we'll evaluate the proposed model on the mentioned real-world datasets (weather, electricity consumption, traffic flow, and solar power generation forecasting).
CONTROLS: Ablation tests to compare with: 1) the standard Transformer model without the adaptive channel attention mechanism, and 2) a model that uses a simple channel-wise attention mechanism that learned a fixed importance weighting for all outputs.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: By incorporating the proposed mechanism, the forecasting model's performance is expected to significantly improve, especially in scenarios where not all channels have equal significance or reliability, such as with the presence of missing or noisy data values. However, the model might struggle to generalize across diverse datasets if the mechanism is overly focused on a few critical variables.

PROPOSAL: Building on recent advances in pre-training for time-series forecasting, we'll develop a novel channel-dependent decoding framework that complements masking-and-reconstruction pre-training. Our approach involves pre-training an encoder-decoder model using partial masking and predicting only the masked fraction for each channel, thereby promoting channel-dependent understanding and leveraging cross-channel dependencies for better forecasting. To integrate this with our adaptive channel attention mechanism (proposed in proposal 2), we'll experiment with combining the two and investigate whether the synergy between them can improve forecasting performance.

PREDICTION: By integrating channel-dependent decoding with masking-and-reconstruction pre-training, we can capture both long-range dependencies and fine-grained relationships between channels, potentially leading to state-of-the-art results. However, tuning the model parameters to balance these competing objectives may be challenging.

TITLE: Scalable Training of Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting Models using Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We'll propose a meta-learning approach to train multivariate time-series forecasting models on various forecasting tasks with different input window sizes and forecasting horizons. This will involve designing a base learner that can be adapted to multiple tasks via a set of parameters learned once and leveraged across multiple forecasting tasks. We'll utilize this approach to scale the training process and improve the generalizability of our forecasting models on a diverse set of real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be conducted to compare our meta-learning approach against a standard cross-validation approach for learning forecasting models on each task individually, as well as an ablation study to evaluate the importance of the meta-learning approach.

However, there may be a risk of overfitting to the meta-learning task and a need to carefully tune the meta-learner to balance learning and adaptation.

We'll evaluate the effectiveness of this combined approach on real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be compared against a baseline that includes only channel-dependent decoding with masking-and-reconstruction tasks, the adaptive channel attention mechanism without masking-and-reconstruction, and the non-conformal temporal information without channel-dependent decoding.
COST: 54000
PREDICTION: By incorporating both adaptive channel attention and non-conformal temporal information, our model should exhibit improved forecasting performance by leveraging channel-wise relationships and localized changes in temporal patterns. However, the model may require careful tuning to achieve benefits without increasing computational cost or overfitting the training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable Training of Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting Models using Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We'll propose a meta-learning approach to train multivariate time-series forecasting models on various forecasting tasks with different input window sizes and forecasting horizons. This will involve designing a base learner that can be adapted to multiple tasks via a set of parameters learned once and leveraged across multiple forecasting tasks. We'll utilize this approach to scale the training process and improve the generalizability of our forecasting models on a diverse set of real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be conducted to compare our meta-learning approach against a standard cross-validation approach for learning forecasting models on each task individually, as well as an ablation study to evaluate the importance of the meta-learning approach.
COST: 60000
PREDICTION: By using meta-learning, we should be able to train our forecasting models more efficiently and improve their generalizability across different forecasting tasks. However, there may be a risk of overfitting to the meta-learning task and a need to carefully tune the meta-learner to balance learning and adaptation.

PROPOSAL: In this revised investigation, we'll explore an alternative to the original masking strategy used in proposal 3. Instead of using fixed-size masking to cover a portion of the input sequence, we'll introduce a novel dynamic masking scheme that adaptively adjusts the masked regions based on the input sequence's temporal patterns and user-defined budget. This flexible masking strategy will allow our model to more effectively learn from the partially observed data, potentially leading to improved performance and reduced overfitting.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be conducted to evaluate the proposed dynamic masking scheme against both the original channel-dependent decoding with masking-and-reconstruction tasks and an ablation study with varying masking ratios and types.
COST: 66000
PREDICTION: By incorporating the dynamic masking strategy, our model should better adapt to the input data's complexity and capture subtle patterns, potentially leading to improved forecasting performance. However, the increased flexibility of the masking scheme may also introduce additional computational overhead and require more careful tuning of the hyperparameters.

TITLE: Ensemble Forecasting Using Diverse Temporal Abstractions
PROPOSAL: We'll explore a novel ensemble forecasting approach that combines diverse temporal abstractions, including local trend extrapolation, intra-seasonal periodic decomposition, and long-term pattern matching. Each component will be learned using a separate model architecture, and the ensemble forecast will be generated by combining the predictions from each component. We'll investigate various methods for combining the predictions, including weighted averaging and stacking with neural networks.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be conducted to evaluate the performance of our ensemble forecasting approach against a range of baselines, including individual models for each temporal abstraction, as well as ablation studies to evaluate the importance of each component and combination method.

However, the model may require careful tuning of hyperparameters, and the combination method may not always lead to the best results for every individual component.

TITLE: Evaluating View Diversity for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will run experiments to investigate the effect of view diversity on contrastive learning performance, by manipulating the number and types of augmentations used for each instance in SimCLR and comparing to a state-of-the-art non-contrastive method (BYOL) as a baseline.

TITLE: Instrumental Mutual Information for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We derive and analyze an instrumental version of mutual information for modeling the concept of individual instance view utility, serving as a measure of the information gained from a view relative to the data distribution. We will study this measure theoretically, proving upper bounds under specific assumptions about the data and model, and experimentally comparing its predictive performance against max and min mutual information as surrogates for view utility on representative synthetic data and subsets of ImageNet, evaluating various evaluation metrics such as mean normalized mutual information, specific occupation ratio and divergence rate. 
CONTROLS: We consider specific initial hypothesis about model choice (e.g., comparison over standard autoencoder architecture like VAE and denoising autoencoder) and for control audacity we will try exploring it in settings with small training data (use MNIST).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive View Expansion through Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: To dynamically expand the representational capacity of each instance while maintaining semantic coherence, we will train a reinforcement learning agent within the SimCLR framework to select new augmentations and expansion steps based on the expected representational gain of each choice. The agent will receive rewards for achieving high accuracy on downstream tasks while controlling for the information gained from the current augmentations.
CONTROLS: Baseline SimCLR, comparing to fixed augmentation strategies and different reinforcement learning objectives.
COST: 2800
PREDICTION: This work should enable adaptive expansion of the view diversity, improving semantic consistency while avoiding overfitting, and allowing models to effectively leverage limited compute resources. However, the effectiveness of reinforcement learning here may be highly sensitive to the chosen reward function and neural architecture design.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Viewwise Information Gain for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will conduct experiments on the ImageNet-1K dataset using the ResNet-50 model family, Train and test the models with various contrastive objectives (e.g., InfoNCE, NSCL) and view augmentation strategies (e.g., random crop, color jittering). For each training iteration, we will extract the information gained through each view for each instance using the conditional entropy, and plot the viewwise information gain over time. We will also measure the relative entropy between the current representation and the final representation, to quantify how much of the representation is drawn from the views. This will help us understand how augmentations contribute to the learned representation and when the model has likely converged to its semantic manifold.
CONTROLS: We will use baseline models trained with fixed augmentation strategies (e.g., Random Erasing, Cutmix) and controlled batch sizes, and compare their performance to our adaptive augmentation method.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By analyzing the viewwise information gain over iterations, we expect to identify when and how the model benefits from certain augmentations more than others. This may suggest that somewhat surprising augmentations could be most informative, where our objective might then steer the learning dynamics. We anticipate, however, potential artifacts from imperfect mutual information estimation that could mask key phenomena we aim to observe.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation Algorithm via Conditional Entropy Minimization
PROPOSAL: Building on the results from proposal 1, we will develop an adaptive augmentation algorithm based on conditional entropy minimization. Given the viewwise information gain extracted from proposal 1, the algorithm will selectively apply augmentations that yield the most information gain while ensuring semantic consistency between views. Specifically, for each instance, the algorithm will compute the conditional entropy of the feature representations given the input data, and then choose the augmentation with the highest decrease in conditional entropy (i.e., lowest conditional entropy). This will iteratively adapt the augmentation strategy during training, rather than relying on static, hand-engineered augmentations.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adaptive augmentation algorithm to traditional static augmentation strategies (e.g., random crop, color jittering), as well as to a baseline that uses a fixed, large batch size to enforce invariance.
COST: 1330 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By allowing the augmentation strategy to adapt to the characteristics of the data, we expect our algorithm to achieve better performance on downstream tasks while maintaining or improving the representational diversity of the learned features. However, a potential challenge lies in automatically determining the optimal trade-off between semantic consistency and representational diversity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Bound on Viewwise Information Gain
PROPOSAL: We will derive an information-theoretic bound on viewwise information gain for contrastive learning, considering the trade-off between alignment and uniformity principles. Specifically, we will leverage the α-divergence framework to provide a lower bound on the mutual information between views, which will help us understand the fundamental limits of information gain through contrastive learning. This bound will also provide insights into the optimal design of augmentation strategies.
CONTROLS: We will investigate the reach of our bound by comparing it to empirical estimates of viewwise information gain on ImageNet-1K.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (lower bound derivation does not require compute-intensive experiments, so the cost is primarily due to theoretical reasoning)
PREDICTION: We expect our derived bound to provide a non-trivial estimate of the maximum achievable viewwise information gain, which will serve as a benchmark for our adaptive augmentation algorithm (proposal 2). However, proving tightness of our bound or deriving it for specific augmentation strategies remains an open problem.

PROPOSAL: Building on the results from proposal 1, we will develop an adaptive augmentation algorithm based on conditional entropy minimization. Given the viewwise information gain extracted from proposal 1, the algorithm will selectively apply augmentations that yield the most information gain while ensuring semantic consistency between views. Specifically, for each instance, the algorithm will compute the conditional entropy of the feature representations given the input data, and then choose the augmentation with the highest decrease in conditional entropy (i.e., lowest conditional entropy). This will iteratively adapt the augmentation strategy during training, rather than relying on static, hand-engineered augmentations.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adaptive augmentation algorithm to traditional static augmentation strategies (e.g., random crop, color jittering), as well as to a baseline that uses a fixed, large batch size to enforce invariance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information Gain-Aware Augmentation Design for Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale experiment on six diverse real-world datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, COCO, Oxford-Pets, Stanford-Cars, and DeepFashion) using a contrastive learning framework with adaptive augmentation design informed by the mutual information score between input views and the output representations. Implement this using CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) as the base model, and substitute its default image encoder with the phonetic transformer block used in vision transformers to effectively learn augmented views with hierarchical emphasis. Additionally, modify the self-learned representation space to be more expressive for prescluding the partition of semantically similar images into different clusters in an early stage of training, in a way that the adequate information is coarsely contained and juxtaposed across both samples while exercising mutual exclusivity between the views slightly augmenting the information landscape quickly.
CONTROLS: Compare against six state-of-art contrastive methods (SimCLR-v2, MoCo-v3, SwAV, BYOL, SimSiam and Barlow Twins) using their baseline schedules and configurations for augmentations, as well as an ablation study on our adaptive augmentation strategy (i.e., from randomly swapping two augmentation operations, to two equally strong augmentation operations swapped every 5 epochs).
COST: 3,325 GPU-h
PREDICTION: The proposed method would acquire substantial improvement over current state of arts in measuring contrastive objectives while pushing overall classification metrics for image recognition tasks quite effectively, more specifically capturing bigger mutual information theoretically. A potential failure might occur due to decreased computational liquidity related to alleviating memory at each repeating iteration for elevated batch sampling intensity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Information Convergence for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Theoretically analyze and mathematically prove that under certain conditions, the representations learned by a contrastive learning model will converge to a common information-theoretic metric, such as mutual information or Kullback-Leibler divergence, across different augmentations and views. This will provide a rigorous foundation for understanding the essential properties of contrastive learning and help to unveil its internal dynamics. To achieve this, we will use tools from information theory, spectral graph theory, and convex optimization to derive a set of sufficient conditions for convergence, and validate our results through a series of experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: The proposed theoretical framework is compared to existing analyses of contrastive learning, and its predictions are validated in comparison to the real-world performance of several state-of-the-art contrastive learning methods (SimCLR, MoCo, and BYOL).
COST: 5,000 GPU-h
PREDICTION: The proposed theoretical framework will provide a valuable insight into the internal workings of contrastive learning, and will help to explain the observed performances of state-of-the-art methods. While the conditions for convergence may be stringent, our analysis will provide a clear understanding of the essential properties of contrastive learning, and will pave the way for the development of more efficient and principled methods.

TITLE: Axiomatic Analysis of Contrastive Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the theoretical properties of contrastive representation learning through axiomatic analysis, focusing on the alignment and uniformity principles that underlie the method. We aim to derive a set of axioms that captures the essential properties of good representations and provides a formal foundation for the contrastive learning framework. This will enable us to rigorously analyze and compare different contrastive learning methods, and to provide a theoretical basis for the design of new approaches.
CONTROLS: Baseline results from existing contrastive learning methods (e.g., SimCLR, MoCo) will be used for comparison.

PREDICTION: Our axiomatic analysis will provide a deeper understanding of the theoretical foundations of contrastive representation learning, and will enable the design of new methods that are both more effective and more interpretable.

We also examine how these metrics change when adaptation is applied to different VLM architectures, such as DALL-E and VILBERT, on a subset of ImageNet.
CONTROLS: We include the three evaluation metrics from our original study (Proposal 1) and compare them against the new metrics. We also explore the impact of different test sets, including ImageNet, Cifar10, and COCO.

PREDICTION: The results will highlight the importance of evaluating adaptation methods across multiple metrics, revealing that while some adaptation methods excel in terms of accuracy, others may provide more robust or interpretable results. However, we anticipate that the performance differences between evaluation metrics might be less pronounced than expected, potentially indicating that adaptation's impact is more nuanced than thought.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Fair Comparison of Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art episodic and online TTA methods on CLIP under consistent experimental settings using the flickr30k and cars196 datasets, measuring accuracy, robustness, and reliability using metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and Brier score. 
CONTROLS: Evaluate each TTA method against the unadapted CLIP model (base model) and compare the performance of the best-performing method in the episodic and online settings. Additionally, ablate training-time fine-tuning of CLIP and compare the performance of TTA methods with and without fine-tuning.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We expect the comparison to reveal that online TTA methods generally outperform episodic methods, but their gains are largely task-specific and dependent on the model architecture. The results may also indicate that combining TTA with training-time fine-tuning is beneficial for improving model performance, especially for robustness. However, the benefits of TTA may come at the cost of increased uncertainty and reduced trustworthiness.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Robustness and Trustworthiness of Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness and trustworthiness of TTA methods by evaluating their performance on images with varying levels of corruption (e.g., noise, blur, and JPEG compression) and on visually similar but different classes (e.g., animals with similar textures). Use the ImageNet-C and ImageNet-V2 datasets and metrics such as the robustness score and trust-calibrated loss to measure the robustness and trustworthiness of TTA models.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness and trustworthiness of the best-performing TTA method from our previous experiment (proposal 1) to the unadapted CLIP model and to a standard robustness-regularized training approach (e.g., adversarial training).
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: We expect TTA methods to show improved robustness compared to the unadapted CLIP model but reduced trustworthiness, suggesting that TTA may not be suitable for safety-critical applications where robustness is crucial. The results may also indicate that robustness-regularized training can improve trustworthiness while degrading robustness.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Generalizability of Test-Time Adaptation Methods across VLM Architectures
PROPOSAL: Extend the evaluation of TTA methods from CLIP to other popular VLM architectures, such as DALL-E and T2T-ViT, and to different modalities, such as text-to-text models. Use the existing evaluation framework and metrics from our previous experiments (proposals 1 and 2) on a range of tasks (e.g., image classification, object detection, and segmentation).
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of TTA methods on each VLM architecture and modality, as well as on the combination of different architectures and modalities. Compare the performance of TTA methods to the unadapted models and to training-time fine-tuned models.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: We expect TTA methods to show improved performance on some VLM architectures and modalities, but reduced performance on others, indicating that TTA is not universally beneficial. The results may also indicate that combining TTA with training-time fine-tuning can lead to improved generalizability across different models and modalities.

PREDICTION: We expect the evaluation to reveal consistent performance improvements for TTA methods on CLIP, while showing more variable results on other VLM architectures. ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Reproducibility-Enhanced Episodic Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Compare and reproduce the existing episodic test-time adaptation methods on CLIP, using a standardized experimental setup with a pre-trained model checkpoint, consistent text prompts, and evaluation protocols. The goal is to establish a fair ground truth for accuracy improvements and to identify the major factors contributing to variations in reported baseline results.
CONTROLS: Unadapted CLIP model with consistent text prompts and evaluation protocols; random baseline of different text prompts; other existing episodic TTA methods with our established experimental setup
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: Our reproduction of existing methods will mostly replicate their reported results, highlighting inconsistent experimental settings in previous works. New techniques to handle variations in prompts and pre-trained model checkpoints will be essential to fair comparisons, and we might find conflicting results that require revisions in previous publications.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluating Test-Time Adaptation via Alternative Metrics
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether episodic and online test-time adaptation methods for VLMs improve not only classification accuracy but also the robustness, reliability, and fairness of VLMs. We will use a combination of metrics such as precision-recall, equalized odds, and predictive entropy to assess the trade-offs between these properties and the adaptation methods.
CONTROLS: Reproducibility-Enhanced Episodic Test-Time Adaptation setup (proposed in proposal 1); original CLIP model and adapted models evaluated on these other metrics; adapted models compared with pre-adapted models when tested on the unseen test dataset
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: Adaptation methods that improve robustness and reliability on average may sacrifice fairness or vice versa. Our results can highlight the need to consider a broader range of metrics when evaluating VLMs and to incorporate fairness into our TTA methods.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Training-Time Fine-Tuning on Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether test-time adaptation methods can complement or conflict with training-time fine-tuning of VLMs, and how these two types of fine-tuning interact. We will design an experiment where we fine-tune a pre-trained VLM model with different amounts of training data and then evaluate the performance of test-time adaptation methods on the fine-tuned models.
CONTROLS: Reproducibility-Enhanced Episodic Test-Time Adaptation setup (proposed in proposal 1); models fine-tuned on various amounts of training data; test-time adaptation methods applied to both fine-tuned and non-fine-tuned models
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: Depending on the amount and distribution of the fine-tuning data, test-time adaptation may either significantly improve the performance of fine-tuned VLMs or even decrease it. Our results can help determine the upper and lower bounds for effectiveness of adaptive methods after pre-trained models have been fine-tuned on data, and therefore provide practical guidance on their appropriate combination in real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Extending Test-Time Adaptation to Other Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Evaluate existing episodic and online test-time adaptation methods on VLMs other than CLIP, to assess their generalizability and identify performance gaps. This will involve adapting existing methods to work with new models and comparing their performance on multiple VLMs, including LLaMA and ViLT.
CONTROLS: Reproducibility-Enhanced Episodic Test-Time Adaptation setup (proposed in proposal 1); existing test-time adaptation methods adapted to work with new VLM models; original CLIP model compared with the adapted VLMs
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: The performance of test-time adaptation methods will vary significantly across different VLM models, highlighting the need to fine-tune adaptation methods to specific VLM architectures. Our results can indicate when a simple adaptation is enough and when deep model-specific hyperparameter tuning might be necessary for achieving better performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1 
TITLE: Enhanced Reproducibility-Enhanced Episodic Test-Time Adaptation with Randomized Model Initialization
PROPOSAL: Enhance the reproducibility-enchanced episodic test-time adaptation setup by introducing randomized model initialization for the adapted model at each run. This will simulate real-world conditions, where fine-tuning the model always includes random weights initialization, and evaluate the effectiveness and robustness of the adaptation methods under such conditions.
CONTROLS: Recording random model weights at each adaptation run; Adaptation metrics comparison between non-randomized and randomized initialization
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: Due to the increased variability in the adapted model weights, some adaptation methods may not perform well under randomized initialization, or may even degrade. This will make some existing results either harder or easier to reproduce and could improve our understanding of how actual adaptation works during real applications.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Embracing Adaptivity with AutoML for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Design a kernel-based meta-learning approach that automatically selects the best test-time adaptation method and hyperparameters from a pool based on its initial performance on a series of mini-batches. This will handle adaptation uncertainty and discover optimal adaptation for a broader range of tasks.
CONTROLS: Enhanced Reproducibility-Enhanced Episodic Test-Time Adaptation setup; different automated adaptation data-driven models queried in combination with kernel dynamics from running batches; unlike the other experiments, here Experiments focused at PL customized guided data sampling
COST: 28000
PREDICTION: By leveraging an automated meta-learning system to personalize test-time adaptation, we will see a noticeable boost in its iterations success rate, expect that the adaptation decision could also include computation on local or spare data points.

PROPOSAL: Examine the transferability of test-time adaptation methods across different domains (image, video, multi-modal) and tasks (classification, segmentation, retrieval). ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Coreset for Long Spatiotemporal Contexts in Discrete Video Generation
PROPOSAL: To alleviate the steep computational cost of long spatiotemporal contexts, we propose representing the historical frames as a low-dimensional coreset, which preserves the essential information for temporal consistency while significantly reducing the sequence length. This can be achieved by subsampling frames based on a learned importance score, which is derived from the video generators' attention weights. We will implement and evaluate this approach using the Summarize- then-Predict (STP) framework in combination with Video-VAE and VQ-VAE architectures on Vimeo-90K, FFHQ, and Netflix video datasets, with metrics of Temporal Consistency Loss (TCL) and Perceptual Path Length (PPL).
CONTROLS: Ablation studies on STP framework, VQ-VAE weights initialization from image tokenizer, and frame subsampling methods.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed coreset method will reduce the computational cost by 30-40% while maintaining 90% of the original temporal consistency, but it may struggle with complex videos that have rapid scene changes and require higher representational capacities.

The mechanism consists of two stages: a short-term attention stage that focuses on adjacent frames, and a long-term attention stage that selectively attends to frames from a coherent temporal segment. We will implement and evaluate this mechanism on Vimeo-90K and Netflix video datasets, with metrics of Temporal Consistency Loss (TCL) and Perceptual Path Length (PPL).
CONTROLS: Ablation study on the two-stage attention mechanism, comparison with a fixed temporal attention mechanism, and evaluation on different video lengths.
COST: 2670 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive temporal attention mechanism will achieve 20-30% reduction in TCL and 15-20% reduction in PPL, but it may struggle with videos that require complex temporal relationships to be captured, leading to temporal inconsistencies.

TITLE: Investigating Coreset for Long Spatiotemporal Contexts in Discrete Video Generation
PROPOSAL: To alleviate the steep computational cost of long spatiotemporal contexts, we propose representing the historical frames as a low-dimensional coreset, which preserves the essential information for temporal consistency while significantly reducing the sequence length. This can be achieved by subsampling frames based on a learned importance score, which is derived from the video generators' attention weights. We will implement and evaluate this approach using the Summarize- then-Predict (STP) framework in combination with Video-VAE and VQ-VAE architectures on Vimeo-90K, FFHQ, and Netflix video datasets, with metrics of Temporal Consistency Loss (TCL) and Perceptual Path Length (PPL).
CONTROLS: Ablation studies on STP framework, VQ-VAE weights initialization from image tokenizer, and frame subsampling methods.
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed coreset method will reduce the computational cost by 30-40% while maintaining 90% of the original temporal consistency, but it may struggle with complex videos that have rapid scene changes and require higher representational capacities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Video Tokenizer for Efficient Discrete Video Generation
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of initializing discrete video tokenizers with high reconstruction quality without prohibitive training cost, we propose a hierarchical architecture for video tokenizers that leverages shared knowledge from static images. Specifically, we will design a two-stage tokenizer: the first stage uses a pre-trained image tokenizer to generate a shared feature space, and the second stage uses a video tokenizer to refine the features based on video-specific information. We will evaluate this approach on Vimeo-90K and Netflix video datasets, with metrics of Frame Reconstruction Error (FRE) and Temporal Consistency Loss (TCL).
CONTROLS: Comparison with three baseline methods: (1) standard discrete video tokenizer, (2) initialzing from discrete image tokenizer, and (3) training from scratch.
COST: 5200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hierarchical tokenizer will achieve 25% reduction in training time while maintaining 95% of the original reconstruction quality, but it may fail to capture nuances in complex videos that require higher-sensitivity tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Granger Causality and Residual Causal Momentum
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the success of autoregressive models in capturing dependencies across different frames in video sequences, we propose to incorporate Granger causality into the residual connections of our discrete autoregressive video model. By enforcing that the information flow in each residual connection is unidirectional (i.e., that the previous frame only affects the current one and not vice versa), we aim to approximate causal relationships between frames. Additionally, we propose to use a causal momentum term to account for changes that have occurred over multiple frames, thereby capturing both immediate and longer-term effects.
CONTROLS: Compare with a non-causal version of the model that uses standard residual connections without Granger causality, and experiment with different orders and combinations of causal residual connections.
COST: 2670
PREDICTION: We expect the incorporation of Granger causality and causal momentum to significantly improve the model's ability to capture causal relationships in the video sequence, resulting in better temporal consistency. However, we anticipate that higher-order causal residual connections may penalize faster convergence and generalizeability, so we will carefully explore and prune these.

We also predict that causal residual connections may diminish some spatial effects (corresponding some form of perfection of practical image enhancement implemented through losses), making it harder to maintain full-fidelity motion.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hindsight Structured Video Prediction with Split Attention
PROPOSAL: Building on the idea of autoregressive models, we propose a novel architecture that utilizes hindsight knowledge to inform the prediction of future frames. By splitting the attention mechanism into two stages – a prediction stage and a hindsight stage – we can leverage both forward and backward information flows to improve visual quality and temporal consistency. In the prediction stage, the model predicts the next frame based on the current context, while in the hindsight stage, the model revises its prediction by considering the previously predicted frames and the actual ground truth. This two-stage attention mechanism enables the model to correct its mistakes and produce more coherent video sequences.
CONTROLS: Compare with a version of the model that uses a single stage attention mechanism and experiment with different subset of frames to include in hindsight stage comparisons.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect the split attention mechanism to significantly improve the model's ability to capture long-term dependencies and coherence, resulting in better visual quality and temporal consistency. However, we anticipate that this may come at the cost of increased computational complexity and training time.

We also predict potential decrease in model's ability to generalize on tasks where the training distribution differs significantly from the testing one, and where large differences appear between model predictions, and reconstructions on frames far enough apart in real-world videos.

TITLE: Long-Range Dependencies through Temporal Modulation
PROPOSAL: Inspired by recent advances in spatial modulation, we propose to inject long-range dependencies into our video generation model through a novel temporal modulation mechanism. By using a specially designed modulation function that operates on the temporal axis, we can effectively capture dependencies between frames that are far apart in the sequence. This can be achieved by introducing a new set of modulation parameters that are learned jointly with the rest of the model. We expect this mechanism to improve the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies and produce more coherent video sequences.
CONTROLS: Compare with a version of the model that uses a fixed modulation function and experiment with different types of modulation functions.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect the temporal modulation mechanism to significantly improve the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies, resulting in better visual quality and temporal consistency. However, we anticipate that this may come at the cost of increased computational complexity and training time.

We also predict potential issues if the long-range dependencies detected by the modulation become too complicated, resulting in model overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Progressive Refinement for Long-Video Generation
PROPOSAL: To tackle the challenges of generating long videos while maintaining coherence and visual quality, we propose a progressive refinement framework. The framework consists of a series of refinement stages, each of which refines the previously generated frames to produce a new set of frames. By iteratively refining the generated video, we can effectively capture the evolving patterns and structures in the video sequence, resulting in improved coherence and visual quality. We expect this framework to significantly improve the model's ability to generate long videos.
CONTROLS: Compare with a version of the model that uses a single refinement stage and experiment with different numbers of refinement stages.
COST: 7344
PREDICTION: We expect the progressive refinement framework to significantly improve the model's ability to generate long videos, with improved coherence and visual quality. However, we anticipate that this may come at the cost of increased computational complexity and training time.

We also predict potential failures if the refinement stages are not carefully designed and aligned, resulting in quality degradation over iterations of refinement

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Context Attention for Temporal Consistency
PROPOSAL: To ensure temporal consistency and coherence in generated videos, we propose a dynamic context attention mechanism that adaptively selects the relevant frames from the video sequence to attend to at each time step. This mechanism learns to focus on the most relevant frames based on the current context and the predicted future frames, allowing the model to maintain coherence and avoid repetition. We expect this mechanism to improve the model's ability to generate high-quality, temporally consistent videos.
CONTROLS: Compare with a uniform attention mechanism and experiment with different context window sizes.
COST: 10700
PREDICTION: We expect the dynamic context attention mechanism to significantly improve the model's ability to generate high-quality, temporally consistent videos. However, we anticipate that this may come at the cost of increased computational complexity and training time.

We also predict potential difficulties in optimizing the attention weights, given the need to balance the trade-off between coherent continuation and repetition.

TITLE: Investigating Gradient-Based Deduction in Transformers with Unknown Implication Targets
PROPOSAL: Develop a mathematical framework to study how transformers acquire reasoning abilities through gradient-based training, focusing on the regime where the model needs to infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed during training. Define a proof technique based on analyzing the optimization dynamics of the transformer architecture, specifically the interplay between the encoder and decoder, to derive a sufficient condition for gradient-driven deduction.

PREDICTION: The framework should provide a clear insight into how gradient-based training enables transformers to infer implications for unseen targets, but may struggle to model the impact of cascading or multiplicative dependencies. Insufficient control over the optimization dynamics might lead to incorrect assumptions about the necessary conditions.

TITLE: Synthetic Dataset for Testing Generalization and Hallucination after Fact Injection
PROPOSAL: Design a synthetic dataset where factual triples (s, r, a) are split into two sets: a training set where subjects (s) are placed in both the fact and its corresponding implication, and a test set where new subjects (s_test) appear only in the fact or implication. Analyze the performance of common knowledge injection protocols (e.g., fine-tuning, prompting) on this synthetic dataset, using metrics such as accuracy, fluency, and factual correctness to differentiate generalization and hallucination.

PREDICTION: The synthetic dataset will show a clear distinction between generalization and hallucination in LLMs after knowledge injection, but performance may be influenced by the underlying distributions and structures of the data, which might not be generalizable to real-world scenarios.
