ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Gradient-Based Deduction in Transformers with Unknown Implication Targets: Local Convergence Analysis
PROPOSAL: Update the proof technique in proposal 1 to incorporate a local convergence analysis of the transformer's optimization dynamics. Specifically, derive conditions under which the iterates of the model converge to a local minimum, and analyze how this convergence relates to the model's ability to infer implications for unseen targets.
CONTROLS: Abate the convergence analysis by considering a simpler transformation of the model's parameters, and compare the results to the original analysis.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: The revised analysis will provide a deeper understanding of the local convergence behavior of the transformer, but may not generalize well to more complex scenarios where multiple local minima are present. Additionally, difficulties in formalizing the relationship between the local convergence and the model's ability to infer implications may lead to a more ambiguous understanding of the underlying mechanisms.

Define a proof technique based on analyzing the optimization dynamics of the transformer architecture, specifically the interplay between the encoder and decoder, to derive a sufficient condition for gradient-driven deduction.

Insufficient control over the optimization dynamics might lead to incorrect assumptions about the necessary conditions.

TITLE: Synthetic Dataset for Testing Generalization and Hallucination after Fact Injection
PROPOSAL: Design a synthetic dataset where factual triples (s, r, a) are split into two sets: a training set where subjects (s) are placed in both the fact and its corresponding implication, and a test set where new subjects (s_test) appear only in the fact or implication. Modeling efforts could struggle to replicate the observed effects, even with adjuvant data augmentation techniques.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Gradient-Based Training on Implication Inference
PROPOSAL: Analyze the gradient flow and target word embeddings in transformers during training, to understand how gradient-based training leads to implication inference. Develop a theoretical framework to predict when a transformer model will deduce unseen implications, in terms of the geometry of the gradient space and properties of the target word embeddings.
CONTROLS: Run the same experiment with a static embedding lookup, to compare the effect of gradient-based training on implication inference.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the gradient flow patterns bear no direct relation to the ability to infer unseen implications, but the structure of target word embeddings might play a crucial role. This would suggest that the model's ability to generalize to unseen implications arises from the way the embeddings encode the relationships between words, rather than the properties of the gradient flow. Failure: if the analysis shows that the model's ability to infer unseen implications correlates strongly with the properties of the gradient flow, this would suggest that the problem is fundamentally related to optimization, rather than the way the embeddings represent the relationships between words.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Theory of Implication Learning in Self-Supervised Transformers
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework for understanding how self-supervised transformers learn to infer implications from training data. Analyze the behavior of transformers as a graph neural network, and show that the way the model updates its embeddings based on masked tokens leads to a form of "inference-as-dense-subgraph" that enables implication learning.
CONTROLS: Apply this framework to explain the strengths and limitations of implication learning in publicly available transformer models.
COST: 26700
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the model's ability to learn implications is closely related to its ability to form dense subgraphs in the embedding space, and that the mechanism can be generalized to other self-supervised training objectives. However, we might also find that the model struggles with implications that require integrating information from multiple graph partitions, or that the required training data is too large or heterogeneous to be efficiently processed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Mechanism Behind Generalization and Hallucination in Factual Knowledge Injection
PROPOSAL: We design a set of synthetic experiments to study how transformer-based LLMs generalize and hallucinate after fine-tuning on new factual knowledge. Specifically, we use the Demonstrational Reasoning (DR) task, which provides multiple scenarios where a subject is related to multiple answers, e.g., (s, lives in, Paris) and (s, speaks, French). We generate a controlled environment where a few training samples contain both facts and their corresponding implications, and the test set contains unseen implications. We fine-tune different versions of a transformer-based LLM on this data with varying strengths of gradient-based training and test its ability to generalize and hallucinate.
CONTROLS: We compare the results with ablations where we remove the gradient-based training or only use a weaker version of the transformer model. We also use a baseline that is not fine-tuned on the new knowledge.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect to see strong generalization abilities in the strongly-trained model, while the weaker-trained model will tend to hallucinate more. If the weaker-trained model fails to generalize, it will raise interesting questions on how gradient-based training contributes to the model's ability to infer implications.

TITLE: Analyzing Relations Between Implications in Factual Knowledge Injection
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical framework to analyze the relationships between implications in factual knowledge injection, specifically focusing on the task of open-domain question answering. We define a graph structure where each node represents a subject, and directed edges represent the relationships between implications. We then study the connectivity of this graph from different perspectives, including the number of paths between nodes, graph centrality measures, and the emergence of communities.
CONTROLS: We compare our framework with existing works on analyzing relationships in knowledge graphs, and we will use a random graph generator to simulate synthetic graphs that mimic real-world knowledge graphs.
COST: 608
PREDICTION: We hope to find that the connectivity of the graph is strongly correlated with the model's ability to generalize and hallucinate, and that graph centrality measures can help explain why some implications are more easily inferred than others.

TITLE: Investigating the Mechanism Behind Generalization and Hallucination in Factual Knowledge Injection
PROPOSAL: We design a set of synthetic experiments to study how transformer-based LLMs generalize and hallucinate after fine-tuning on new factual knowledge. Specifically, we use the Demonstrational Reasoning (DR) task, which provides multiple scenarios where a subject is related to multiple answers, e.g., (s, lives in, Paris) and (s, speaks, French). We generate a controlled environment where a few training samples contain both facts and their corresponding implications, and the test set contains unseen implications. We fine-tune different versions of a transformer-based LLM on this data with varying strengths of gradient-based training and test its ability to generalize and hallucinate.
CONTROLS: We compare the results with ablations where we remove the gradient-based training or only use a weaker version of the transformer model. We also use a baseline that is not fine-tuned on the new knowledge.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect to see strong generalization abilities in the strongly-trained model, while the weaker-trained model will tend to hallucinate more. If the weaker-trained model fails to generalize, it will raise interesting questions on how gradient-based training contributes to the model's ability to infer implications.

TITLE: Analyzing Relations Between Implications in Factual Knowledge Injection
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical framework to analyze the relationships between implications in factual knowledge injection, specifically focusing on the task of open-domain question answering. We define a graph structure where each node represents a subject, and directed edges represent the relationships between implications. We then study the connectivity of this graph from different perspectives, including the number of paths between nodes, graph centrality measures, and the emergence of communities.
CONTROLS: We compare our framework with existing works on analyzing relationships in knowledge graphs, and we will use a random graph generator to simulate synthetic graphs that mimic real-world knowledge graphs.
COST: 1830
PREDICTION: We hope to find that the connectivity of the graph is strongly correlated with the model's ability to generalize and hallucinate, and that graph centrality measures can help explain why some implications are more easily inferred than others.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Focal-Stack Regularization on Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We will train a baseline 3D convolutional neural network (3D CNN) architecture on the NYU Depth V2 dataset for the task of indoor depth estimation from focal stacks, and evaluate its performance under different regularization schemes that utilize the spatial and focal structure of the input data. The experimentation involves replacing the traditional L1, L2 regularization, and drop-out methods with and exploring the following custom focal-stack regularization methods: a) focal-depth coherence loss, which encourages the network to produce consistent depth predictions across the focal stack; b) spatial-focal attention, which adaptively weights the contributions of different focal planes to spatial locations; c) slice-wise batch normalization, which normalizes the input at each focal plane individually. In addition to these custom schemes, we will evaluate the performance of the baseline network with traditional L1, and L2 regularizations.
CONTROLS: Baseline 3D CNN without any focal-stack regularization, traditional L1, and L2 regularizations; and L1-dropout.
COST: 180 
PREDICTION: We expect the custom focal-stack regularization methods a) and b) to improve depth estimation accuracy, especially in regions with fine textures or abrupt depth changes, as they better leverage the complementary spatial and focal information of the focal stack. On the other hand, c) may degrade the performance in low-texture regions due to its sensitivity to noise. Traditional methods may fail to reach the level of performance of the custom focal-stack regularization methods due to their simplicity and the trade-off between regularization strength and over-smoothing.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Exploring Focal-Stack Features via Multi-Scale Attention Mechanism
PROPOSAL: We propose to incorporate a multi-scale attention mechanism into the focal-stack processing pipeline to effectively exploit varying spatial and focal information. This attention mechanism, specifically designed for focal-stack data, focuses on modeling hierarchical relationships between images at different focal distances. The proposed model, Focal-Stack Multi-Scale Attention Network (FS-MSAN), consists of three main components: a focal-depth extractor, which extracts focal-depth features from individual images in the stack; a multi-scale attention module, which aggregates and focuses on the most informative features from all scales; and a deformable convolutional decoder, which generates the final depth map by refining the focal-depth features with the spatial contextual information. Our goal is to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed multi-scale attention mechanism in accurately capturing depth variations across the focal stack.
CONTROLS: Baseline 3D CNN with the previously proposed focal-stack regularization methods, a variant of FS-MSAN without the deformable convolutional decoder.
COST: 360 
PREDICTION: FS-MSAN is expected to outperform the baseline and other variants due to its ability to model hierarchical representations and contextually refine focal information, leading to accurate depth estimation, especially in scenes with abrupt depth changes or repetitive textures. Challenges to our success might come from efforts to further enlarge the model's capacity and compute resource imbalance during testing.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Exploring Focal-Stack Features via Multi-Scale Attention Mechanism
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to make it more tractable by replacing the deformable convolutional decoder with a more lightweight component: a conventional convolutional decoder with upsampling layers. The goal remains to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed multi-scale attention mechanism in accurately capturing depth variations across the focal stack, but now with a more computationally efficient architecture.
CONTROLS: Baseline 3D CNN with the previously proposed focal-stack regularization methods, a variant of FS-MSAN without the multi-scale attention module.
COST: 300 
PREDICTION: The revised FS-MSAN is expected to achieve comparable accuracy to our original model, with the primary difference being the trade-off between performance and computational efficiency. Remaining challenges include optimizing the number of scales in the multi-scale attention module and ensuring that the model is not over-reliant on certain features. 

Note: The added computational efficiency might compensate for potential reduction in accuracy, possibly improving model's robustness to unseen test sets.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Physics-Informed Neural Network for Depth Estimation via Shape-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: To better exploit the physics of focus and focal stack, we propose incorporating a physics-informed neural network (PINN) component into our model. Specifically, we will use a PINN to model the focus behavior of light in a camera, allowing our model to learn the underlying physical principles of focusing and integrate these into its depth estimation process. This will be achieved by incorporating an additional focusing energy term into the PINN's loss function, which encourages the network to generate depth maps that satisfy the focus-sharpness relationshippredicted by the camera's physics.
CONTROLS: Baseline 3D CNN with the previously proposed focal-stack regularization methods, our revised FS-MSAN model from proposal 2, a variant of FS-MSAN that omits the PINN component.
COST: 660 
PREDICTION: Incorporating the PINN component is expected to bring significant improvements in depth estimation accuracy, as the model will be better equipped to handle complexities in focal stack and exploit the physics-based focus-sharpness relationship. However, challenges may arise when dealing with limited training data and approximating complex physical relationships.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Focal-Stack Regularization on Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to investigate the effect of focal-stack regularization on a broader range of focus measures, including not only the commonly used Laplacian and frequency-domain contrast operators, but also more novel and physics-inspired measures, such as the blur-kernel analysis and focus-sharpness gradient-based methods. Our goal is to evaluate the extent to which these different focus measures can contribute to the robustness and accuracy of depth estimation models in challenging scenarios such as fine textures and low-texture regions.
CONTROLS: Baseline 3D CNN without any focal-stack regularization; Focal-Stack Multi-Scale Attention Network (FS-MSAN) from proposal 2; the PINN-based focus-sharpness model from proposal 3; the baseline 3D CNN with traditional L1 and L2 regularizations.
COST: 450 
PREDICTION: We expect that the physics-inspired focus measures will outperform the traditional methods in challenging scenarios, while the novel focus measures may still be vulnerable to noise and mislead the model in ambiguous situations.

PROPOSAL: To assess the deployment-readiness of the proposed models, we will conduct experiments on a diverse range of real-world datasets, including indoor and outdoor scenes, with varying levels of complexity and texture. Our focus will be on accurately estimating depth at both macro and micro levels, including low-texture regions, fine structures, and repetitive patterns.

PREDICTION: The proposed models will achieve high accuracy on the real-world datasets, particularly on scenes with high visual complexity and texture, demonstrating their capabilities in real-world deployment. However, we anticipate that some models might struggle with scenes having low texture, as features might not enough descriptive and may not capture the actual scene depth in general.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Physics-Informed Neural Network for Depth Estimation via Shape-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to incorporate an additional self-supervised learning component that jointly optimizes the depth estimation and defocus simulation processes. This self-supervised learning component will involve a separate network that predicts the defocused images from the estimated depth map, serving as a proxy for the actual defocus process. By jointly optimizing both the depth and defocus components, we aim to improve the accuracy and robustness of the depth estimation model, particularly in challenging scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baseline 3D CNN with traditional L1 and L2 regularizations; Focal-Stack Multi-Scale Attention Network (FS-MSAN) from proposal 2; the original PINN-based focus-sharpness model from proposal 3, minus the self-supervised learning component.
COST: 540 
PREDICTION: The revised model with self-supervised learning is expected to achieve higher accuracy in challenging scenarios, as the joint optimization process will better capture the relationships between depth, defocus, and camera parameters. However, the additional complexity of the model may lead to overfitting if not properly regularized.

TITLE: Evaluating Real-World Depth Estimation Performance on Diverse Scenes
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to incorporate explicit calibration and adaptation mechanisms to make the depth estimation models more robust and adaptable to different real-world scenarios. This will involve injecting domain knowledge, such as scene understanding and real-world constraints, into the depth estimation process to bridge the gap between controlled laboratory settings and real-world deployments. Specifically, we will leverage recent advances in scene understanding and generative models to inject visual and semantic context into the depth estimation pipeline.
CONTROLS: Baseline 3D CNN with traditional L1 and L2 regularizations; Focal-Stack Multi-Scale Attention Network (FS-MSAN) from proposal 2; the PINN-based focus-sharpness model with self-supervised learning from proposal 3, without the explicit calibration mechanism; a domain-adversarial training variant of FS-MSAN, which adapts to unseen domains during inference.
COST: 630 
PREDICTION: The revised evaluation protocol with explicit calibration and adaptation will lead to improved depth estimation accuracy and robustness in real-world scenarios, particularly in diverse and complex scenes. However, the added complexity may require careful tuning of model parameters and computational resources.

Participants will be presented with various depth maps and focus cues, and their subjective ratings of accuracy, sharpness, and comfort will be collected. The goal is to identify the key characteristics of depth maps and focus cues that are perceived as most salient and intuitive by humans, and to explore the potential implications for the design of more user-friendly and intuitive depth estimation systems.
CONTROLS: None, as this is a qualitative study that will inform the development of future quantitative models.
COST: 450 
PREDICTION: The perception studies will provide valuable insights into human perception and preferences, and will likely reveal important differences between the results of human subjects and automated depth estimation models. These findings can be used to guide the development of more human-centered and user-friendly depth estimation systems.

TITLE: Learning Focus-Conditional Spatial Features for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a new end-to-end convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that learns focus-conditional spatial features to enhance depth estimation from focal stacks. Our model combines U-Net-type encoder-decoder structure with an attention mechanism conditioned on the focus maps. This enables the network to distinguish true depth edges from texture-induced gradients, disambiguate noisy or misleading focus cues, and produce accurate and sharp depth maps. We will train and evaluate our network on the NileCrops and MPI Sintel datasets using depth-ground truth, focal stack images, and evaluate its performance using metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE) and the effectiveness of the learned focus maps in disambiguating noise.
CONTROLS: We will set aside one of our models to simply serve as our baseline for comparison – this baseline will be an U-Net model tackling the task without taking focus into account.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Our results should be competitive with existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in terms of the quality of the focal maps produced by the model and how well it handles ambiguous regions, but may struggle with the large texture patterns typical in some indoor scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Informed Convolutional Neural Networks for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Motivated by the understanding of the physics of focusing, we design and train physics-informed convolutional neural networks (PICNNs) to model the connection between focal stacks and depth maps. Specifically, we introduce a deblurring loss function that directly relates the sharpness of image features to the focal distance. We also formulate the depth loss as a residual error between predicted and true depth maps, while incorporating a smoothness regularization term to favor plausible depth discontinuities. We expect our approach to improve the robustness and accuracy of depth estimation in scenes with varying illumination and texture content. We will train and test our PICNNs on a diverse set of real-world indoor scenes and datasets such as NYU Depth v2 and MatterPort3D.
CONTROLS: We will compare the PICNNs with our baseline model in Learning Focus-Conditional Spatial Features for Depth Estimation, as well as two alternative methods: a cascade of U-net models for deblurring and depth estimation, and an ordinary U-net model without physics-informed regularization.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: Our PICNNs approach is expected to outperform our baseline and alternative methods, especially in scenarios with ambiguous focus cues and texture-induced noise. Some of the results may, however, also highlight challenges in modeling complex physical phenomena in the CNN framework.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Learning Focus-Conditional Spatial Features for Depth Estimation with Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We extend our previous model by incorporating domain adaptation to improve the robustness and generalizability of depth estimation across various scenes and environments. To adapt to new domains, we use a source-target similarity loss-based framework that involves learning a domain-specific feature transformation and a weighting mechanism to balance source and target distributions. This allows our network to develop a robust and adaptive understanding of focus patterns and structural variations in depth images. We will evaluate this extension on multiple datasets, including the NYU Depth v2, MatterPort3D and the KITTI depth benchmark, to assess its performance under different domain shifts.
CONTROLS: Our revised baseline will be the domain-adapted U-Net model that distinguishes from the non-domain-adapted one only by the inclusion of source-target similarity loss.
COST: 324
PREDICTION: Our revised model is expected to maintain or improve the accuracy and robustness observed in our previous work, while demonstrating its ability to generalize better across different environments, especially when there is a significant difference in lighting or texture content. Still, adapting to the specifics of a new environment might prove challenging for the domain adaptation mechanism, which may impact the performance in customs cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Mutual Information between Spatial and Focal Information for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: To better integrate spatial and focal information for robust depth estimation, we propose to leverage mutual information as an objective function that encourages the model to learn informative and complementary representations from both modalities. Specifically, we introduce a novel mutual information-based regularizer that maximizes the confidence in the predicted depth maps when conditioned on both the image and the focal stack. Our approach can help the model distinguish between true depth edges and texture-induced gradients by exploiting the differences in focus patterns between regions of different depths. We expect our method to achieve state-of-the-art performance on depth estimation benchmarks and be particularly effective in scenes with ambiguous focus cues.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method with our previous models as well as an alternative approach based on entropy-based spatial and focal feature fusion.
COST: 350
PREDICTION: Our method will likely outperform existing state-of-the-art methods due to its ability to accurately capture the inter-relationship between spatial and focal information, which might lead to more accurate depth estimates, especially in scenarios with complex texture patterns or focusing cues. However, the model may struggle to handle too complex or ambiguous scenes where depth correlates poorly with focal or other cues, potentially resulting in suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improved Focal Stack Quality through Denoising and Defocus Map Refinement
PROPOSAL: To improve the quality of focal stacks, a crucial component for depth estimation, we propose a multi-stage approach that first denoises the input images using a BM3D-based denoising algorithm, and then refines the defocus maps by incorporating a CNN-based defocus map refinement module into our framework. Our denoising method can effectively remove various types of noise (Gaussian, impulse, etc.) that may degrade the quality of focal stacks, while the defocus map refinement module helps recover subtle details that may have been lost due to image blur and optical aberrations. We will evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on a range of datasets, including the popular MPI Sintel dataset and real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: As a baseline, we will use a simple denoising algorithm that is limited to removing Gaussian noise alone, along with two additional models, our previous spatial feature learning models, for direct comparison on focal stack qualification.
COST: 429.5
PREDICTION: Our approach should lead to improved depth estimation results in scenes with corrupted or noisy focal stacks, as denoised and refined focal stacks contribute to a more confident and detailed depth prediction. Although it is possible to further optimize our method for specific noise types, our generalized approach may not cover the entire range of possible image corruption scenarios, which could lead to suboptimal performance on particularly difficult cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly-Supervised Depth Estimation with Focal-Ensemble Learning
PROPOSAL: In response to the limited availability of labeled depth data, we propose a weakly-supervised depth estimation framework that leverages the strength of focal stacks. Our approach involves an ensemble of multiple models that are trained to predict depth maps using weak supervision (i.e., focusing cues alone) and then aggregates their predictions through a focal-ensemble learning strategy. This strategy enables our framework to capture subtle depth cues that might be overlooked by individual models. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we will evaluate our approach on a variety of benchmarks, including several public datasets with partial and weak supervision.
CONTROLS: As a baseline, we will compare our approach against a conventional strong supervision baseline where each model is trained with finer-grained (but more expensive) labels, our previous spatial and focal feature learning models.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: Our framework has the potential to achieve competitive results with strong supervision and often surpass them under certain conditions, because our ensemble approach effectively captures weak depth cues – but our performance may be noticeably worse under conditions of very strong noise, given the reduced weight of stronger supervision, it may observe under-rated depth values.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Physics-Informed Convolutional Neural Networks for Depth Estimation with Optimal Focal Distance Estimation
PROPOSAL: To improve the accuracy and robustness of our previously proposed physics-informed CNN framework for depth estimation, we focus on optimizing the estimation of focal distances. We expect this optimized focal-distance estimation to critically improve the accuracy of depth estimation results in a range of challenging scenarios.
CONTROLS: As a baseline, we'll use our previous physics-informed CNN without focal-distance prediction sub-network; also include an ablation study to evaluate the impact of estimation accuracy on depth-estimation performance.

PREDICTION: With this optimized focal-distance estimation capability, our framework should significantly improve its ability to estimate accurate depth maps, especially in scenes with ambiguous focusing cues, discontinuities, and variations in texture and reflectance. Still, challenges remain as overly confident estimation in certain scenarios may ultimately cause suboptimal inference in overall depth map predictability.

TITLE: Hierarchical Depth Estimation using Multi-Modal Focal Maps and Refinement with Graph Convolutional Networks
PROPOSAL: Building upon our previous methods, we propose a hierarchical depth estimation framework that combines multi-modal focal maps and refinement with the power of graph convolutional networks (GCNs). By learning a hierarchical representation of focal information from multiple input modalities, including intensity and depth maps, our approach enables accurate depth estimation at various scales and resolutions. The GCN-based refinement module further enhances depth accuracy by aggregating neighborhood relationships and structural patterns. We will evaluate our framework on a suite of depth estimation benchmarks, including the NYU Depth v2 and KITTI datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach against state-of-the-art hierarchical depth estimation methods, our previous weakly-supervised depth methods, and alternative refinement methods based on GCNs without hierarchical focal maps.

PREDICTION: Our hierarchical framework should exhibit competitive performance in depth estimation due to its ability to effectively integrate and refine focal information from various modalities and scales – though strong noise patterns in fine-grained depth-maps could compromise the precision of refined results, especially at higher hierarchical levels.

TITLE: Investigating Learning-based Focal Stack Parsing for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel learning-based paradigm that leverages the physical principle of focus and the multi-focus information in focal stacks to segment focus patterns from a focal stack into multiple regions, each representing a distinct depth segment. We utilize a U-Net architecture with a novel focal attention mechanism that selectively aggregates features across the focal stack, allowing the model to capture sharpness-driven depth cues and distinguish noisy focus cues. The model is trained on a large-scale dataset comprising images from various indoor scenes captured at multiple focal distances.
CONTROLS: We compare our model against several baseline models, including a classical DFF method, a self-supervised model that jointly reconstructs depth and all-in-focus images, and a state-of-the-art learning-based DFF model. We also conduct ablation studies to evaluate the effectiveness of the focal attention mechanism.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our model achieves significant improvements in benchmark performance, particularly in complex indoor scenes with fine textures and abrupt depth changes, while maintaining high accuracy and sharpness. However, it may struggle with certain types of ambient reflections, which could lead to misleading focus cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-aware Feature Representation for Learning-based DFF
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the physical principle of focus, we design a novel feature representation that incorporates a combination of gradient-based and sharpness-driven features for better capturing the geometry of a scene. Our feature representation is composed of multiple channels, including the gradient magnitude and orientation, Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) features, and a novel sharpness-oriented feature extracted using a frequency-domain approach. We demonstrate that this physics-aware feature representation significantly improves the robustness and accuracy of learning-based DFF models in challenging scenes.
CONTROLS: We compare our feature representation against traditional hand-crafted features (e.g., Sobel and LoG) and a baseline where we add a random feature channel. We also examine the impact of each individual component on the overall performance of the DFF model.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our feature representation improves the state-of-the-art performance in a variety of challenging indoor scenes, while maintaining robustness across different texture types and depth changes. However, integrating this new feature representation may require calibration of hyperparameters specific to each dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Focal Stack Sampling for Efficient Learning-based DFF
PROPOSAL: To alleviate the computational bottleneck of training deep neural networks on densely sampled focal stacks, we propose an adaptive sampling scheme that dynamically selects the most informative frames from the stack. Our approach uses a novelty-based sampling strategy, which evaluates the focus patterns across the stack and identifies frames that provide the highest contrast between sharp and blurred regions. By adaptively sampling the most informative frames, we reduce the computational burden while maintaining the accuracy of our learning-based DFF model.
CONTROLS: We compare our adaptive sampling scheme against traditional fixed sampling strategies (e.g., regular grid, random selection) and a baseline where all frames are used in training.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our adaptive sampling scheme reduces the computational requirements of training by approximately 50% while retaining the state-of-the-art performance. However, it may suffer from inconsistent performance in scenes with varying lighting conditions and fine textures.

TITLE: Multi-task Learning for Joint Depth Estimation and Defocus Map Inference
PROPOSAL: Leveraging the complementary information provided by the focal stack, we propose a multi-task learning approach that jointly trains a model to estimate depth and infer a defocus map from the stack. Our approach uses a shared backbone architecture that fuses the features extracted from the depth estimation and defocus map inference branches. By learning to predict both depth and defocus maps simultaneously, our model benefits from a richer representation of the scene geometry and photometric properties.
CONTROLS: We compare our multi-task learning approach against single-task depth estimation methods, a baseline that only trains the defocus map inference network, and a classical DFF method that relies on post-hoc smoothing for depth estimation.
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our multi-task learning approach leads to a significant improvement in depth estimation accuracy and defocus map quality, particularly in scenes with fine textures and complex geometry. However, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the contributions of the two tasks.

TITLE: Self-supervised Focal Stack Reconstruction for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a self-supervised learning approach that leverages focal stack reconstruction as a pretext task to improve depth estimation accuracy. TITLE: Self-supervised Focal Stack Reconstruction for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a self-supervised learning approach that leverages focal stack reconstruction as a pretext task to improve depth estimation accuracy. Our approach trains a model to reconstruct the all-in-focus image from a deeply degraded stack, where the degradation is modeled using a learned defocus simulation. By optimizing the depth estimation task and the focal stack reconstruction task jointly, our model learns a robust and efficient representation of the scene geometry and photometric properties.
CONTROLS: We compare our self-supervised focal stack reconstruction approach against a supervised baseline where the model is trained on a depth estimation dataset and a self-supervised baseline where the model is trained only on the focal stack reconstruction task.

PROPOSAL: We propose a unified neural model that jointly estimates depth and infers a defocus map from a focal stack, while also predicting additional scene attributes such as the camera pose and scene structure. Our model uses a modular architecture that seamlessly integrates the depth estimation and defocus map inference branches, leveraging a shared feature extraction component to capture the interplay between scene geometry and photometry.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Spatial-Focal Unsupervised Monocular Depth Estimation using a Focal Stack Autoencoder
PROPOSAL: Train an unsupervised focal stack autoencoder with a spatial-focal discriminator, which disentangles depth, albedo, and geometry from multi-focus images and produces sharp and accurate depth maps by leveraging synergies between spatial structure and focus evolution across the stack. The model is trained on the challenging KITTI-Depth benchmark with focal stacks captured at 5 focal distances. Our novel reconstruction loss terms for depth and albedo will be based on a scaled-Cosine similarity metric. 
CONTROLS: Supervised DFF (SCP, Zhang et al. 2019) and Deep filling-In for Depth from Focus (DIFI, Sa et al. 2020)
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: This method should better distinguish true depth edges from texture-induced gradients and generate more accurate depth maps compared to the baselines, but might suffer from the difficulties of unsupervised learning on complex real-world scenes, including loss of structural detail.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploiting Multiple Levels of Focal Map Features for DFF via a Hierarchical Model
PROPOSAL: Design a hierarchical model consisting of an encoder-decoder deep network that combines multiple feature-level representations of focal maps, each capturing distinct aspects of depth and focus patterns. The focal maps will be derived from a variety of focal measures to encode rich focus information at multiple scales. The decoder will refine the spatially-regressed depth maps using a depth-informed focal map regularization term to produce sharp depth outputs that accurately recover structure. We will test this method on the NTU SES Depth Dataset and NYU Depth V2 Dataset with focal stacks captured at 3-5 focal points.
CONTROLS: Self-Supervised Depth from Focus via Learned Defocus Simulation (SDFD, Li et al. 2020) and Residual refinement for focal depth (ReDeF, Hazan & Bronstein, 2019)
COST: 6936
PREDICTION: This model should achieve significant improvements in estimating depth from focal stacks by better leveraging multiple scales of focal map features and providing better depth-informed regularization, but may be time-consuming due to the added complexity of a hierarchical architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Focal Depth Estimation via Monte Carlo Sampling and Bayesian Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Propose a method that incorporates Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) and Monte Carlo sampling to estimate the uncertainty of depth maps from focal stacks. TITLE: Joint Spatial-Focal Unsupervised Monocular Depth Estimation using a Focal Stack Autoencoder
PROPOSAL: Train an unsupervised focal stack autoencoder with a spatial-focal discriminator, which disentangles depth, albedo, and geometry from multi-focus images and produces sharp and accurate depth maps by leveraging synergies between spatial structure and focus evolution across the stack. The model is trained on the challenging KITTI-Depth benchmark with focal stacks captured at 5 focal distances. Our novel reconstruction loss terms for depth and albedo will be based on a scaled-Cosine similarity metric. 
CONTROLS: Supervised DFF (SCP, Zhang et al. 2019) and Deep filling-In for Depth from Focus (DIFI, Sa et al. 2020)
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: This method should better distinguish true depth edges from texture-induced gradients and generate more accurate depth maps compared to the baselines, but might suffer from the difficulties of unsupervised learning on complex real-world scenes, including loss of structural detail.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploiting Multiple Levels of Focal Map Features for DFF via a Hierarchical Model
PROPOSAL: Design a hierarchical model consisting of an encoder-decoder deep network that combines multiple feature-level representations of focal maps, each capturing distinct aspects of depth and focus patterns. The focal maps will be derived from a variety of focal measures to encode rich focus information at multiple scales. The decoder will refine the spatially-regressed depth maps using a depth-informed focal map regularization term to produce sharp depth outputs that accurately recover structure. We will test this method on the NTU SES Depth Dataset and NYU Depth V2 Dataset with focal stacks captured at 3-5 focal points.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Disentangling MoE Routing Heuristics in DiTs
PROPOSAL: Given the inconsistent results from previous MoE variants for DiTs, we plan a comprehensive comparison of different token-choice and expert-choice routing strategies. Using lineups of diverse image datasets (e.g., CelebA-HQ and LSUN) and high-performance DiT models, we'll examine the efficiency and effectiveness of routing mechanisms like token-distribution, competitive routing, and sparse routing, and their combinations. This study will be replicated with real-world, large-scale datasets (e.g., COCO-Stuff, and iNaturalist2019).
CONTROLS: Dense DiT baseline, variants with token-choice routing (DiT-MoE), and expert-choice routing (EC-DiT), with the least used number of experts to test for efficiency.
COST: 645
PREDICTION: Our experiments may uncover important insights into the limitations of existing MoE routing strategies and provide evidence for a superior or hybrid approach, improving efficiency and generation quality of MoE variants for DiTs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Visual Token Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: We design a series of experiments to analyze whether diffusion model tokens have a comparable basis for specialization as text tokens in language modeling. We construct a variant of a DiT that randomly assigns tokens to experts, effectively "masking" their spatial information, and compare its performance to a normal DiT and a random tokenizer. We use theFlyingThings3D dataset and the PSNR metric for evaluation. Controls include ablated models where either spatial assignment or expert masking is disabled.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect a moderate performance degradation (~1-3 PSNR drop) for masked DiTs compared to normal ones, indicating the dependence of MoE performance on token context. Where it might fail lies in an abysmal outcome, where expert masking gives mildly better results, leading to abandonment of MoE paradigm.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Expert Attribute Analysis for Diffusion Model Tokens
PROPOSAL: We investigate whether specific attributes of diffusion model tokens, such as size, position, or frequency of occurrence, influence the capacity for expert specialization. We use a set of pre-trained DiTs and compute metrics measuring attribute diversity among assigned tokens. We then train MoE variants using token assignment schemes that either promote or hinder attribute diversity and compare their performance on the LegendDenario dataset. Controls include MoE models with token attribute-based routing. 
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect attribute diversity to be an important aspect of token specialization, with models promoting diversity (PSNR baseline ~101, no diversity ~99) and discouraging it (PSNR baseline ~101, discouraged diversity ~102) fitting these expectations. However, without carefully accounting for attribute interaction, the expert router may overfit.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Adaptive Multi-Task Learning for Mixture-of-Experts with Dynamic Routing
PROPOSAL: Investigate the possibility of leveraging adaptive multi-task learning (AMTL) to further enhance the performance of MoE-based DiTs with dynamic routing. In this setting, the routing mechanism and the experts themselves are jointly trained to solve multiple tasks (e.g., image generation and image discrimination) simultaneously, while adapting to the changing requirements of each task. This adaptive framework is hypothesized to promote rapid and agile learning, as well as improved knowledge transfer between experts, leading to superior performance on downstream tasks. The AMTL framework is instantiated using a constrained variational Bayes to tackle the challenges of interaction between components, efficiently refining the inference process.
CONTROLS: Traditional dense DiTs, MoE-DiTs with fixed routing, and existing multi-task learning methods.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: This experiment is expected to demonstrate significant improvements in performance and adaptability, as well as showcasing more efficient use of computational resources compared to state-of-the-art MoE-DiTs.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating MoE Routing for Visual Tokens in DiTs
PROPOSAL: We propose a thorough empirical study of various token-choice routing strategies for MoE in DiTs using a series of ablation experiments, including vanilla token-choice, spatial aware token-choice, and learning a content-based token embedding to inform routing decisions. For each strategy, we will evaluate its performance on text-to-image tasks with metrics including Inception Score (IS), Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). We will compare our implementations to the DiT-MoE baseline.

COST: 600
PREDICTION: Token-choice with spatial awareness (with/without token embedding) should significantly outperform the DiT-MoE baseline. Spatially aware token-choice might help assign correct tokens to experts due to image spatial coherence. This might not work as well with smaller images or few experts. 

Given the multitude of roles MoE can play in improving performance, rarity of understanding the failure modes of MoE in images, I estimated the cost to be higher due to difficulty and potential numerous control distributions.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Expert Design for Visual Tokens in DiTs
PROPOSAL: We propose designing a set of novel expert architectures for DiTs, each optimized for specific visual token properties such as spatial location, patch size, and feature complexity, to benefit from expert specialization. By analyzing the characteristics of visual tokens in DiTs, we design experts as variants of efficient vision architectures like EfficientNet and MobileNet, and evaluate their performance on text-to-image tasks. We also experiment with pre-training experts on specialized tasks (e.g., object detection, image segmentation) before integrating them into the MoE module to encourage expert-domain specialization.
CONTROLS: DiT-MoE (with pre-defined experts), pre-trained experts (using tasks such as image segmentation, object detection)
COST: 746.8
PREDICTION: Training experts for specific tasks or designing them with visual token properties in mind should result in better performance, with notable gains in IS and FID scores, due to better specialization and utilization of visual tokens. 

MoE expert efficiencies, and applicability may be limited depending on the space complexity of the specific model, training process, and resulting scalability. ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Improving MoE Routing for Visual Tokens in DiTs with Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose improving token-choice routing in MoE DiTs using contrastive learning, a technique that encourages experts to specialize on specific visual tokens by contrasting them with negative examples. We will design a contrastive loss function that pushes the representations of positive tokens (i.e., tokens matched with their corresponding experts) closer together while pulling the representations of negative tokens (i.e., tokens not matched with their corresponding experts) further apart. This will help the MoE module to learn more robust and discriminative expert representations.
CONTROLS: DiT-MoE (token-choice), DiT-MoE with contrastive learning
COST: 955.4
PREDICTION: Contrastive learning will improve expert specialization and overall MoE performance by learning more discriminative expert representations, but might have a limited effect on smaller models or tasks with a very small token vocabulary, as they lack the capacity to capture subtle token features.

TITLE: Improving MoE Routing for Visual Tokens in DiTs with Transferable and Adversarial Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose enhancing token-choice routing in MoE DiTs using a more robust and transferable contrastive learning framework that incorporates adversarial training. We will design a modified contrastive loss function that leverages both positive and negative tokens, as well as adversarial samples to penalize the model for using overly specialized expert representations. This will help the MoE module to learn more generalizable and expert specialization resistant expert representations that can adapt to novel visual token distributions.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Analyzing Expert Interactions in MoE DiTs using Graph-Based Methods
PROPOSAL: We propose analyzing the interactions between experts in MoE DiTs using graph-based methods, where experts are represented as nodes, and their interactions are represented as edges. We will use graph neural networks to learn the relationships between experts and identify key patterns, such as expert co-specialization, hubness, and cliques. By examining these expert interactions, we can gain insights into how experts work together to produce accurate visual tokens and how the MoE module leverages expert collaboration to improve performance.
CONTROLS: DiT-MoE (token-choice), Graph-based expert interaction analysis with different graph neural network architectures
COST: 1140
PREDICTION: Graph-based analysis of expert interactions will reveal complex patterns and relationships between experts that can inform the design of more effective MoE modules. However, analyzing large-scale MoE models may be computationally expensive and require significant resources.

TITLE: Improving MoE Routing for Visual Tokens in DiTs with Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose improving token-choice routing in MoE DiTs using contrastive learning, a technique that encourages experts to specialize on specific visual tokens by contrasting them with negative examples. We will design a contrastive loss function that pushes the representations of positive tokens (i.e., tokens matched with their corresponding experts) closer together while pulling the representations of negative tokens (i.e., tokens not matched with their corresponding experts) further apart. This will help the MoE module to learn more robust and discriminative expert representations.
CONTROLS: DiT-MoE (token-choice), DiT-MoE with contrastive learning
COST: 2872
PREDICTION: Contrastive learning will improve expert specialization and overall MoE performance by learning more discriminative expert representations, but might have a limited effect on smaller models or tasks with a very small token vocabulary, as they lack the capacity to capture subtle token features.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Improving MoE Routing for Visual Tokens in DiTs with Transferable and Adversarial Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose enhancing token-choice routing in MoE DiTs using a more robust and transferable contrastive learning framework that incorporates adversarial training. We will design a modified contrastive loss function that leverages both positive and negative tokens, as well as adversarial samples to penalize the model for using overly specialized expert representations. This will help the MoE module to learn more generalizable and expert specialization resistant expert representations that can adapt to novel visual token distributions.
CONTROLS: DiT-MoE (token-choice), DiT-MoE with transferable and adversarial contrastive learning, DiT-MoE with only adversarial training
COST: 3170
PREDICTION: The updated contrastive learning approach will significantly improve the adaptability and generalization ability of the MoE module, but might require a larger dataset or more extensive fine-tuning to learn the target task.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Analyzing Expert Interactions in MoE DiTs using Graph-Based Methods
PROPOSAL: We propose analyzing the interactions between experts in MoE DiTs using graph-based methods, where experts are represented as nodes, and their interactions are represented as edges. We will use graph neural networks to learn the relationships between experts and identify key patterns, such as expert co-specialization, hubness, and cliques. By examining these expert interactions, we can gain insights into how experts work together to produce accurate visual tokens and how the MoE module leverages expert collaboration to improve performance.
CONTROLS: DiT-MoE (token-choice), Graph-based expert interaction analysis with different graph neural network architectures
COST: 3415
PREDICTION: Graph-based analysis of expert interactions will reveal complex patterns and relationships between experts that can inform the design of more effective MoE modules. However, analyzing large-scale MoE models may be computationally expensive and require significant resources.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: "Robust Offset Correction through Synthetic Contamination"
PROPOSAL: We propose an offline reinforcement learning algorithm, namely OffsetCorrectedQ-Learning (OCQ-Learning), that uses synthetic contamination of the observation dataset to learn an offset correction policy. The method adds artificial, temporally correlated offsets to a clean dataset to mimic the behaviours of real-world data, where a single offset applies across an episode. The agent learns to correct these added offsets, which serve as a proxy for the true, temporally correlated offsets that are present in the real world. OCQ-Learning is then tested in synthetic experiments using Mujoco robot simulation environments, including robotic arm and wheel environments, which can mimic some of the attributes of real-world robot manipulation and navigation tasks.
CONTROLS: The baselines used will be vanilla Q-Learning and a noise-robust version of Q-Learning, that adds Gaussian noise to the observation space.
COST: 3200
PREDICTION: We expect OCQ-Learning to generalize better to perturbed observations, show higher task success rates under unseen perturbations and perform well under the previously-mentioned synthetic environments but might struggle with non-linear offset patterns if not refined properly.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: "Curriculum Learning for Robust Online Adaptation"
PROPOSAL: We develop a curriculum learning approach to enable offline-trained agents to adapt robustly to unseen patterns of non-stationarity. Our Curricular Offset Tuner (COT) trains the agent on an increasingly difficult series of tasks, each with a recalibrated level of synthetic offset contamination. This allows the agent to learn an offset correction policy from scratch on easy tasks and refine its knowledge progressively as it is trained on harder tasks with higher levels of contamination.
CONTROLS: Vanilla training and curriculum learning without offset contamination are used as controls to examine the effect of the offset tuning mechanism on the agent's performance.
COST: 4400
PREDICTION: COT is expected to improve the agent's ability to adapt to online and unseen offset patterns, generalize to new offsets, and reduce the training time required to reach task completion.

TITLE: "Robust Offset Correction through Multi-scale Contamination and Correction"
PROPOSAL: "Robust Offset Correction through Synthetic Contamination" is revised by incorporating both multi-scale offset contamination and multi-scale offset correction learning. The revised approach adds artificial, temporally and spatially correlated offsets to the clean dataset to mimic the real-world data, and then learns an offset correction policy of varying temporal and spatial scales.
CONTROLS: The baselines used are vanilla Q-Learning, a noise-robust version of Q-Learning, and multi-scale perturbation baselines, both with and without the correction signal.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect the revised model to better correct various scales of temporal offsets and generalize to a greater variety of real-world offset patterns in both training and test environments but might still struggle with arbitrary and non-linear patterns of contamination if not further refined.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: "Predictive Offset Modeling through Time-series Analysis"
PROPOSAL: We explore the use of time-series analysis techniques, such as ARIMA and LSTMs, to model and predict the offset patterns in the environment. This Predictive Offset Model (POM) learns to forecast the offsets for the next time step, given the past offset sequence. This can be used to correct the agent's perception of the environment, and improve its performance in the face of non-stationarity.
CONTROLS: POM will be compared to the offset correction methods in OCQ-Learning and COT, as well as a baseline that uses random offset forecasting.
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: We expect POM to provide accurate predictions of offset patterns, allowing the agent to adapt and correct its perception more effectively, and lead to better performance in both training and test environments. However, its performance may be affected by the complexity and stationarity of the offset patterns.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Discovering Stationary Components in a Time-Varying State Representation
PROPOSAL: 
We propose to utilize Independent Component Analysis (ICA) to extract stationary components from the observation function, while treating the episode-wide offsets as non-stationary. This decomposition can help the model learn the time-invariant parts of the environment, potentially mitigating the effect of offsets. The ICA model will be trained on the offline dataset in an unsupervised manner.
CONTROLS: This proposal will be implemented with the state-of-the-art FastICA algorithm and compared to results from k-means clustering for unsupervised dimensionality reduction.
COST: 400
PREDICTION:  We expect the ICA-based model to succeed in discovering robust state representations but may fail if the offsets are highly correlated with the observed states, as the ICA may incorrectly attribute both to a single stationary component.

TITLE: Map-based State Estimation with Virtual Sensors
PROPOSAL: 
We propose the implementation of a map-based state estimation method that utilizes virtual sensors to track the cumulative effect of time-varying offsets across episodes. This approach constructs a map of the environment in a landmark-based representation, associating each landmark with a learned virtual sensor that attempts to estimate its true position and the accumulated offset in each episode. The model will be trained offline to learn when and how the offsets introduce systematic errors in the state representation.
CONTROLS: This proposal will be tested with a range of virtual sensor types, including Kalman filters and machine learning-based estimation, and benchmarked against the TAR-based and ICA-based models, to assess the feasibility and effectiveness of this novel approach.
COST: 834
PREDICTION: We expect the map-based state estimation method to work well for obstacle-rich environments with clear landmarks but may fail if the offsets are highly correlated with the environmental features, causing the virtual sensors to incorrectly adjust tracking.

TITLE: Transfer Learning from Similar Environments
PROPOSAL: 
For environments where similar non-stationary patterns are observed or expected, we propose transferring knowledge from an offline dataset collected in a source environment with known offset patterns to an online environment with partially or completely unknown offset patterns. This will be achieved through transfer learning and fine-tuning techniques, allowing for adapting the pre-trained model to the new target environment.
CONTROLS: We will explore different transfer learning strategies (e.g., using source domain's dataset to pre-train, domain adaptation or multi-task learning) and assess the effect of model adaptation on non-stationarity handling across domains with varying offset profiles.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: We expect the transfer learning approach to expedite adaptation to new environments with similar offset patterns, but it may fail if the offset distributions in the source and target environments are significantly dissimilar, resulting in knowledge that does not generalize effectively.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Robust Transfer Learning: Handling Out-of-Distribution Offset Distributions
PROPOSAL: 
To improve the robustness and adaptability of transfer learning in handling varying offset distributions across environments, we propose incorporating data augmentation techniques that explicitly simulate out-of-distribution offset patterns and outlier robust estimation methods during the source domain's dataset collection and transformation process. This will enhance the model's ability to generalize and serve as a more robust proxy for the unknown offset distributions in the target domain.
CONTROLS: We will apply and compare several data augmentation strategies (e.g., simulated additive noise or sudden changes in offset values) to the source domain's data, along with different outlier detection and robust estimation techniques, to gauge their effects on model performance in out-of-distribution offset scenarios.
COST: 2332.8
PREDICTION: We expect the revised transfer learning approach to show significant improvement in its ability to adapt to environments with out-of-training-distribution offset patterns; however, the enhanced complexity may lead to additional training difficulties if insufficient data is available to effectively capture the diversity of possible offset patterns.

These datasets should cover diverse shifting behaviors, signal-to-noise characteristics, and correlated or uncorrelated offset variations, thereby emulating complex real-world conditions in a controlled manner.

PREDICTION: We expect the synthetic dataset generation to significantly streamline the evaluation process for all non-stationary state estimation and transfer learning methods, aiding in accelerated research but may be computationally resource-heavy if it involves completely sampling novel up-to-date offset patterns and phenomena, potentially outweighing the deployment efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Offset Recovery through Temporal Differentiation
PROPOSAL: We design an agent who estimates the per-episode offset using differences in observations across multiple time-steps: the derivative of observation w.r.t. time. To be more robust, we average derivatives over several time-steps, using a sliding window. The agent trains offline on stationary data to learn the observation dynamics, then at test-time it estimates the offset at each time-step by taking the derivative of each dimension's observation.
CONTROLS: Zero-shot learning baseline (uses only offline data to estimate state space reward), No Offsets baseline (does not account for offsets during test-time), Differentiation w/o Sliding Window (uses no sliding window for averaging derivatives)
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: The sliding window helps recovery of complex, abrupt offsets, and the method should perform close to No Offsets for some easier patterns, such as additive noise or periodic offsets.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: BISTRO: Adversarial Bilevel Learning for Online Offset Correction
PROPOSAL: We propose BISTRO, which jointly trains a state estimator and an offset predictor using bilevel optimization. The state estimator, which handles the stationary transition dynamics, is parameterized using a standard offline RL model (e.g., BCQ). The offset predictor, which is a separate model that uses observations from each episode, aims to minimize the difference between the predicted state and true state, while also learning a representation of the offset that minimizes state estimation bias at the level of episode-specific predictions. We estimate the true state through a proxy by measuring the divergence between predicted and true state under perturbations, where the perturbations are estimated by differentiating observations as described in Online Offset Recovery through Temporal Differentiation (proposed earlier).
CONTROLS: Online Offset Recovery through Temporal Differentiation, Epsilon Constrained BCQ: standard BCQ with additive epsilon bias correction, CLIP+Adversarial Perturbations: learns multiple offline agent's distributions with a KL divergence objective circa 2 that tries to produce unseen seqeunces of outliers
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: BISTRO is expected to accurately learn offsets when sufficient data is available, showing improved generalization and reproducing various real-world scenarios of offsets. Possible failure: notable state estimation bias when negative transfer from stationary RL is significant or the parameters learned from BCE objective with episodes become dissimilar.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Particle Filter-Based Online Offset Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach for online offset estimation using a particle filter. The particle filter represents the uncertainty in the observation function by means of a set of particles, each of which represents a potential observation function. The particles are propagated through time using a forward filtering step, and the weights of the particles are updated using a backward smoothing step. At each time step, the particles are resampled to preserve the most informative particles. We use the particle filter to estimate the offset by weighting the particles based on their likelihood of producing the observed measurements. This approach allows for robust online offset estimation in the presence of measurement noise and uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Temporally Consistent Hann Window Offset Estimation, Online Offset Recovery through Temporal Differentiation, Particle Filter without Resampling (particle filter without resampling step)
COST: 14080
PREDICTION: The particle filter-based approach is expected to provide robust online offset estimation in scenarios with high measurement noise and uncertainty, especially in applications where the offset patterns change frequently. Possible failure: if the number of particles is not sufficient, the particle filter may not accurately capture the uncertainty in the observation function.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Agent Offset Estimation for Cooperative Robot Systems
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach for multi-agent offset estimation in cooperative robot systems. Each robot learns to estimate the offset of its own observation function using an online learning algorithm, such as the particle filter-based approach. The robots also communicate with each other to share their estimates and improve the overall estimation accuracy. We use a Bayesian consensus algorithm to fuse the estimates from each robot, taking into account the uncertainty in each robot's estimate. This approach allows for robust multi-agent offset estimation in cooperative robot systems, where the agents need to adapt to changing environments and communicate with each other.
CONTROLS: Particle Filter-Based Online Offset Estimation (single-agent), Temporally Consistent Hann Window Offset Estimation (single-agent), Multi-Agent Consensus without Bayesian Consensus (simple consensus algorithm without considering uncertainty)
COST: 16560
PREDICTION: The multi-agent offset estimation approach is expected to improve the accuracy of offset estimation in cooperative robot systems, especially in scenarios where the agents need to adapt to changing environments and communicate with each other. Possible failure: if the Bayesian consensus algorithm is not accurately implemented, it may lead to reduced performance or instability in the system.

TITLE: Particle Filter-Based Online Offset Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach for online offset estimation using a particle filter. The particle filter represents the uncertainty in the observation function by means of a set of particles, each of which represents a potential observation function. The particles are propagated through time using a forward filtering step, and the weights of the particles are updated using a backward smoothing step. At each time step, the particles are resampled to preserve the most informative particles. We use the particle filter to estimate the offset by weighting the particles based on their likelihood of producing the observed measurements. This approach allows for robust online offset estimation in the presence of measurement noise and uncertainty.

COST: 42500

Possible failure: if the number of particles is not sufficient, the particle filter may not accurately capture the uncertainty in the observation function.

CONTROLS: Baselines: standard offline RL and the stochastic model-based offline RL approach. Ablations: different combinations of the individual components.

PREDICTION: This comprehensive model will exhibit improved robustness and adaptability in handling non-stationary environments, but may require careful tuning of the multiple components and model hyperparameters.

TITLE: Temporally-Ordered, Task-Agnostic Estimation of Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: Design a simple yet efficient algorithm to estimate the unknown time-varying offsets by analyzing the statistical properties of a sequence of clean, fully observable training data without assuming any specific distribution for the offsets, exploiting the property that the clean data is temporally ordered.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be performed with and without partial access to past offsets to understand if and when omitting this information hinders estimation.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: This algorithm should be able to accurately estimate offsets from the training data sequence for synthetic series with an independent but not necessarily identically distributed, non-Markovian pattern, but may not work as well when the true pattern cannot be inferred from the training data; robustness to large shifts within an episode will also be a concern.

PROPOSAL: Investigate methods to extract and utilize useful information from limited past offset values, without making strong assumptions about the pattern of evolution, for guiding online adaptation through relatively simple decision-making mechanisms, exploiting the property of fixed shifts within an episode.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Benchmarking of Visual Interleaving Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of visual interleaving reasoning using a modified version of the CoT architecture (PaLM-E) on a set of challenging visual reasoning tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving and instruction-based image editing. We will evaluate model performance on these tasks using metrics such as jigsaw accuracy and instruction-based edit quality, and compare it to the performance of a text-only CoT baseline.
CONTROLS: Text-only CoT baseline on the same tasks and data, and a visually-grounded CoT baseline (e.g., ViLT) which uses separate visual and text components but doesn't interleave them.
COST: 16,560
PREDICTION: We expect to find that visual interleaving reasoning significantly outperforms the text-only baseline, but may struggle with tasks requiring high-level spatial reasoning. An unexpected finding could be that the visually-grounded CoT baseline performs surprisingly well, indicating potential for visual representation improvements in those models.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improved Training Stability through Simulated Visual Reasoning Steps
PROPOSAL: To address training instability in visual interleaving models, we will simulate shorter visual reasoning steps using data augmentation techniques such as spatial warping and inpainting, to create "negative" visual inputs that mimic the effects of longer visual processing chains. We will train the CoT model on these simulated visual steps, as well as real visual inputs, and evaluate its performance on the simulated steps as well as real-world tasks.
CONTROLS: The same visual interleaving model trained without simulated steps, and a model trained with a more standard architecture that doesn't capture visual information.
COST: 40,000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that adding simulated visual steps to the training data significantly improves training stability and convergence, and that the model's ability to perform well on the simulated steps is correlated with its ability to perform well on real-world tasks. However, the fixed data augmentation methods might fail to capture the full complexity of visual interleaving, leading to suboptimal performance.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Autoregressive Visual Reasoning with Recursive Predictive Coding
PROPOSAL: To alleviate the computational burden of autoregressive visual reasoning, we will incorporate recursive predictive coding into the visual encoder, learning to compress and represent intermediate visual states as probabilistic latent variables. This approach will enable the model to reason about visual changes in a more hierarchical and efficient manner, reducing the quadratic cost of autoregressive generation.
CONTROLS: The same visual interleaving model without recursive predictive coding, and a model using a non-autoregressive visual encoder.
COST: 60,000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that including recursive predictive coding significantly reduces the sequence length and computational cost of visual reasoning, enabling the model to reason about complex visual scenes more efficiently. However, the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies and complex visual transformations might be diminished, leading to suboptimal performance in certain tasks.

PROPOSAL: We will modify the real-world benchmarking experiment to evaluate the visual interleaving model's performance across multiple tasks, including reasoning-driven text-to-image generation, instruction-based image editing, and jigsaw puzzle solving. To account for the cross-task generalizability, we will use a multi-task learning setup where the model learns to balance the objectives across tasks simultaneously.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visual Interleaving through Self-Supervised Visual-Linguistic Alignment
PROPOSAL: We will introduce a self-supervised loss function that encourages the visual interleaving model to align its generated visual and textual outputs. Specifically, we will use a masked language model objective to predict the text and visual tokens of the previous steps given the current step's outputs. By aligning the visual and textual representations in a self-supervised manner, we aim to improve the model's ability to reason about visual changes through text.
CONTROLS: The same visual interleaving model without self-supervised visual-linguistic alignment, and a model using a non-alignment based self-supervised objective.
COST: 73,440
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the self-supervised visual-linguistic alignment significantly improves the model's ability to reason about visual changes through text, and enhances its performance on visually-intensive tasks. We will train the CoT model on these simulated visual steps, as well as real visual inputs, and evaluate its performance on the simulated steps as well as real-world tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: MUlti-Modal Chain-Of-Thought (MuCoT) Model 
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel transformer architecture, MuCoT, that simultaneously generates textual logic and visual state transitions through an efficient multi-modal attention mechanism. MuCoT consists of two sub-modules: a text-encoder that generates intermediate reasoning steps, and a visual-encoder that produces and updates visual state transitions. The interaction between the two modules is facilitated through a novel symmetric multi-modal attention mechanism, allowing for fast and efficient inference.
CONTROLS: Compare to baseline performances of standard transformer models and separately trained text-generating and visual-generating models.
COST: 2400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MuCoT should significantly outperform existing approaches on reasoning-intensive tasks, such as instruction-based image editing and jigsaw puzzle solving, with a notable improvement in coherent visual transitions. However, it may struggle with tasks requiring a large number of image generations due to the increased computational burden.

TITLE: MUlti-Modal Chain-Of-Thought (MuCoT) Model 
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel transformer architecture, MuCoT, that simultaneously generates textual logic and visual state transitions through an efficient multi-modal attention mechanism. MuCoT consists of two sub-modules: a text-encoder that generates intermediate reasoning steps, and a visual-encoder that produces and updates visual state transitions. The interaction between the two modules is facilitated through a novel symmetric multi-modal attention mechanism, allowing for fast and efficient inference.
CONTROLS: Compare to baseline performances of standard transformer models and separately trained text-generating and visual-generating models.

However, it may struggle with tasks requiring a large number of image generations due to the increased computational burden.
