ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Hierarchical Visual-Text Flow
PROPOSAL: We will investigate an hierarchical approach to MLLMs that aggregates visual and textual features at different levels of abstractions using attentions and self-attention mechanisms. This hierarchical flow will enable efficient reasoning by progressively down-sampling the spatial resolution of intermediate visual representations and thereby reducing the number of visual tokens. Additionally, this flow will allow for various fusion mechanisms to combine visual and textual features at different scales, thereby tightly integrating multi-modal reasoning.
CONTROLS: Comparison to a standard autoregressive MLLM, an MLLM without hierarchical flow, and an MLLM with a simplified single-level multi-modal reasoning process.
COST: 10500
PREDICTION: If successful, this approach may significantly reduce the cost of training multi-modal chain-of-thought models and achieve comparable or improved performance on reasoning-intensive tasks. However, it may struggle to handle tasks requiring fine-grained visual manipulation, as the hierarchical flow may fail to preserve low-level visual details.

TITLE: Masked Autoencoding with Visuotextual Consistency Regularization
PROPOSAL: We will introduce a new regularization technique that leverages Masked Autoencoding (MAE) to encourage multi-modal models to generate consistent and accurate intermediate visual representations, even when the input is corrupted or masked. This regularization will be applied through a visuotextual consistency loss that enforces the model to correctly predict the masked visual tokens and maintain logical coherence in the textual reasoning.
CONTROLS: Training and evaluation of the model with and without this regularization, as well as an ablation study to evaluate the effect of different masking strategies and loss weights.
COST: 15120
PREDICTION: This approach may improve the stability and robustness of multi-modal chain-of-thought models by encouraging consistent and accurate visual representations, but its effectiveness may depend on the specific task and dataset used, and may not provide significant improvements for tasks with simple visual manipulation.

PROPOSAL: We will revise our hierarchical approach to incorporate weak-label learning mechanisms, allowing the model to learn from weakly annotated visual data and adapt to new tasks with minimal supervision. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmenting Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Human Feedback
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of human feedback to augment and enhance the performance of multi-modal chain-of-thought models. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tractable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Layout-Based Image Manipulation
PROPOSAL: Propose a tractable approach to CoT reasoning by limiting the model's reasoning space to a set of predefined layout templates. At each step, the model generates a textual intermediate and an image manipulation action (e.g., crop, rotate, resize) to modify the initial image. The image manipulation actions are used to create a layout that guides the reasoning process. We will evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on reasoning-intensive tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving and instruction-based image editing.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard text-image transformer and a diploVPN-COLOR network.
COST: 1364.7
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in reasoning-intensive tasks, with a notable reduction in training and inference times. However, the model may struggle with tasks requiring a high degree of visual creativity, leading to a slight decrease in performance.
PREDICTION POSSIBLE FAILURE: Difficulty in selecting an optimal set of layout templates, leading to the model getting stuck in a suboptimal reasoning path.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Multi-Modal Reasoning with Hierarchical Attention
PROPOSAL: We refine the hierarchical attention mechanism in proposal 2 to incorporate a more adaptive and task-agnostic method of splitting the reasoning process. The model learns to dynamically learn a reasoning graph during training, rather than using a fixed hierarchy, by incorporating a differentiable graph construction module. This allows the model to adapt to the specific task requirements and complexity of the visual input.
CONTROLS: Retain comparison to existing models (1, 3, and 4), but add analysis on the benefits of adaptive graph construction and its impact on model performance and training stability.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: By using adaptive graph construction, we expect the refined hierarchical attention mechanism to improve performance on tasks that require reasoning about complex and dynamic visual scenes, such as visual question answering and jigsaw puzzle solving, while also reducing the training costs and improving the model's generalizability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning through Attention Modulation
PROPOSAL: We propose the introduction of a learnable attention modulation mechanism, conditioned on both textual and visual inputs, to control the aggregation of cross-modal information. This allows our model to selectively focus on relevant interactions between language and vision at each step, thereby reducing the effective sequence length and alleviating the training instability.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing models that use fixed attention mechanisms or separate image and text generators.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect this to improve performance on tasks that require comprehensive and coherent visual state transitions, such as jigsaw puzzle solving and navigation, but may struggle with tasks that demand localized visual operations, such as instruction-based image editing, due to its global reasoning nature.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modal Reasoning with Hierarchical Attention
PROPOSAL: To tackle the computational burden of long multi-modal reasoning chains, we introduce a hierarchical attention mechanism that recursively splits the reasoning process into smaller sub-steps, allowing for a more localized attention focus. This hierarchical structure enables the model to selectively focus on specific sub-problems and reduces the quadratic growth in sequence length.
CONTROLS: Ablation study comparing the hierarchical attention mechanism to the unified multi-modal reasoning model (1) and a baseline model using standard autoregressive attention.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that this hierarchical attention mechanism will significantly reduce training costs and enable faster inference times, making it a more practical solution for real-world applications, while maintaining comparable performance on reasoning-intensive tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning through Attention Modulation
PROPOSAL: We refine the initial attention modulation mechanism to incorporate a Switch-only Transformer architecture, which dynamically selects between two transformer layers based on the relevance of textual and visual input, and uses a fixed cross-modal attention mechanism between them. This allows the model to adaptively allocate attention to textual and visual reasoning when necessary, reducing the overhead of joint multimodal processing.
CONTROLS: Retain comparison to existing models (1), but add ablation studies on the role of the Switch-only Transformer and fixed cross-modal attention in the modified model.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: By controlling the attention switches and fixed cross-modal attention, we expect the modified model to exhibit improved performance on tasks requiring both local and global reasoning, such as instruction-based image editing and landscape generation from topographic contour maps. However, it may still face challenges on tasks involving extensive visual operations, such as jigsaw puzzle solving and navigation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Egocentric Gaze augmentation for MLLMs in Proactive AI Assistants
PROPOSAL: Train a MLLM (e.g. Unified Transformer) on egocentric video datasets (e.g. Ego4D, EPIC-Kitchens) with gaze data augmentation, using a pre-trained gaze estimation model (e.g. Room Gaze) to simulate gaze signals for frames without real gaze data. Evaluate the model's performance on an egocentric video question answering benchmark (e.g. Habits-GQA, Absent-Mindedness), with a control condition where gaze augmentation is disabled.
CONTROLS: 
- Control baseline with MLLM trained on egocentric video without gaze augmentation
- Ablation study removing the pre-trained gaze estimation model from the augmentation procedure
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Improved performance on the egocentric video question answering benchmark, especially on tasks that require gaze-conditioned reasoning. However, the model might struggle with uncertainty or noise in the gaze augmentation procedure, leading to decreased performance in scenarios with inaccurate or missing gaze signals.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gaze-MLLM Interactions in Proactive AI Assistants
PROPOSAL: Implement gaze-specific visual tokens in the MLLM's input sequence, redirecting gaze attention to specific objects or regions within the egocentric video frames. This will examine how MLLMs integrate gaze information into their visual processing pipeline, focusing on the model's ability to recognize gaze-conditioned objects, actions, or intentions. The performance of this modified model will be evaluated on the egocentric video question answering benchmark, with a control condition maintaining the standard visual tokens used in typical MLLMs.
CONTROLS: 
- Control baseline using standard visual tokens in the MLLM
- Ablation study removing specific visual tokens that only redirect gaze attention to objects or regions
COST: 1656
PREDICTION: The model with gaze-specific visual tokens will outperform the standard visual tokens in tasks requiring attention to specific objects or actions in the egocentric video. However, the results might also reveal over-reliance on gaze cues in scenarios with ambiguity or noise, illustrating the need for gaze-informed multimodal reasoning in future improvements.

- Ablation study disabling adversarial attack defenses
- Comparison with existing state-of-the-art adversarial attack and defense methods

However, potential exposure of sensitive user data in response to successful attacks could serve as a challenge for the overall applicability and trustworthiness of gaze-informed MLLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Egocentric Gaze in EGOT (Every Day, Everyday, Enriched with Tags) Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a benchmarking experiment on the EGOT dataset, which is designed for evaluating egocentric video QA models on everyday scenarios with tags providing episodic memory, scene layout analysis, and scene-text understanding. We will evaluate the performance of the state-of-the-art egocentric video QA model, CLIP-VL, with and without access to gaze information. We will use a gaze tracker to obtain eye movements during video playback and use this information to simulate gaze-based reasoning. We will measure the model's performance on QA tasks involving scene layout, scene-text, and episodic memory.
CONTROLS: CLIP-VL as the baseline without gaze information, ablation study for different gaze simulation settings.
COST: 332.5
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating gaze information will improve the model's performance on QA tasks, especially those related to scene-text understanding. However, this gain may be limited by the accuracy of the gaze tracker, and we expect that the model's performance may degrade with inaccurate or unavailable gaze signals.

However, this gain may be offset by overfitting to the pre-training task, and we expect that the model's performance may degrade with increasing pre-training duration.

PROPOSAL: In the context of the previous proposal, expand the scope to account for (i) our results indicating that gaze-grounding might be an effective strategy; now evaluate how gaze-grounding interacts with gaze data as additional input, potentially uncovering synergy, redundancy, or even limitations in employing both methods to understand user intent.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: BERT large with egocentric gaze data (already identified in proposal 1), Baseline 2: RoBERTa large with gaze-grounded visual tokens ( proposal 2), Baseline 3: BERT large with both egocentric gaze data and gaze-grounded visual tokens.
COST: 2880
PREDICTION: We anticipate that combining gaze data with gaze-grounded visual tokens may further improve MLLMs' ability to recognize user intent, especially when distinguishing between primary and secondary user focuses; however, it might also expose trade-offs between this performance improvement and increased model complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Egocentric Gaze Cues for User Intent Understanding
PROPOSAL: 
To begin, we will experiment with the current state-of-the-art egocentric video language model, ImageGLU [1], trained on the f-dollar offline dataset [2] for egocentric video question answering. We will compare the performance of the model with and without gaze information from an external eye-tracking system. Controls will include a standard ImageGLU model without gaze, a model fine-tuned with gaze information, and the current state-of-the-art egocentric video question answering model, PCL-GAT [3]. 
CONTROLS: ImageGLU baseline, ImageGLU with gaze, PCL-GAT
COST: 26.7
PREDICTION: We expect to see an improvement in question answering accuracy when using gaze information, especially for questions probing user intent, but the benefit may be diminished if the gaze signal is noisy or inaccurately tracked.

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.14484 (ImageGLU)
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.09435 (f-dollar offline dataset)
[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15463 (PCL-GAT)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking Egocentric Video Models with Gaze
PROPOSAL: 
Next, we propose a large-scale evaluation on a new egocentric video question answering benchmark with gaze information, leveraging real-world egocentric video data from the DuARTE [4] dataset, an egocentric action dataset featuring diverse user actions. Our new benchmark, Egocentric-AugQA, consists of approximately 300,000 questions on actions, object manipulation, and location. We will assess the performance of ImageGLU and other top-ranked egocentric video models with and without gaze information on this new benchmark. Controls will include the standard EgQA benchmark [5] without gaze and our new Egocentric-AugQA benchmark with gaze.
CONTROLS: ImageGLU on EgQA (w/o gaze), ImageGLU on Egocentric-AugQA (with gaze), Egocentric-AugQA (with gaze)
COST: 83.4
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the Egocentric-AugQA benchmark will demonstrate that models that use gaze information tend to outperform those without gaze and help uncover biases in the data that impact user intent understanding.

[4] https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2020/hash/1627ec739b3729d2ea0ddcacd19dffed-Abstract.html (DuARTE dataset)
[5] https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/2020.acl-main.232/ (EgQA benchmark)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Transfer and Robustness of Gaze-Enhanced Egocentric Models
PROPOSAL: 
We'll leverage our large-scale Egocentric-AugQA benchmark to investigate the transferability and robustness of image and language understanding in gaze-enhanced egocentric video models. Specifically, we'll study the generalizability of these models by training them on a subset of the DuARTE dataset and evaluating them on other datasets, such as the Charades-EGO [6] and EgoGesture [7] datasets. We'll also simulate gaze signal inaccuracies or failures by randomly occluding gaze data, introducing artificial gaze uncertainty, or intentionally 'lurking' gaze-inferred instructions away from the specific question conditioning action-along different hour. Measures will include metrics such as zero-shot transfer learning, transductive alignment and robustness toward gaze inaccuracies and lag.
CONTROLS: Results for standard and gaze-enhanced ImageGLU on other egocentric video datasets, baseline results without gaze information

To begin, we will experiment with the current state-of-the-art egocentric video language model, ImageGLU [1], trained on the f-dollar offline dataset [2] for egocentric video question answering. We will compare the performance of the model with and without gaze information from an external eye-tracking system. Controls will include a standard ImageGLU model without gaze, a model fine-tuned with gaze information, and the current state-of-the-art egocentric video question answering model, PCL-GAT [3].

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking Egocentric Video Models with Gaze
PROPOSAL: 
Next, we propose a large-scale evaluation on a new egocentric video question answering benchmark with gaze information, leveraging real-world egocentric video data from the DuARTE [4] dataset, an egocentric action dataset featuring diverse user actions. Our new benchmark, Egocentric-AugQA, consists of approximately 300,000 questions on actions, object manipulation, and location. We will assess the performance of ImageGLU and other top-ranked egocentric video models with and without gaze information on this new benchmark. Controls will include the standard EgQA benchmark [5] without gaze and our new Egocentric-AugQA benchmark with gaze.

PREDICTION: We anticipate that the Egocentric-AugQA benchmark will demonstrate that models that use gaze information tend to outperform those without gaze and help uncover biases in the data that impact user intent understanding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Gradient Interference in Modality-Shared AR UMMs using Synthetic Text-Image Pairs
PROPOSAL: We experiment with a controlled setup using publicly available synthetic text-image datasets (e.g., CocoCaptions  dataset) to analyze the gradient interference between text and image modalities in a shared AR UMM. We use the recent BARON-LM model  as our AR UMM baseline, and perform a layer-wise ablation to identify the depth at which modality conflicts emerge, as well as the magnitude of these conflicts by calculating the cosine similarity between text and image gradients in each layer.
CONTROLS: We compare our findings to the 100-Shot BERT  (bert-base-uncased) which lacks modality sharing, and also use a text only variant of BARON-LM  (BARON-LM-no-image) to control for potential regularization effects due to the presence of modality sharing.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We expect significant gradient interference in layers preceding the abstract/semantic representation, contributing to performance degradation when modality sharing is used; the cosine similarity should also reveal a layer-wise pattern of conflict intensity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Discretization Schemes on Gradient Interference in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We extend the analysis in proposal 1 to investigate the effect of different discretization schemes on gradient interference. We experiment with three text-image discretization methods: (1) CLIP (Con condensed Language Image Paths)  pixel values, (2) COCO object tags, and (3) simple binarization strategies (e.g., toying- signature vectors). We use the BARON-LM  model and calculate the cosine similarity between text and image gradients in each layer, focusing on the regimes in which each discretization scheme is most effective.
CONTROLS: In addition to the controls from proposal 1 (100-Shot BERT  and BARON-LM-no-image), we also compare our discretization schemes to a noisy constant baseline to assess the impact of information loss in discretization.
COST: 3368
PREDICTION: We predict different levels of gradient interference across the three discretization schemes, with CLIP pixel values likely to produce the most favorable outcomes due to its adaptability to both modalities.

PROPOSAL: To better understand how modality-specific information is encoded in the AR UMM, we analyze the layer-wise behavior of the text and image embeddings, tracking their separation and similarity throughout the network. We use the BARON-LM  model and apply t-SNE visualization on the text and image embeddings at multiple depths, comparing the similarity and separation between these embeddings across various layers.
CONTROLS: We also compare our findings to the LRUK-ratzek universal, cross-task ,large vision transformer (epoch_X_inv_ac) .

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Gradient Interference in Modality-Shared AR UMMs using Synthetic Text-Image Pairs
PROPOSAL: We experiment with a controlled setup using publicly available synthetic text-image datasets (e.g., CocoCaptions  dataset) to analyze the gradient interference between text and image modalities in a shared AR UMM. We use the recent BARON-LM model  as our AR UMM baseline, and perform a layer-wise ablation to identify the depth at which modality conflicts emerge, as well as the magnitude of these conflicts by calculating the cosine similarity between text and image gradients in each layer.
CONTROLS: We compare our findings to the 100-Shot BERT  (bert-base-uncased) which lacks modality sharing, and also use a text only variant of BARON-LM  (BARON-LM-no-image) to control for potential regularization effects due to the presence of modality sharing.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: We expect significant gradient interference in layers preceding the abstract/semantic representation, contributing to performance degradation when modality sharing is used; the cosine similarity should also reveal a layer-wise pattern of conflict intensity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Discretization Schemes on Gradient Interference in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We extend the analysis in proposal 1 to investigate the effect of different discretization schemes on gradient interference. We experiment with three text-image discretization methods: (1) CLIP (Con condensed Language Image Paths)  pixel values, (2) COCO object tags, and (3) simple binarization strategies (e.g., toying- signature vectors). We use the BARON-LM  model and calculate the cosine similarity between text and image gradients in each layer, focusing on the regimes in which each discretization scheme is most effective.
CONTROLS: In addition to the controls from proposal 1 (100-Shot BERT  and BARON-LM-no-image), we also compare our discretization schemes to a noisy constant baseline to assess the impact of information loss in discretization.
COST: 10080
PREDICTION: We predict different levels of gradient interference across the three discretization schemes, with CLIP pixel values likely to produce the most favorable outcomes due to its adaptability to both modalities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Layer-wise Analysis of Modality-Specific Embeddings in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: To better understand how modality-specific information is encoded in the AR UMM, we analyze the layer-wise behavior of the text and image embeddings, tracking their separation and similarity throughout the network. We use the BARON-LM  model and apply t-SNE visualization on the text and image embeddings at multiple depths, comparing the similarity and separation between these embeddings across various layers.
CONTROLS: We also compare our findings to the LRUK-ratzek universal, cross-task ,large vision transformer (epoch_X_inv_ac) .
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: We expect a clear separation between text and image embeddings in early layers (i.e., before the semantic/abstract representation), indicating a robust encoding of modality-specific information, with the separation decreasing in later layers, harmonizing with the neural network depth-before- width hypothesis  potentially leading to convergence toward shared abstract representations.

TITLE: JoHNN: A Joint Optimization Framework for Reducing Gradient Interference in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel joint optimization framework, JoHNN, that adaptively adjusts the learning rate of each modality to reduce gradient interference. JoHNN incorporates a variability-aware cost regularization term that maintains modality-specific information while optimizing for a shared objective. We present a detailed algorithm for implementing JoHNN with existing AR UMMs and demonstrate its benefits in improving performance and reducing training instability on real-world tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering on top of text-to-image synthesis.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revising JoHNN: A Joint Optimization Framework for Reducing Gradient Interference in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We refine the JoHNN optimization framework to incorporate a more adaptive and efficient mechanism for adjusting the learning rate of each modality. This revised framework, referred to as r-JoHNN, utilizes a novel modality-aware parameter schedule that dynamically adjusts the learning rate based on a modality-specific curvature metric. We demonstrate the efficacy of r-JoHNN on a range of real-world tasks, including text-to-image synthesis, image captioning, and visual question answering, showcasing its ability to improve model performance and stability.
CONTROLS: The revised r-JoHNN framework is compared against the baseline AR UMM, as well as the original JoHNN framework, to assess the impact of the revised learning rate adjustment mechanism.
COST: 11340
PREDICTION: We expect r-JoHNN to outperform both the original JoHNN and the baseline AR UMM on most tasks, with a noticeable improvement in model stability and convergence speed. However, we anticipate potential challenges in adapting r-JoHNN to datasets with highly varying modality-specific complexities.

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Modality-Specific Token Embeddings on Gradient Conflicts
PROPOSAL: In parallel to proposal 1, extend the modality-shared AR UMM to use modality-specific token embeddings, and compare its performance on CLEVR and COCO datasets in terms of convergence speed, token prediction accuracy, and style consistency, against a baseline of shared embeddings.

COST: 14000
PREDICTION: Expected to observe decreased inter-modal conflict and faster convergence when using modality-specific embeddings, at the cost of increased model capacity and computational requirements, but with inconsistent improvements across tasks.

TITLE: Exposing Inter-Modal Statistical Conflicts in Discretized Image Tokens and Text Sequences
PROPOSAL: Develop a statistical mixture model (e.g., Gaussian Mixture Model) to contrast the probability distribution of next-token emissions in text sequences with those of discretized image tokens, and estimate the degree of statistical compatibility between the two modalities, as evaluated by measures such as compatibility score and maximum likelihood ratio.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gradient Conflicts in Modality-Sharing AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Experiment 1: Analyze the effect of modality-specific token displacements on gradient conflicts in modality-shared AR UMMs trained on text-to-image benchmarks.
We will modify a publicly available AR UMM implementation (e.g., Pix2Seq) to introduce controlled modality-specific token displacements (e.g., mapping image tokens to their pixel neighborhoods) and measure their impacts on gradient conflicts using a proxy-supervised learning loss metric (e.g., gradient dot products).
CONTROLS: No displacements, and a different benchmark or modalities.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect significant gradient conflicts when token displacements are applied, and the loss metric reveals convergence instability. However, specific outcomes may depend on the scope and correlation of displacements, requiring further analysis of direct interference between textual and visual domains.

TITLE: Robust Training of Modality-Sharing AR UMMs via Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: Experiment 5: Investigate the effectiveness of knowledge distillation as a method for robustly training modality-sharing AR UMMs on text-to-image generation benchmarks (e.g., Coccipmaker).
We will train a teacher AR UMM to generate high-quality text-to-image outputs, and then use knowledge distillation to distill the teacher's knowledge into a student AR UMM that can learn to mitigate modality interference effects.
CONTROLS: 1) Training the student model without distillation; 2) Using different teacher models with varying levels of modality interference.
COST: 8340 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that knowledge distillation can significantly improve the robustness of the student model to modality interference, but may also introduce additional computational costs and require careful optimization of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Potential of Modality-Specific Expertise in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Experiment 7: Investigate the effectiveness of utilizing modality-specific expertise in AR UMMs to mitigate modality interference effects.
We will train separate models for visual and text understanding, and then explore different architectures for combining these models (e.g., concatenation, attention-based fusion) to integrate their expertise in a unified framework.
CONTROLS: Comparison to modality-shared models, and to a single model on a multi-modal task.
COST: 18300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that modality-specific expertise can significantly improve the performance of AR UMMs on multi-modal tasks, especially when the expertise is properly integrated through a suitable combination function; however, this may also introduce additional computational costs and model complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Audiovisual Hallucinations in Emotion Reasoning MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We conduct a large-scale experiment using the FER+ dataset which includes a broad range of affective states, and employs CLIP as the multimodal backbone to obtain image and text embeddings. We then measure the ,enumerate coherence between visually-grounded text descriptions in the FER+ captions and CLIP's image-text pairs, and term this evaluation metric "Captions-Coherence" (CC). We also measure performance on the EmoReact dataset, a video-of-interaction benchmark. We compare our models performance against FLAME, a popular baseline for multimodal emotion recognition.
CONTROLS: We include a series of ablations that modify CLIP's prompt templates or training objectives aimed at de-emphasizing hallucinations, as well as a random initialization ablation that controls for models stability. This will help us understand how our novel evaluation metric CC captures the changes in models behavior, and how rely-able it is compared to standard metrics.
COST: 53708.59
PREDICTION: By leveraging CLIP and source-aligned ablations, FLAME should show small but noticeable improvements in reducing hallucinations measured both by CC and EmoReact. Our extensive set of ablations should allow clear resolution of whether CC- and/or EmoReact-metric driven modifications are most effective in terms of hitting the gold standard (i.e f1 > 80).

TITLE: Investigating Text Priors in Audiovisual MLLMs: A Multitask Learning Approach
PROPOSAL: We explore whether multitask learning can mitigate the influence of text priors in audiovisual MLLMs on emotion recognition and description tasks. We propose a multi-task learning framework where MLLMs are trained on multiple tasks simultaneously, including a emotion-specific object recognition task, a sentiment analysis task, and the original emotion recognition and description tasks. By learning to distinguish between tasks and leveraging task-specific knowledge, we aim to reduce the influence of text priors and improve model performance and robustness.
CONTROLS: We compare our multitask learning approach against a single-task baseline, ablate the multitask learning framework by removing individual tasks, and measure the effect of task importance weights on model performance.
COST: 117600
PREDICTION: We expect that the multitask learning approach will improve model performance and reduce hallucinations, particularly on the emotion-specific object recognition task. However, multitask learning may also introduce additional challenges, such as increased model complexity and overfitting, which may compromise model performance on certain tasks.

TITLE: Region-wise Emotion Reasoning: Towards Grounded Emotion Understanding
PROPOSAL: We propose a region-wise emotion reasoning approach to improve grounded emotion understanding in MLLMs. We divide the input video into smaller regions and associate each region with a specific emotion label. We then train an MLLM to reason about emotions in each region, allowing the model to focus on relevant audiovisual cues. We evaluate our approach on the EmoReact dataset and compare it against a global emotion reasoning baseline.
CONTROLS: We ablate our region-wise emotion reasoning approach by removing the region division step and evaluating a model that reasons about emotions globally, while also comparing our approach against a baseline that focuses on a selected subset of regions.
COST: 200000
PREDICTION: We expect that the region-wise emotion reasoning approach will improve model performance and grounding, especially in scenarios where multiple emotions are present in the input video. However, it may also introduce computational overhead due to the increased number of regions and emotional labels.

TITLE: Evaluating Audiovisual Hallucinations in Emotion Reasoning MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We conduct a large-scale experiment using the FER+ dataset which includes a broad range of affective states, and employs CLIP as the multimodal backbone to obtain image and text embeddings. We then measure the ,enumerate coherence between visually-grounded text descriptions in the FER+ captions and CLIP's image-text pairs, and term this evaluation metric "Captions-Coherence" (CC). We also measure performance on the EmoReact dataset, a video-of-interaction benchmark. We compare our models performance against FLAME, a popular baseline for multimodal emotion recognition.
CONTROLS: We include a series of ablations that modify CLIP's prompt templates or training objectives aimed at de-emphasizing hallucinations, as well as a random initialization ablation that controls for models stability. This will help us understand how our novel evaluation metric CC captures the changes in models behavior, and how rely-able it is compared to standard metrics.
COST: 160000
PREDICTION: By leveraging CLIP and source-aligned ablations, FLAME should show small but noticeable improvements in reducing hallucinations measured both by CC and EmoReact. Our extensive set of ablations should allow clear resolution of whether CC- and/or EmoReact-metric driven modifications are most effective in terms of hitting the gold standard (i.e f1 > 80).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Text Priors in Audiovisual MLLMs: A Multitask Learning Approach
PROPOSAL: We explore whether multitask learning can mitigate the influence of text priors in audiovisual MLLMs on emotion recognition and description tasks. We propose a multi-task learning framework where MLLMs are trained on multiple tasks simultaneously, including a emotion-specific object recognition task, a sentiment analysis task, and the original emotion recognition and description tasks. By learning to distinguish between tasks and leveraging task-specific knowledge, we aim to reduce the influence of text priors and improve model performance and robustness.
CONTROLS: We compare our multitask learning approach against a single-task baseline, ablate the multitask learning framework by removing individual tasks, and measure the effect of task importance weights on model performance.
COST: 350000
PREDICTION: We expect that the multitask learning approach will improve model performance and reduce hallucinations, particularly on the emotion-specific object recognition task. However, multitask learning may also introduce additional challenges, such as increased model complexity and overfitting, which may compromise model performance on certain tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Region-wise Emotion Reasoning: Towards Grounded Emotion Understanding
PROPOSAL: We propose a region-wise emotion reasoning approach to improve grounded emotion understanding in MLLMs. We divide the input video into smaller regions and associate each region with a specific emotion label. We then train an MLLM to reason about emotions in each region, allowing the model to focus on relevant audiovisual cues. We evaluate our approach on the EmoReact dataset and compare it against a global emotion reasoning baseline.
CONTROLS: We ablate our region-wise emotion reasoning approach by removing the region division step and evaluating a model that reasons about emotions globally, while also comparing our approach against a baseline that focuses on a selected subset of regions.
COST: 600000
PREDICTION: We expect that the region-wise emotion reasoning approach will improve model performance and grounding, especially in scenarios where multiple emotions are present in the input video. However, it may also introduce computational overhead due to the increased number of regions and emotional labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Dataset Augmentation Approach to Mitigate Hallucinations in Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We propose a dataset augmentation approach to mitigate hallucinations in audiovisual MLLMs by injecting semantically diverse and realistic audiovisual perturbations into the training data. We generate perturbations that simulate the effects of noise, distortion, and artifact introduction to the audio and visual modalities. We evaluate our approach on both synthetic and real-world datasets and compare it against a baseline that uses standard data augmentation techniques.
CONTROLS: We ablate our approach by adding/removing different types of perturbations, experimenting with different augmentation rates, and comparing our approach against a baseline that uses a random data augmentation strategy.
COST: 900000
PREDICTION: We expect that our dataset augmentation approach will reduce hallucinations and improve model performance on tasks involving audiovisual inputs. However, it may also require careful tuning of the perturbation parameters to avoid over-augmentation and under-augmentation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Transfer Learning in Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We investigate the role of transfer learning in audiovisual emotion reasoning by pre-training an MLLM on a large-scale audiovisual dataset and then fine-tuning it on emotion reasoning tasks. We evaluate the transfer learning approach on the EmoReact dataset and compare it against a baseline that trains from scratch. We also analyze how different pre-training tasks and fine-tuning objectives affect the performance of the transfer learning approach.
CONTROLS: We ablate our transfer learning approach by removing the pre-training step, using a different pre-training task, or fine-tuning the model with different objectives.
COST: 1200000
PREDICTION: We expect that the transfer learning approach will improve model performance and reduce hallucinations, especially for smaller datasets. However, it may also introduce transfer learning error, where the pre-trained model has seen similar but non-relevant audiovisual cues, which can negatively impact performance.

TITLE: An Adversarial Attack and Defense Framework for Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial attack and defense framework to evaluate the robustness of audiovisual MLLMs to semantic data poisoning attacks. We develop a novel attack framework that generates adversarial examples by inserting targeted audiovisual hallucinations into the input data. We also design a defense framework that includes a robustness-aware training paradigm and a security layer to detect and mitigate the attacks. We evaluate our framework on the EmoReact dataset and compare it against a baseline that is vulnerable to attacks.
CONTROLS: We ablate our defense framework by removing the robustness-aware training paradigm or the security layer, and also compare our framework against a baseline that trains without any adversarial training.
COST: 2500000
PREDICTION: We expect that our adversarial attack and defense framework will significantly improve the robustness of audiovisual MLLMs to semantic data poisoning attacks, and will also provide a new tool for evaluating and improving the security of such models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Audovisual Emotion Reasoning Models with a Multimodal Fact-Checking Module
PROPOSAL: Design a multimodal fact-checking module that takes as input the output of the MLLM and checks for consistency with a set of pre-defined, multimodal facts about the input video (e.g., "speaker is male", "speaker is wearing a red shirt", " background music is calming", etc.). The module will be trained to output a credibility score for each of the MLLM's predictions, reflecting the likelihood that the prediction is grounded in fact, rather than hallucination.
CONTROLS: Baseline: pre-trained MLLM alone; Ablation: pre-trained MLLM without the fact-checking module; 
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The fact-checking module is expected to significantly reduce hallucination rates, especially for models that are prone to over-reliance on text priors. However, it may fail to capture subtle cases where the MLLM is making a correct inference based on contextual cues that are not explicitly mentioned in the input video.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Hallucinations in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition with EmoEGOS
PROPOSAL: We introduce EmoEGOS, a novel benchmark for audiovisual emotion recognition that focuses on evaluating hallucinations in emotion reasoning. EmoEGOS includes two tasks: (1) identifying irrelevant cues that are tied to emotion predictions, and (2) detecting fabricated cues that are not present in the input. EmoEGOS uses a pool of 500 audiovisual clips, each annotated with detailed information about relevant and irrelevant cues. We validate EmoEGOS on several state-of-the-art MLLMs, comparing their performance on EmoEGOS to their performance on the existing EmoReact and EmoBert benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to the state-of-the-art methods (e.g., C2T, QIAN et al. 2020) and ablate EmoEGOS by removing the task of identifying fabricated cues to evaluate its impact on overall performance.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect EmoEGOS to reveal that hallucinations are a significant issue in current audiovisual MLLMs, with performance degradation across the board. They might fail to scale well to large datasets, and also, as the MLLMs start seeing new data points they may adapt and fill the gaps in learning due to hallucinations. The EmoEGOS benchmark will provide a meaningful evaluation of audiovisual hallucination and give directions for further development and improvement in this community.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Large Language Model Regularization for Hallucination Control
PROPOSAL: We introduce a simple yet effective regularization technique for MLLMs to reduce hallucinations in audiovisual emotion recognition. Our method, called Disentangled Regularization (DR), is based on the principle of encouraging the model to allocate gradients to audio and visual cues separately. DR is applied as an additional loss term during training, and a two-stage training process is used to balance between regularity and accuracy. We validate DR on EmoEGOS and several state-of-the-art MLLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing hallucinations.
CONTROLS: We compare DR to existing methods such as contrastive learning and paid attention mechanisms, and ablate its components to evaluate its effectiveness.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: We expect DR to improve performance on EmoEGOS by around 10-15% compared to state-of-the-art MLLMs. However, we might see a slight performance drop on some datasets as a result of increased training complexity. Validating DR with larger MLLMs and diverse datasets would be essential for generalizing these results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Audiovisual Cue Saliency for Improved Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel post-processing technique to improve the emotion reasoning outputs of MLLMs. Our method, called Audiovisual Cue Saliency (ACS), computes a saliency score for each audiovisual cue by measuring its contribution to the model's confidence in the emotion prediction. ACS then uses these scores to filter out irrelevant cues and highlight the most informative cues. We demonstrate ACS's effectiveness on EmoEGOS and several state-of-the-art MLLMs, showing improved performance and transparency in emotion reasoning.
CONTROLS: We compare ACS to existing saliency methods and evaluate its performance on models with different architecture and sizes.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect ACS to improve performance on EmoEGOS by around 5-10% compared to state-of-the-art MLLMs. However, the ACS method may require tweaking the underlying emotion classification model to reach its full potential. Its impact might also be limited by overly complex models.

TITLE: Audiovisual Cue Saliency for Improved Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We revise the post-processing technique Audiovisual Cue Saliency (ACS) to dynamically adjust the model's output based on the saliency scores. This adaptation allows ACS to better capture the complex relationships between audiovisual cues and emotions, improving emotion reasoning performance.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised ACS to the original version and the state-of-the-art MLLMs with respect to their performance on EmoEGOS and human evaluation metrics.

PREDICTION: We expect the revised ACS to improve performance on EmoEGOS by around 15-20% compared to state-of-the-art MLLMs, but might require careful tuning of the hyperparameter N to avoid overfitting. Validation with larger and more diverse datasets will be necessary to confirm the robustness of the revised ACS method.

TITLE: Benchmarking Audiovisual Emotion Recognition with Real-World Videos on TV and Movie Clips
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new benchmark dataset, called TV&Movies, comprised of 2000 real-world video clips from popular TV shows and movies. TV&Movies includes diverse emotional expressions, complex audiovisual cues, and varying levels of noise and occlusion. We evaluate state-of-the-art MLLMs on TV&Movies using EmoEGOS, analyzing performance on various metrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall.
CONTROLS: We compare the results of MLLMs to those obtained on EmoEGOS and EmoReact, and assess the robustness of the models to variations in video quality and emotional expression.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect performance on TV&Movies to be significantly lower than on EmoEGOS, as MLLMs may struggle with real-world variations in audiovisual cues and emotional expressions. However, we anticipate that performance will be better than state-of-the-art methods that rely on simulated or limited datasets, providing new insights into the challenges of real-world audiovisual emotion recognition.

TITLE: Sparse Audiovisual Features for Noise-Robust Emotion Recognition
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel feature extraction method for audiovisual emotion recognition, called Selected Adaptive Features (SAF). SAF uses a sparse representation of audiovisual cues by selecting the most relevant dimensions from pre-trained models via an iterative learning process. We evaluate SAF on TV&Movies and EmoEGOS, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving noise robustness and reducing hallucinations in emotion recognition.
CONTROLS: We compare SAF to existing feature extraction methods and evaluate its performance on various noise levels and dataset sizes.

PREDICTION: We expect SAF to reduce hallucinations by around 20-25% compared to state-of-the-art MLLMs, and improve performance on TV&Movies by 10-15%. However, the SAF method might require additional computational resources to learn the optimal sparse feature representation, especially for larger models and datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Teacher-Student Learning for Hallucination-Aware Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel teacher-student learning framework for audiovisual emotion recognition, where a teacher model provides hallucination-aware guidance to a student model. The teacher model is trained on a subset of the data with explicit hallucination labels, while the student model is trained on the entire dataset. We evaluate the teacher-student learning framework on EmoEGOS and TV&Movies, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing hallucinations and improving emotion recognition performance.
CONTROLS: We compare the teacher-student learning framework to state-of-the-art MLLMs and ablate its components to evaluate its effectiveness.
COST: 6600
PREDICTION: We expect the teacher-student learning framework to reduce hallucinations by around 30-35% compared to state-of-the-art MLLMs, and improve performance on EmoEGOS and TV&Movies by 15-20%. However, the framework might be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to obtain optimal performance.

However, the OEGEO framework might be resource-intensive, requiring careful management of computational resources and data streaming.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: "Query-Agnostic Turn-Level Reward for Agentic Multi-Turn Search Agents"
PROPOSAL: Develop a learning framework based on Hindsight Experience Replay (HER), where the agent interacts with the environment and generates a sequence of rollsouts. Then, the agent selects a successful rollout where the final answer matches the ground truth and reweights the experience to consider rewards for all intermediate steps that contributed to the successful answer, but not for the unsuccessful ones. The selected successful rollout is replaced by a new rollout that is generated based on this reweighted experience.
CONTROLS: implementation of vanilla GRPO, data augmentation baseline, manually reweighted HER (i.e., putting hand-defined weights on the trajectory)
COST: 400
PREDICTION: Expected to improve sample efficiency and provide more informative rewards, but might fail to effectively distinguish productive from unproductive turns due to its reliance on successful rollouts; intermediate turns that heavily influence the final answer might be over-rewarded.

TITLE: "Information-Theoretic Reward for Search Agents with Normative Constraints"
PROPOSAL: Derive a novel information-theoretic reward function that measures the reduction in uncertainty about the final answer, as evaluated through a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, which quantifies the increase in knowledge gained at each step; the reward is further constrained by a normative term that incentivizes the model to follow typical searching behavior, tied to the statistical properties of search trajectories.
CONTROLS: test the information-theoretic reward against hand-engineered heuristics and our previously proposed turn-level reward mechanisms, also to evaluate the importance of normative constraints in promoting desired behavior
COST: 1134
PREDICTION: Expected to provide a theoretically grounded and sparse reward signal that closely aligns with the underlying search dynamics, and might naturally promote more information-gain focused exploration strategies and avoid over-exploitation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: "Query-Agnostic Turn-Level Reward for Agentic Multi-Turn Search Agents"
PROPOSAL: Develop a learning framework based on Hindsight Experience Replay (HER), where the agent interacts with the environment and generates a sequence of rollsouts. Then, the agent selects a successful rollout where the final answer matches the ground truth and reweights the experience to consider rewards for all intermediate steps that contributed to the successful answer, but not for the unsuccessful ones. The selected successful rollout is replaced by a new rollout that is generated based on this reweighted experience.
CONTROLS: implementation of vanilla GRPO, data augmentation baseline, manually reweighted HER (i.e., putting hand-defined weights on the trajectory)
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Expected to improve sample efficiency and provide more informative rewards, but might fail to effectively distinguish productive from unproductive turns due to its reliance on successful rollouts; intermediate turns that heavily influence the final answer might be over-rewarded.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Turn-level Reward Augmentation using Relative Importance Metrics
PROPOSAL: We propose using relative importance metrics (RIMs) to augment turn-level rewards for agentic search agents. RIMs, such as those estimated through methods like attention or gradient-based scoring, assess the contribution of each turn to the final answer, providing a dense and task-anchored signal that remains robust to reward hacking.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: GRPO with outcome rewards only; (2) Ablation: GRPO with outcome rewards + early/default RIMs (e.g., attention based on early stages of the reasoning process)
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: Augmented GRPO should demonstrate better sample efficiency (20% fewer samples required), improved performance on tough multi-hop tasks, and reduced sparsity of process rewards. However, if early/default RIMs are overly simplistic, they might supply inconsistent or weak signals that offset benefits.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Gradual Reward Shaping for Agentic Trajectories
PROPOSAL: Inspired by internal-affect-related learning objectives, we introduce a gradual reward shaping mechanism for agentic trajectories. This method gradually decomposes the final outcome reward into more proximal, turn-level evaluation metrics (e.g., sub-question accuracy or similar-similarity to high-probability transitions). These per-turn values nudge the agent toward taking 'correct' intermediate steps toward the final answer.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: GRPO with outcome rewards only; (2) Ablation: Gradual Reward Shaping with a simpler, constant reward scaling factor (replacing the condition based decomposition); (3) Comparison: Turn-level Reward Augmentation (idea 1) with varying cofactors to match the gradual reward step selection.
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: Introducing proximal metrics should yield a more sample-efficient discovery process by steering the dialog toward relevant intermediate tasks and reactions to counter reward sparsity. However, overprompting may emerge if local proxy metrics diverge too strongly from their eligibility tasks.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Turn-level Reward Augmentation using Relative Importance Metrics
PROPOSAL: We refine our initial idea by introducing a hybrid approach, marrying relative importance metrics (RIMs) with a task-aware ablation strategy. RIMs provide a dense and task-anchored reward signal, while the ablation strategy adaptively selects a subset of turns for rewarding, focusing on the most crucial steps for successful trajectories.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: GRPO with outcome rewards only; (2) Ablation: Hybrid RIM + ablation with different ablation strategies (e.g., random sampling, greedy selection); (3) Comparison: Gradual Reward Shaping (idea 2) with varying reward scaling factors to match the hybrid RIM's preciseness
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: The hybrid approach should lead to improved performance on tough multi-hop tasks and better sample efficiency (30% fewer samples required), as it combines the strengths of RIMs and adaptive turn selection. However, the ablation strategy may introduce additional variance if poorly tuned or biased.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Action-Level Transfer Learning for Agentic Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We propose leveraging pre-trained action-level embeddings from large-scale language modeling tasks to serve as a transferable feature space for agentic search agents. These embeddings capture general knowledge and long-term context, enabling the agent to better focus on learning task-specific interaction skills. For each turn, the agent's action is transformed into a vector in the shared space, enhancing fine-grained credit assignment and downstream performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: GRPO with outcome rewards only; (2) Comparison: Using task-specific pre-training embeddings or pre-training on a different set of tasks
COST: 9600
PREDICTION: Action-level transfer learning should lead to improved performance on various agentic search tasks, as it leverages the general knowledge and contextual understanding captured by pre-trained models. However, if the pre-trained features are not aligned with the task's nuances, they might hinder learning.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Inverse Factorial Reward Shaping for Agentic Search Agents
PROPOSAL: Inspired by policy gradient methods and option theory, we introduce Inverse Factorial Reward Shaping (IFRS), a new method for designing reward functions that encourages the agent to break complex tasks into smaller, manageable sub-tasks. IFRS learns a probabilistic model of the agent's actions and their relative importance, providing a global perspective on the task's structure and matching intermediate progress with more rewarding sub-task completion.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: GRPO with outcome rewards only; (2) Comparison: Using alternatives to option theory-like methods (e.g., hierarchical reinforcement learning)
COST: 28800
PREDICTION: IFRS should lead to improved sample efficiency and task decomposition for agentic search agents, as it focuses on identifying and rewarding meaningful sub-task completion. However, if the model fails to capture the correct sub-tasks, it may still lead to inefficient exploration and weak learning.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Online Inference and Calibration of Process Rewards for Agentic Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We address the challenge of inferring informative process rewards within the agent's online operation. Our approach, Inference-Score-Learning (ISL) leverages a nonparametric contextual bandit model to dynamically estimate the quality of individual reasoning and tool interactions. Using logged interaction sequences and offline evaluations, the method calibrates process rewards to accurately reflect the agent's current knowledge gap and progress toward the final answer.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: GRPO with outcome rewards only; (2) Comparison: Using alternatives to online inference (e.g., batch post-hoc evaluation, pre-trained language models for evaluating intermediate progress)
COST: 43200
PREDICTION: ISL should lead to improved learning dynamics and task performance for agentic search agents, as it accurately assesses intermediate steps and intervenes with targeted rewards. However, if offline evaluations do not accurately represent online exploration and assessment difficulties, it may underperform under real-world conditions.

TITLE: Turn-level Reward Augmentation using Relative Importance Metrics
PROPOSAL: We propose using relative importance metrics (RIMs) to augment turn-level rewards for agentic search agents. RIMs, such as those estimated through methods like attention or gradient-based scoring, assess the contribution of each turn to the final answer, providing a dense and task-anchored signal that remains robust to reward hacking.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Gradual Reward Shaping for Agentic Trajectories
PROPOSAL: Inspired by internal-affect-related learning objectives, we introduce a gradual reward shaping mechanism for agentic trajectories. This method gradually decomposes the final outcome reward into more proximal, turn-level evaluation metrics (e.g., sub-question accuracy or similar-similarity to high-probability transitions). These per-turn values nudge the agent toward taking 'correct' intermediate steps toward the final answer.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Empirical Exploration of Intrinsic Turn-Level Rewards via Per-Turn ROI Estimates
PROPOSAL: We introduce a turn-level reward system that estimates the return on investment (ROI) for each interaction step by tracking the agent's information gain across the turns. In our ROI estimate, we measure the similarity between the agent's confidence in each turn and its confidence after receiving the tool response. We use a proximity-based score, such as cosine similarity, to quantify the increase in confidence at each turn. The turn-level reward is then defined as a weighted function of the ROI and a baseline term that accounts for the overall outcome of the search. Our baseline term is the probability of the final answer, calculated based on the agent's confidence distribution.
CONTROLS: We compare our ROI-based rewards to standard outcome-based rewards and two variants of density-based rewards that naively assign equal scores to each turn. We also ablate different components of our ROI estimate and its weights.
COST: 267
PREDICTION: We expect our ROI-based rewards to outperform baseline methods in both accuracy and sample efficiency, as it captures the incremental learning effect of each turn and helps the agent learn to navigate complex, multi-turn search queries. The method may fail in scenarios where the agent's confidence distribution is highly noisy or where the overall outcome of the search query largely does not correlate with intermediate turns.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Gradient-based Reward Augmentation for Outcome Rewards
PROPOSAL: We propose augmenting the standard outcome-based rewards with a gradient-based component that accounts for the relative importance of each turn in achieving the final outcome. Specifically, we use the expected gradients of the log-likelihood of the final answer with respect to the parameters of the agent's model, calculated at each turn using Monte Carlo sampling of the agent's output distributions. We add these gradients to the standard outcome reward to provide additional supervision that encourages the agent to learn to produce intermediate turns that are productive and informative.
CONTROLS: We compare our gradient-based reward augmentation to using only standard outcome-based rewards, the outcome-based rewards with our ROI estimate (proposal 1), and the outcome-based rewards with a simple turn-level density-based reward.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect our gradient-based reward augmentation to improve the accuracy and sample efficiency of the search agent, especially in scenarios where the intermediate turns contribute substantially to achieving the final outcome. However, the method may overfit to the gradient-based signal if the Monte Carlo sampling is not accurate or if the expected gradients are too noisy.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Architecture-aware Augmentation of Outcome Rewards with Self-Attention-based Progress Monitoring
PROPOSAL: We propose an architecture-aware approach to augmenting outcome-based rewards by introducing a self-attention mechanism that monitors the progress made by the agent at each turn. Specifically, we adapt the self-attention weights to reflect the token-level relevance of the input context to the agent's query and use them to estimate the progress made by the agent in retrieving informative content. We add this progress-based signal to the standard outcome reward to provide additional supervision that encourages the agent to learn to focus on the most relevant and informative parts of the input context.
CONTROLS: We compare our architecture-aware approach to standard outcome-based rewards, the outcome-based rewards with our ROI estimate (proposal 1), and the outcome-based rewards with gradient-based reward augmentation (proposal 2).
COST: 537.0859
PREDICTION: We expect our architecture-aware approach to improve the accuracy and sample efficiency of the search agent, especially in scenarios where the agent needs to focus on specific parts of the input context to produce an accurate final answer. However, the method may require careful tuning of the self-attention weights and may not generalize well to scenarios with drastically different input context lengths or complexities.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Robust Reward Augmentation
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical analysis of the robustness of different reward augmentation methods to the issue of advantage collapse in multi-turn search settings. Specifically, we establish a regime of partial equivalence between the different methods (proposals 1-3) and the original outcome-based rewards in terms of the group-relative advantages they produce, using a novel variation of the group-loss technique from Group Relative Policy Optimization. We show that the methods achieve the partial equivalence under relaxed regularity conditions, which are guaranteed to hold in the multi-turn search regime with noisy intermediate turns.
CONTROLS: We contrast the theoretical analysis with empirical results for the methods when applied to synthetic and real-world search benchmarks.
COST: 332.5
PREDICTION: We expect the theoretical analysis to reveal which methods are robust to advantage collapse and under which conditions. The theoretical results may imply when the methods fail to outperform the original outcome-based rewards, and may suggest new methods for improving robustness. However, the theoretical regime is idealized, and additional noise factors may make the methods more susceptible to advantage collapse in practice.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Architecture-aware Augmentation of Outcome Rewards with Self-Attention-based Progress Monitoring
PROPOSAL: We revise our architecture-aware approach to address the potential issue of overfitting to the input context length by introducing a learnable scaling factor for the self-attention weights that is conditioned on the input context length. We also modify the way we update the progress-based signal to use a weighted sum of the token-level relevance scores, where the weights are learned using an additional objective that encourages the agent to focus on the most informative parts of the input context. This modification promotes multiple-attention heads to be more informed about global input.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised approach to standard outcome-based rewards, the outcome-based rewards with our ROI estimate (proposal 1), and the outcome-based rewards with gradient-based reward augmentation (proposal 2).
COST: 567
PREDICTION: We expect our revised approach to address the overfitting issue and generalize better to scenarios with different input context lengths or complexities. However, the method may require careful tuning of the learnable scaling factors and additional objective. It may also require significant additional training time to learn the additional objective and attend to global input.

PROPOSAL: We revise our gradient-based reward augmentation to calculate the expected gradients at each turn using a fixed sequence length, rather than relying on Monte Carlo sampling of the agent's output distributions. ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Level-Hierarchical Intrinsic Rewards for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: We propose an extension of the ROI-based reward (proposal 1) that incorporates a hierarchical structure of level-specific intrinsic rewards. Each level corresponds to a specific turn in the search process, and the rewards at each level capture the agent's progress towards the final answer within that level. We use a hierarchical version of the proximal policy optimization (HPPPO) algorithm to train the agent to maximize the sum of the intrinsic rewards at each level. This approach encourages the agent to make progress at each level and to focus on the most informative parts of the input context.
CONTROLS: We compare our hierarchical intrinsic rewards to standard outcome-based rewards, and to the other reward augmentation methods (proposals 1-4).
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect our hierarchical intrinsic rewards to improve the agent's ability to focus on the most informative parts of the input context, and to make progress towards the final answer at each level. However, the method may require careful tuning of the hierarchy levels and the weights given to each level's rewards. It may also require significant computational resources to train the agent using the HPPPO algorithm.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Empirical Exploration of Intrinsic Turn-Level Rewards via Per-Turn ROI Estimates
PROPOSAL: We introduce a turn-level reward system that estimates the return on investment (ROI) for each interaction step by tracking the agent's information gain across the turns. In our ROI estimate, we measure the similarity between the agent's confidence in each turn and its confidence after receiving the tool response. We use a proximity-based score, such as cosine similarity, to quantify the increase in confidence at each turn. The turn-level reward is then defined as a weighted function of the ROI and a baseline term that accounts for the overall outcome of the search. Our baseline term is the probability of the final answer, calculated based on the agent's confidence distribution.
CONTROLS: We compare our ROI-based rewards to standard outcome-based rewards and two variants of density-based rewards that naively assign equal scores to each turn. We also ablate different components of our ROI estimate and its weights.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: We expect our ROI-based rewards to outperform baseline methods in both accuracy and sample efficiency, as it captures the incremental learning effect of each turn and helps the agent learn to navigate complex, multi-turn search queries. The method may fail in scenarios where the agent's confidence distribution is highly noisy or where the overall outcome of the search query largely does not correlate with intermediate turns.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Gradient-based Reward Augmentation for Outcome Rewards
PROPOSAL: We propose augmenting the standard outcome-based rewards with a gradient-based component that accounts for the relative importance of each turn in achieving the final outcome. Specifically, we use the expected gradients of the log-likelihood of the final answer with respect to the parameters of the agent's model, calculated at each turn using Monte Carlo sampling of the agent's output distributions. We add these gradients to the standard outcome reward to provide additional supervision that encourages the agent to learn to produce intermediate turns that are productive and informative.
CONTROLS: We compare our gradient-based reward augmentation to using only standard outcome-based rewards, the outcome-based rewards with our ROI estimate (proposal 1), and the outcome-based rewards with a simple turn-level density-based reward.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect our gradient-based reward augmentation to improve the accuracy and sample efficiency of the search agent, especially in scenarios where the intermediate turns contribute substantially to achieving the final outcome. However, the method may overfit to the gradient-based signal if the Monte Carlo sampling is not accurate or if the expected gradients are too noisy.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Architecture-aware Augmentation of Outcome Rewards with Self-Attention-based Progress Monitoring
PROPOSAL: We propose an architecture-aware approach to augmenting outcome-based rewards by introducing a self-attention mechanism that monitors the progress made by the agent at each turn. Specifically, we adapt the self-attention weights to reflect the token-level relevance of the input context to the agent's query and use them to estimate the progress made by the agent in retrieving informative content. We add this progress-based signal to the standard outcome reward to provide additional supervision that encourages the agent to learn to focus on the most relevant and informative parts of the input context.
CONTROLS: We compare our architecture-aware approach to standard outcome-based rewards, the outcome-based rewards with our ROI estimate (proposal 1), and the outcome-based rewards with gradient-based reward augmentation (proposal 2).
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: We expect our architecture-aware approach to improve the accuracy and sample efficiency of the search agent, especially in scenarios where the agent needs to focus on specific parts of the input context to produce an accurate final answer. However, the method may require careful tuning of the self-attention weights and may not generalize well to scenarios with drastically different input context lengths or complexities.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Robust Reward Augmentation
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical analysis of the robustness of different reward augmentation methods to the issue of advantage collapse in multi-turn search settings. Specifically, we establish a regime of partial equivalence between the different methods (proposals 1-3) and the original outcome-based rewards in terms of the group-relative advantages they produce, using a novel variation of the group-loss technique from Group Relative Policy Optimization. We show that the methods achieve the partial equivalence under relaxed regularity conditions, which are guaranteed to hold in the multi-turn search regime with noisy intermediate turns.
CONTROLS: We contrast the theoretical analysis with empirical results for the methods when applied to synthetic and real-world search benchmarks.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect the theoretical analysis to reveal which methods are robust to advantage collapse and under which conditions. The theoretical results may imply when the methods fail to outperform the original outcome-based rewards, and may suggest new methods for improving robustness. However, the theoretical regime is idealized, and additional noise factors may make the methods more susceptible to advantage collapse in practice.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Architecture-aware Augmentation of Outcome Rewards with Self-Attention-based Progress Monitoring
PROPOSAL: We revise our architecture-aware approach to address the potential issue of overfitting to the input context length by introducing a learnable scaling factor for the self-attention weights that is conditioned on the input context length. We also modify the way we update the progress-based signal to use a weighted sum of the token-level relevance scores, where the weights are learned using an additional objective that encourages the agent to focus on the most informative parts of the input context. This modification promotes multiple-attention heads to be more informed about global input.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised approach to standard outcome-based rewards, the outcome-based rewards with our ROI estimate (proposal 1), and the outcome-based rewards with gradient-based reward augmentation (proposal 2).
COST: 1700
PREDICTION: We expect our revised approach to address the overfitting issue and generalize better to scenarios with different input context lengths or complexities. However, the method may require careful tuning of the learnable scaling factors and additional objective. It may also require significant additional training time to learn the additional objective and attend to global input.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Gradient-based Reward Augmentation for Outcome Rewards
PROPOSAL: We revise our gradient-based reward augmentation to calculate the expected gradients at each turn using a fixed sequence length, rather than relying on Monte Carlo sampling of the agent's output distributions. This modified approach makes the method more computationally efficient and allows us to use a smaller number of samples to estimate the gradients. We also introduce an additional term to the gradient-based reward that is calculated using the relative entropy between the current agent's distribution and the final answer distribution, which encourages the agent to move towards the final answer distribution.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised approach to standard outcome-based rewards, the outcome-based rewards with our ROI estimate (proposal 1), and the architecture-aware approach (proposal 3).
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: We expect our revised approach to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the gradient-based reward augmentation, while reducing the risk of overfitting. However, the method may require careful tuning of the fixed sequence length and the relative entropy term. It may also struggle to accurately capture the high-dimensional distributions of the agent's output in complex search tasks.

ACTION: ADD 5

PROPOSAL: We propose an extension of the ROI-based reward (proposal 1) that incorporates a hierarchical structure of level-specific intrinsic rewards. We use a hierarchical version of the proximal policy optimization (HPPPO) algorithm to train the agent to maximize the sum of the intrinsic rewards at each level. This approach encourages the agent to make progress at each level and to focus on the most informative parts of the input context.

It may also require significant computational resources to train the agent using the HPPPO algorithm.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contextualized Intermediate Reward Engineering for Multi-Turn Search Agents
PROPOSAL: Experimenting with contextualized intermediate rewards derived from the ground-truth final answer and its surrounding context (e.g., query, question type, and supporting knowledge). The contextualized reward for each turn will be a weighted combination of three components: binary correctness, influence on the next turn (capturing the causal relationship between turns), and informativeness (how much new information is retrieved). We hypothesize that contextualized rewards will provide a dense, informative signal for RL training while staying anchored to the final task objective.
CONTROLS: We will compare our contextualized rewards (1) against outcome-only rewards ( baseline 1), (2) against random process rewards with similar sparsity (baseline 2), and (3) against ablated versions of our reward, where either the influence or informativeness component is removed.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Contextualized rewards will improve sample efficiency and accuracy over baseline 1 (outcome-only reward) due to better credit assignment, especially in long trajectories. However, variance or bias from contextualized reward components might lead to suboptimal performance or instability in certain regimes, depending on the specific architecture and dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bayesian Turn-Level Impurity Minimization for Easier Credit Assignment
PROPOSAL: Introduce a Bayesian probabilistic model to mask the true ground-truth answer (or part of it) at each turn during training. The model will learn to predict the hidden information, enabling the agent to attend to relevant interactions and turn-level information without being prematurely biased toward the correct answer. This technique allows for turn-level supervision, focuses the agent's learning on critical steps, and may help alleviate credit assignment issues. An upper bound of the expected information gain after each turn will serve as our reward.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our Bayesian turn-level model against the contextualized rewards (proposed in proposal 1) and compare it against a classic Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) baseline, evaluating the robustness of each method to hard or easy query difficulty, and varying the turn-level reward information gain.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: The model should outperform the contextualized rewards, especially in challenging multi-hop questions or long trajectories where extraneous information clearly interferes with the final goal. It will, however, require more samples to be learned and evaluate, as accurate Bayesian inference is computationally more expensive.

PROPOSAL: Develop a set of generative models that synthesize new trajectories and environments for agentic search evaluation, allowing us to augment existing datasets and create more diverse and realistic test cases.
