ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Hybrid Pseudo-Labeling with Confident Reminder
PROPOSAL: We propose to design a hybrid pseudo-labeling approach that not only uses vision-language detectors to generate pseudo-labels from the target test data but also maintains a confidence-driven reminder mechanism. When a test image lacks high-quality pseudo-labels (due to a confidence threshold), our mechanism will selectively recall a fixed number of previously generated pseudo-labels with high confidence from previous test batches that are similar to the current image. This strategy aims to balance the trade-off between adapting to the new target domain and preserving the pre-trained generalization capability of the vision-language detector.
CONTROLS: comparing against state-of-the-art self-training methods, a condition where the memory mechanism is disabled
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: The new approach can achieve better test-time adaptation performance by leveraging historical pseudo-labels, while escalating the risk of overfitting if the memory mechanism is too aggressive or uses insufficient historical data.

TITLE: Adaptive Attention Weighting for Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: To mitigate the limitations of vision-language detectors when adapting to cross-domain and cross-category target data, we propose to dynamically adjust the attention weighting mechanism of these detectors during test-time adaptation. By learning to adaptively select the most relevant attention weights for the target domain, we can enhance the detector's ability to focus on task-relevant features while ignoring domain-specific biases. This approach builds upon recent advancements in adaptive attention mechanisms and meta-learning.

PROPOSAL: Design a novel capacity-aware learning strategy that adapts the learning process to the fixed capacity of the model, simulating projected effects of scaling up the solution and representation spaces. This constraint directly helps the model's capacity by fixing an upper bound on the linear dimension and potentially reduces overfitting by making the model robust to overly large graphs, and the high-dimensional latent traits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual Web Data Selection with Cross-lingual Contrastive Loss
PROPOSAL: Train a multilingual BERT-based classifier on high-quality samples from multiple languages (Wikipedia, news corpora) and then fine-tune it on a large unlabeled multilingual dataset (e.g., CC100). Use cross-lingual contrastive loss as the objective to learn a universal representation of data quality. In each language, use in-language evaluation metrics (e.g., ROUGE, BLEU) as auxiliary objectives to adapt the quality judgment to the specific language's characteristics.
CONTROLS: Compare with FineWeb2-HQ, DCLM, and a baseline with no selection using standard web data deduplication and filtering techniques.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The proposed multilingual classifier will achieve better performance than existing model-based data selection strategies on a test set of in-language quality evaluations, outperforming FineWeb2-HQ and DCLM. However, it may fall short compared to the performance of language-specific fine-tuned models like QuRating, especially for low-resource languages.

PREDICTION: The proposed multilingual classifier will achieve better performance than existing model-based data selection strategies on a test set of in-language quality evaluations, outperforming FineWeb2-HQ and DCLM. However, it may fall short compared to the performance of language-specific fine-tuned models like QuRating, especially for low-resource languages.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revising Cross-lingual Contrastive Loss
PROPOSAL: Refine the previous proposal by incorporating a domain adaptation step where the multilingual classifier is fine-tuned on a set of translated documents from each language, inducing a common representation shared across all languages. Then, maintain the cross-lingual contrastive loss objective to further refine the representation. In each language, continue using in-language evaluation metrics as auxiliary objectives to ensure language-specific adaptation. Evaluate on a set of languages where domain knowledge (e.g., recipes, FAQs) differs significantly from other domains.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original proposal, multilingual BERT with only in-language evaluation metrics, and a state-of-the-art domain adaptation baseline.
COST: 54000
PREDICTION: Domain adaptation will improve the classifier's ability to generalize across language domains, reducing performance drops when shifting across languages, whereas simply including in-language evaluation metrics without domain adaptation may not fully address this issue.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Improving Robustness Against Synthetic and Manipulated Data
PROPOSAL: 1. Multilingual Web Data Selection with Cross-lingual Contrastive Loss:
 Revise the original proposal by training a adversarial noise model on a mix of synthetic and malicious samples and then using this model as an additional objective during training, which will increase robustness against data tampering attempts and "adversarial" manipulation of samples used for pretraining.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on data that contains synthetic and manipulated samples, compare against the original proposal and existing state-of-the-art data selection methods.
COST: 63000
PREDICTION: The addition of the adversarial objective will provide increased robustness, however, over-optimization of the noise model might make the overall learning process less effective thus possibly losing some signal coming from the contrastive loss.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-based Selection vs Heuristic Filtering: A Hybrid Approach
PROPOSAL: Create a hybrid system that combines the multilingual classifier from the first proposal with a set of heuristics based on common filtering techniques (e.g., deduplication, stemming/lemmatization). The model will selectively use the heuristics to augment its predictions when dealing with complex, content-heavy samples where the heuristics are effective, but use its classification output as the primary decision when dealing with high-confidence predictions.

PROPOSAL: Introduce a curriculum learning approach to the multilingual classifier, where the model is first trained on an easier subset of the multilingual dataset (e.g., high-quality documents, well-formed text) and then gradually exposed to increasingly complex samples. PREDICTION: Transfer learning will allow the model-based data selection approach to be easily adapted to new languages and domains, reducing the need for extensive re-training and improving the overall efficiency of the approach, although it might require more careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability and Parallelization for Multilingual Data Selection
PROPOSAL: Develop a scalable and parallelizable implementation of the multilingual classifier and data selection pipeline using distributed computing techniques (e.g., data parallelism, model parallelism) to enable the selection of large-scale multilingual datasets efficiently.

PREDICTION: Distributed computing will significantly speed up the data selection process, enabling the scalability of the approach on massive multilingual datasets, although it might require careful optimization of the implementation to avoid communication overhead and ensure efficient data parallelism.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model-Based Multilingual Data Selection using Prompt-Based Evaluation Criteria
PROPOSAL: We will extend the QuRating approach to multilingual settings by training language-specific raters using prompt-based evaluation criteria from mC4 and XSum in multiple languages. Each rater will be trained with its native language in addition to three other languages: Spanish, French, and Hindi. We will also evaluate these raters on three metric tasks: loss of a cross-lingual LLM as it only sees training samples labeled by QuRating as higher-quality, average KL-divergence between predicted and actual quality labels, and the percentage of selected samples that contain relevant knowledge about the given topic.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach against baseline prompts asking borderline-quality mC4 samples if they "should be included in a high-quality LLM training corpus" or asking relevant but small fine-tuning tasks on LLMs trained on worsening-quality mC4 samples. Additionally, we will perform an ablation study on decreasing the number of auxiliary languages from 3 to 2 and then to 1.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: This experiment will help us discover whether language-specific prompt-based evaluation criteria can learn multilingual ground truth for data quality effectively, and whether this helps them outperform traditional bilingual LLM training tests. High predictive power could lie at difficulties stemming from blurriness of certain languages via multilingual LLM sizes.

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Model-Based Data Selection on Out-of-Distribution Performance
PROPOSAL: We propose evaluating the impact of model-based data selection on out-of-distribution performance by training a multilingual LLM on selected data and evaluating its performance on unseen languages, domains, and topics. We will compare our results to those obtained by training on randomly sampled data and on data selected using existing heuristic methods such as LCD.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Multilingual Data Quality Rating with Observable Risk
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the performance of language-agnostic data quality ratings trained on diverse multilingual datasets (e.g., CC-Net, ParaCrawl) with observable risk assessment using noise-robust metrics (e.g., Confidence Scoring, Anomaly Detection), to instances trained with supervision from benchmark-derived labels (e.g., evaluation metrics on portions of the test set not yet seen during training). We hypothesize that observable risk assessment can generalize better even across rare languages and domains. We compare these models to fine-tuned language-specific raters on English and other languages (e.g., Spanish, Arabic, Chinese).
CONTROLS: We compare with benchmark-derived models including DCLM, AskLLM and FineWeb2-HQ, as well as language-agnostic baselines that use standard heuristics and perplexity-based filters.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: We anticipate that observable risk assessment will reduce model bias and improve performance on unseen data across languages, with potential failure in representing edge cases involving very few datapoints.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training With Noise as a Mechanism for Multilingual Data Quality 
PROPOSAL: This experiment focuses on using noise_augmented training of a multilingual LLM during the pretraining phase. We specifically inject noise in line with real-world error types (label noise, missing values, typos) while training, to allow the model to derive robustness and generalization ability across diverse languages. We evaluate performance and compare to our 'Unified Multilingual Data Quality Rating with Observable Risk' setup from earlier on English and several non-English languages.
CONTROLS: Baselines include standard pretraining with no added noise, as well as the previously mentioned language-specific raters and benchmark-derived models. 
COST: 834 
PREDICTION: By leveraging noise-augmented training during pretraining and building on low risk assessment, we anticipate an additional boost in the generalization ability of the model across different languages, although potential issues could arise from consideration of "labels" to augment data which isn't available in large quantities for each non-english language.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multitask Learning for Quality Rating and Downstream Task Alignment
PROPOSAL: We explore multitask learning by simultaneously training the quality rating model to predict quality scores for pretraining data and to align with downstream task objectives. By doing so, the quality rating model learns to prioritize content quality that is relevant to the downstream tasks. We evaluate its effectiveness on tasks such as text classification and sentiment analysis in multiple languages.
CONTROLS: Baselines include the existing quality rating models, language-specific raters, and a version of the multitask learning approach that doesn't align with the downstream task.
COST: 1176 
PREDICTION: By multitask learning and aligning the quality rating model with downstream task objectives, we anticipate a significant improvement in the model's ability to select high-quality pretraining data for multiple languages, with potential failure in aligning with very diverse or language-specific downstream tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Multilingual Data Quality Rating with Observable Risk
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the performance of language-agnostic data quality ratings trained on diverse multilingual datasets (e.g., CC-Net, ParaCrawl) with observable risk assessment using noise-robust metrics (e.g., Confidence Scoring, Anomaly Detection), to instances trained with supervision from benchmark-derived labels (e.g., evaluation metrics on portions of the test set not yet seen during training). We hypothesize that observable risk assessment can generalize better even across rare languages and domains. We compare these models to fine-tuned language-specific raters on English and other languages (e.g., Spanish, Arabic, Chinese).
CONTROLS: We compare with benchmark-derived models including DCLM, AskLLM and FineWeb2-HQ, as well as language-agnostic baselines that use standard heuristics and perplexity-based filters.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We anticipate that observable risk assessment will reduce model bias and improve performance on unseen data across languages, with potential failure in representing edge cases involving very few datapoints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training With Noise as a Mechanism for Multilingual Data Quality 
PROPOSAL: This experiment focuses on using noise_augmented training of a multilingual LLM during the pretraining phase. We specifically inject noise in line with real-world error types (label noise, missing values, typos) while training, to allow the model to derive robustness and generalization ability across diverse languages. We evaluate performance and compare to our 'Unified Multilingual Data Quality Rating with Observable Risk' setup from earlier on English and several non-English languages.
CONTROLS: Baselines include standard pretraining with no added noise, as well as the previously mentioned language-specific raters and benchmark-derived models. 
COST: 2500 
PREDICTION: By leveraging noise-augmented training during pretraining and building on low risk assessment, we anticipate an additional boost in the generalization ability of the model across different languages, although potential issues could arise from consideration of "labels" to augment data which isn't available in large quantities for each non-english language.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Unified Multilingual Data Quality Rating with Observable Risk
PROPOSAL: We extend the original proposal to use contrastive learning to further enhance the robustness and generalization capability of the unified quality rating model in low-resource languages. This involves defining two types of contrastive pairs: 1) positive-negative pairs (high-quality-low-quality documents in the same language) and 2) cross-lingual pairs (documents with the same quality in different languages).
CONTROLS: We keep the controls as previously mentioned and add contrastive learning as an additional variant to be compared with.
COST: 10000 
PREDICTION: By utilizing contrastive learning in conjunction with observable risk assessment, we anticipate even better performance and a more robust generalization capability across languages and resources, with possible challenges in forming coherent contrastive pairs in low-resource languages.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Unified Multilingual Data Quality Rating with Observable Risk
PROPOSAL: We extend the original proposal to use transfer learning from English to non-English languages, utilizing the multilingual variant of BERT (mBERT) as a baseline to pre-process the text and then training the quality rater on translated documents. This setup should leverage the strengths of the pre-trained model and potentially transfer knowledge across languages.
CONTROLS: We keep the controls as previously mentioned and add the contrastive learning variants, including those with and without pre-processing by mBERT.
COST: 12000 
PREDICTION: By pre-processing non-English text with the mBERT model and leveraging its transfer knowledge, we anticipate improving the performance and generalization capability of the quality rating model, although we may face challenges when transferring linguistic knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multitask Learning for Quality Rating and Downstream Task Alignment
PROPOSAL: We explore multitask learning by simultaneously training the quality rating model to predict quality scores for pretraining data and to align with downstream task objectives. By doing so, the quality rating model learns to prioritize content quality that is relevant to the downstream tasks. We evaluate its effectiveness on tasks such as text classification and sentiment analysis in multiple languages.
CONTROLS: Baselines include the existing quality rating models, language-specific raters, and a version of the multitask learning approach that doesn't align with the downstream task.
COST: 3500 
PREDICTION: By multitask learning and aligning the quality rating model with downstream task objectives, we anticipate a significant improvement in the model's ability to select high-quality pretraining data for multiple languages, with potential failure in aligning with very diverse or language-specific downstream tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Training With Noise as a Mechanism for Multilingual Data Quality
PROPOSAL: We refine the existing "Training With Noise as a Mechanism for Multilingual Data Quality" setup by incorporating self-supervised learning techniques to improve the noise robustness of the model and better generalize to diverse languages and domains. Specifically, we add a contrastive learning component to the noise-augmented pretraining process.
CONTROLS: We keep the existing baselines and controls, including the refined contrastive learning variant used in the revised unified quality rating model.
COST: 18000 
PREDICTION: By incorporating self-supervised learning and contrastive learning into the noise-augmented pretraining setup, we anticipate significant improvements in the model's ability to robustly select high-quality pretraining data across languages and domains, with potential challenges in tuning the noise injection and self-supervised learning schedules.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge Distillation for Multilingual Data Quality Transfer
PROPOSAL: We explore knowledge distillation as a method for transferring knowledge from a pre-trained quality rating model to smaller, more efficient models that can be easily deployed on embedded devices or for specific downstream tasks. We evaluate its effectiveness in retaining the quality rating performance on diverse languages and domains.
CONTROLS: Baselines include the pre-trained quality rating models, the distilled models, and a version of the distillation process that uses a proxy task or synthetic data.
COST: 4500 
PREDICTION: By leveraging knowledge distillation, we anticipate a significant reduction in the computational requirements and memory usage of the quality rating models, with potential trade-offs in terms of their performance on low-resource languages or edge cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Human-in-the-Loop for Quality Rating and Downstream Task Alignment
PROPOSAL: We design a human-in-the-loop system where expert annotators provide quality labels or corrections to the pre-training data, with the model learning from these human feedbacks to improve its quality rating and downstream task alignment. We evaluate its effectiveness in retaining the quality rating performance and downstream task accuracy on diverse languages and domains.
CONTROLS: Baselines include the existing quality rating models, the human-in-the-loop setup, and a version of the human feedback that is used as an additional proxy task for self-training.
COST: 8000 
PREDICTION: By incorporating human feedback and expert annotators, we anticipate significant improvements in the quality rating performance and downstream task accuracy, with potential challenges in scaling the human annotation process or achieving consistent quality in the human-annotated data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferable Explanation and Understandability for Multilingual Data Quality
PROPOSAL: We develop a framework that generates transferable explanations and understandability metrics for multilingual data quality ratings. This framework aims to provide insights into the model's decision-making process and allows for more transparent and explainable quality ratings. We evaluate its effectiveness in improving the interpretability and trustworthiness of the quality rating model.
CONTROLS: Baselines include the existing quality rating models, and a version of the explanation framework that uses proxy tasks or synthetic data.
COST: 23000 
PREDICTION: By generating transferable explanations and understandability metrics, we anticipate significant improvements in the interpretability and transparency of the quality rating model, with potential challenges in balancing the complexity and comprehensibility of the explanations.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Knowledge Distillation for Multilingual Data Quality Transfer
PROPOSAL: We refine the existing "Knowledge Distillation for Multilingual Data Quality Transfer" setup by incorporating the previously proposed transferable explanation and understandability metrics as an additional distillation target. This allows the distilled models to retain not only the knowledge of the quality rating model but also its ability to provide transparent and explainable quality ratings. We evaluate its effectiveness in achieving both high-quality transfers and explanation retention.
CONTROLS: We keep the existing baselines and controls, including the distilled models with and without explanation retention.
COST: 36000 
PREDICTION: By incorporating transferable explanations and understandability metrics into the knowledge distillation process, we anticipate a significant improvement in the ability of the distilled models to provide high-quality transfers while retaining their transparency and explainability, with potential challenges in balancing the complexity of the explanations with the efficiency of the distillation process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual Universal Quality Evaluator via Score Matching
PROPOSAL: Train a multilingual deep generative model (e.g., VQ-VAE or MIL-G for conditional text generations) on a large, diverse dataset of pre-training data (e.g., Pile, MLDoc) where quality labels are assigned randomly to chunks of text. This will encourage the model to capture either inherent, general quality features or correlations with certain specific linguistic features, and we will learn to score the model's likelihoods under an approximate maximum likelihood (AML) objective with a relaxed and universal quality score inferred by adjusting the mean token perplexity and specifically accounting for genre seeming disjointness. Modal scoring analysis, based on attention heads of the projected samples, will be used to combine the AML loss with a quality-theory- evidentiary likelihood to produce quality-labels for new codeblocks that match the style using a operational mapping through examples resembling samples used during the prior process.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing benchmark methods using identical evaluation setup and training conditions.
COST: 360000
PREDICTION: This universal quality rater could achieve performance comparable or exceeding current SOTA benchmarks for author-trustworthiness on monolingual data, requiring a plethora of classification improvement, model extracted mappings recall accuracy of >94%.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-Grained Quality Assessment through Hierarchical Rater Learning
PROPOSAL: Train a hierarchical model (e.g., cascade of transformers) where each stage's output, i.e., quality scores, serves as an input to the next stage. We'll fine-tune the raters to learn fine-grained quality criteria specific to each language family (e.g., Sino-Tibetan, Indo-European, Afro-Asiatic) or writing system (e.g., logographic vs. alphabetic) to capture nuances in linguistic diversity. By leveraging hierarchical learning, we can effectively decouple the universal and language-specific quality aspects and improve the rater's ability to adapt to diverse linguistic contexts.
CONTROLS: Compare with the pre-trained multilingual quality evaluator from proposal 1, examine how hierarchically learned quality assessment benefits LLMs in fine-grained tasks (e.g., fact-checking, question-answering) specific to each language family or writing system.
COST: 485000
PREDICTION: This hierarchical approach can improve the accuracy and adaptability of fine-grained quality assessment, with up to 15% increase in F1-score for specific language families, but may require additional domain expertise to design an optimal hierarchy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robust Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Perturb the input data with adversarial noise to improve the robustness of the quality evaluator. We'll use a generator to produce adversarial samples that are hard to predict and use a discriminator to differentiate between high-quality and low-quality samples. Train the quality evaluator with a combination of clean and adversarial samples to improve its ability to generalize to unseen data and robustness to noise and outliers.
CONTROLS: Compare performance of quality evaluator trained with adversarial samples with controls in proposals 1-3, examining the benefit of robust training.
COST: 750000
PREDICTION: This approach can achieve up to 10% improvement in quality assessment accuracy under noisy or outlier-prone conditions, making it a valuable addition to existing quality evaluation methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Time-Efficient Training of Joint Geometric and Reflectance Fields for Scalable Object Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Investigate a domain parallelization and knowledge distillation approach for the joint representation to reduce training times by a significant margin without compromising accuracy, thereby enabling efficient adaptation to new objects and scenes in real-time applications.
CONTROLS: Compare to a standard parallel implementation (e.g., using standard data parallelism) and to a baseline using regular learn-to-generate techniques.
COST: 7500
PREDICTION: Expected to achieve real-time performance, reducing training times to approximately 1-3 hours on a single high-end GPU, and maintaining a geometric and reflectance accuracy comparable to the non-parallelized baseline.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Geometric and Reflectance Fields for Realistic 3D Object Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel 3D representation that combines signed distance fields for geometry and neural radiance fields for view-dependent appearance, enabling the joint learning of an object's shape, material properties, and reflectance without pre-processing or post-processing steps.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art geometry-only latent representations (e.g., Occupancy Networks) and view-dependent appearance-only methods (e.g., NeRF).
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: Expected to outperform geometry-only models on appearance metrics and view-dependent effects, but could underperform for complex scenes with multiple occluding objects due to limitations in current Neural Radiance Field (NRF) models handling self-occlusion.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Generalizability of Joint Geometric and Reflectance Fields to Novel Scenes and Viewpoints
PROPOSAL: Conduct an experiment to test the generalization capabilities of the proposed joint representation, by measuring its performance on unseen scenes, viewpoints, and object categories, while also assessing its ability to capture subtle changes in appearance induced by varying lighting conditions and textures.
CONTROLS: Compare to strong baselines that incorporate multiple views (e.g., learned features from a multi-view 3D reconstruction method) and robust global representations (e.g., pre-trained weights for the neural network, a well-performing distance field).
COST: 9600
PREDICTION: Expected to outperform the baselines in capturing nuanced appearance changes, but might fail to generalize across drastic scene changes, such as those involving significant changes in lighting or texture, highlighting a potential research direction for future improvements.

CONTROLS: Compare to the original joint representation and to a geometric only baseline that uses a state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction method incorporating 3D primitives (e.g., NTU method).

PREDICTION: Expected to improve view-dependent effects and material properties recovery, but might require substantial data and compute resources due to additional complexity, and could be difficult to optimize.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multiview Feature Merging for Compact Latent Representation
PROPOSAL: Train a neural network that learns to merge multiview features from precomputed appearance and geometry descriptors, such as pix2code features [1] for appearance and Occupancy Normals [2] for geometry, and outputs a compact, view-invariant latent vector that captures both geometric and appearance information from a given dataset of 3D objects with RGB images.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art geometry-only representations like Occupancy Normals and Signed Distance Fields, as well as appearance-only models like primitive-based representations.
COST: 332.5
PREDICTION: This method should outperform geometry-only models in tasks that require appearance, but fall short of appearance-only models in tasks that prioritize geometric accuracy; with significant improvements in view-dependent effects like reflections and highlights due to the merged multiview features.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: View-Dependent Latent Decoder with Conditioned Normal Distributions
PROPOSAL: Develop a new latent decoder component that takes the view-invariant latent vector from Proposal 1 and conditionally samples normal distributions for 3D points based on the cosine similarity between the input image and the object's view directions; use these normal distributions to modulate the geometry and appearance channels of the latent vector, allowing for view-dependent effects like reflections and shading.
CONTROLS: Compare variants of the latent decoder component with and without conditioning on view directions, as well as without the view-dependent modulation.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: This decoder component should significantly improve view-dependent effects and realism in generated 3D objects, with noticeable improvements in tasks like image-to-3D asset generation, but require additional optimization to not decrease performance in tasks that prioritize geometric accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Based Rendering of Generated 3D Objects
PROPOSAL: Integrate a rendering engine that uses physically-based rendering (PBR) techniques to visually evaluate the generated 3D objects from Proposal 1 and Proposal 2, incorporating real-world materials and lighting conditions to assess the realism and view-dependent effects of the generated objects.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the PBR-rendered images against real-world images of the corresponding objects, as well as user studies to assess the perceived realism and view-dependent effects.
COST: 6720
PREDICTION: The generated 3D objects should exhibit significant improvements in realism and view-dependent effects when rendered with PBR techniques, but potential limitations may arise from the representation's inability to capture extremely complex or dynamic real-world lighting conditions, and suboptimal material properties learned from the training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Stage Latent Refining for Image-to-3D Asset Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a multi-stage latent refining framework that takes the compact latent representation from Proposal 1 and iteratively refines it through multiple stages, each focusing on specific aspects of geometry and appearance, such as geometry detail, texture, and material properties; each refinement stage can be conditioned on the input image and the previously refined latent representation.
CONTROLS: Compare against direct generation from compact latents and variants that remove or modify individual stages of refinement.
COST: 2000

TITLE: Model-Based Adversarial Loss for Latent 3D Object Representations
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel model-based adversarial loss function that encourages the latent 3D object representation to capture realistic views and appearances by adversarially training a separate model to predict the input image from the latent representation and evaluating its realism.
CONTROLS: Compare against variants with different types of adversarial losses, as well as direct evaluations of realism through quantitative metrics and user studies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly-Supervised Training for Image-to-3D Asset Generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a weakly-supervised training framework that leverages a pretext task of image-to-image translation to pretrain the latent 3D object representation and its associated neural components, followed by a coarse-to-fine refinement process that optimizes the representation for image-to-3D asset generation.
CONTROLS: Compare against fully-supervised and self-supervised training variants, as well as direct evaluations of 3D asset generation in a range of downstream tasks.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: This weakly-supervised training framework should significantly reduce the requirement for large-scale annotation data and computational resources, while still improving the quality and realism of generated 3D objects, but may introduce additional complexity in the training pipeline and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

COST: 9000

PROPOSAL: Develop a multi-scale sparse voxel occupancy representation that conditions on both the input image and a set of related images (e.g., differing only by viewpoint or lighting) to better model the intricate view-dependent appearance of complex real-world objects.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Deformable Signed Distance Functions
PROPOSAL: Improve Deformable Signed Distance Functions (Proposal 3) by incorporating a differential loss function for occlusion boundaries, enabling more accurate representation of object structures with regions of partial occlusion and adding robustness to the learned deformations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Voxel-Based 3D Latent Representation with View-Dependent Appearance
PROPOSAL: Train a state-of-the-art 3D generator (e.g., Modern 3D Diffusion model or Latent Diffusion I Moffat) on a voxel-based representation (e.g., sparse voxel grid), where each voxel contains not only occupancy but also material properties such as color, roughness, and metallicity. Incorporate view-dependent effects by conditioning the generator on camera poses and lighting conditions. Use the REAL-57 dataset for training and evaluation.
CONTROLS: Compare with our ablation study on geometry-only representations (Sparse Voxel-Distance Field model) and a state-of-the-art appearance-only model (Primitive-based Signed Distance model).
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The model will improve upon existing methods in both geometry and appearance representation, but may struggle with intricate view-dependent effects such as subtle shading changes; it may fail to generalize to other datasets with significant variations in lighting and material properties.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating View-Dependent Effects in 3D Models using Mixed Reality and User Studies
PROPOSAL: Develop a custom mixed reality setup to collect user studies on existing 3D models (e.g., from REAL-57) in various real-world environments with varied lighting conditions. Ask participants to identify and rate view-dependent effects such as reflections, highlights, and shading. Use this data to quantify the importance of view-dependent representation for realism and to compare with the generated models from proposal 1.
CONTROLS: Compare ratings with human-expert ratings on view-dependent effects in existing 3D models and generated models.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: The study will reveal the importance of view-dependent effects for realism and highlight limitations of existing models; it may struggle to collect sufficient participant ratings for robust evaluation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimizing View-Dependent Appearance using Physics-Based Rendering and Multi-View Supervision
PROPOSAL: Use the rendering equation and physically-based rendering (PBR) to train a view-dependent appearance model that merges photometric-stereo-based material properties with view-conditioned geometry. This will enable the model to accurately capture view-dependent effects such as depth cues, specularity, and ambient occlusion. Train and evaluate on a dataset of multi-view images of 3D objects with varying lighting conditions (e.g., ShapeNet with lighting variations from Cats 3D).
CONTROLS: Compare with existing view-conditioned geometry-only models (e.g., proposal 1) and appearance-only models.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: The model will improve upon existing methods in capturing view-dependent effects, but may struggle with scenes containing complex textures and occlusions; it may require significant computational resources to train accurately.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reformulating Image Autoregressive Models for Equivariant Learning
PROPOSAL: We explore whether reformulating image AR models to exploit equivariant structures in the input image can lead to more efficient one-step sampling. Specifically, we propose to represent the image as a set of local tokens that correspond to specific visual features (e.g., edges, textures) and design the AR model to be equivariant to spatial transformations of these local tokens. This can simplify the modeling of spatial correlations between tokens and potentially reduce the computational requirements for one-step sampling.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: If the reformulation successfully captures the spatial correlations, we can achieve comparable or even better performance than the original AR model, while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend heavily on the choice of local tokens and the design of the equivariant AR model, which could lead to complications if not carefully handled.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Latent Codebook Splitting for One-Step Sampling
PROPOSAL: We propose to split the codebook used in the image AR model into multiple sub-codebooks, each corresponding to a specific subset of the visual features represented by the local tokens. We design a separate AR model to generate tokens from each sub-codebook, and then use a mixture-of-experts-like strategy to combine the predictions from each sub-model. This approach allows the model to focus on the most relevant features for each token and potentially reduce the computational requirements for one-step sampling.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the number of sub-codebooks and the design of the mixture-of-experts strategy.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: If the codebook splitting is done effectively, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the sub-codebook design and the mixture-of-experts strategy, which could lead to overfitting or loss of feature interactions.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Generative Model for Image Autoregression
PROPOSAL: We introduce a hierarchical generative model for image autoregression, where the teacher AR model is used to predict high-level features (e.g., object categories, scene contexts), and these predictions are then used as inputs to a pixel-level decoder to generate the detailed image structure. This hierarchical design can help the model to capture long-range dependencies and spatial correlations between tokens, making it more efficient for one-step sampling.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the hierarchy depth and the design of the high-level feature predictor.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: If the hierarchical design is effectively used, we can achieve comparable or even better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the high-level feature predictor and the hierarchical design, which could lead to loss of detailed image information.

TITLE: REVISED: Hierarchical Generative Model for Image Autoregression
PROPOSAL: We modify the hierarchical generative model to use a set of intermediate latent variables to condition on the high-level features and facilitate the pixel-level decoder to generate detailed image structure. These intermediate latent variables can capture additional information learned from the teacher AR model, and help the model to generate a more coherent image. We also introduce a new loss function to better align the intermediate latent variables with the teacher AR model's predictions.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the hierarchy depth, the design of the high-level feature predictor, and the intermediate latent variables.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: If the modified hierarchical design effectively captures the high-level features and utilizes the intermediate latent variables, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the high-level feature predictor, the intermediate latent variables, and the new loss function, which could lead to increased complexity and computational cost.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Optimization of Teacher and Student Models for One-Step Sampling
PROPOSAL: We propose a joint optimization approach that learns both the teacher AR model and the one-step generator (student model) simultaneously. The teacher model is used to generate the target images and the student model is trained to match the teacher's output distribution. We introduce a novel loss function that combines the reconstruction error and a term that encourages the student model to output a probability distribution that is close to the teacher's output distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the joint optimization approach and the design of the novel loss function.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: If the joint optimization approach effectively captures the complexities of the teacher AR model and the student model, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the initial teacher model, the design of the novel loss function, and the computational cost of joint optimization.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Refine the Student Model's Output Distribution
PROPOSAL: We propose a technique to refine the output distribution of the student model, which is learned through the joint optimization approach. The refinement process involves generating additional samples from the student model and selecting the ones that have high likelihood under the teacher model's probability distribution. We use these selected samples to update the student model's output distribution, effectively refining it to match the teacher's output distribution more closely.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the refinement process and the selection of samples.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: If the refinement process successfully captures more details of the teacher model's output distribution, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the initial student model and the selection of samples, which could lead to overfitting or underutilization of the updated output distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving One-Step Sampling with Meta-Learning for Teacher AR Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach to improve the performance of teacher AR models. During meta-training, the teacher model is trained on a set of diverse datasets, and during adaptation, the teacher model is fine-tuned on a target dataset with few-shot learning. We also propose a new way to adapt the Meta-Teacher to a specific class of images using the largest n classes w.r.t the meta-training dataset. 
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the meta-learning approach and the adaptation process.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: If the meta-learning approach effectively adapts the teacher model to the target dataset, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the meta-training dataset, the adaptation process, and the number of shots used for few-shot learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Overcoming Mode Collapse with Normalizing Flows in One-Step Sampling
PROPOSAL: We propose to use normalizing flows to transform the output distribution of the student model and prevent mode collapse. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reformulating Image Autoregressive Models for Equivariant Learning
PROPOSAL: We explore whether reformulating image AR models to exploit equivariant structures in the input image can lead to more efficient one-step sampling. Specifically, we propose to represent the image as a set of local tokens that correspond to specific visual features (e.g., edges, textures) and design the AR model to be equivariant to spatial transformations of these local tokens. This can simplify the modeling of spatial correlations between tokens and potentially reduce the computational requirements for one-step sampling.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: If the reformulation successfully captures the spatial correlations, we can achieve comparable or even better performance than the original AR model, while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend heavily on the choice of local tokens and the design of the equivariant AR model, which could lead to complications if not carefully handled.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Latent Codebook Splitting for One-Step Sampling
PROPOSAL: We propose to split the codebook used in the image AR model into multiple sub-codebooks, each corresponding to a specific subset of the visual features represented by the local tokens. We design a separate AR model to generate tokens from each sub-codebook, and then use a mixture-of-experts-like strategy to combine the predictions from each sub-model. This approach allows the model to focus on the most relevant features for each token and potentially reduce the computational requirements for one-step sampling.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the number of sub-codebooks and the design of the mixture-of-experts strategy.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: If the codebook splitting is done effectively, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the sub-codebook design and the mixture-of-experts strategy, which could lead to overfitting or loss of feature interactions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Generative Model for Image Autoregression
PROPOSAL: We introduce a hierarchical generative model for image autoregression, where the teacher AR model is used to predict high-level features (e.g., object categories, scene contexts), and these predictions are then used as inputs to a pixel-level decoder to generate the detailed image structure. This hierarchical design can help the model to capture long-range dependencies and spatial correlations between tokens, making it more efficient for one-step sampling.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the hierarchy depth and the design of the high-level feature predictor.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: If the hierarchical design is effectively used, we can achieve comparable or even better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the high-level feature predictor and the hierarchical design, which could lead to loss of detailed image information.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Hierarchical Generative Model for Image Autoregression
PROPOSAL: We modify the hierarchical generative model to use a set of intermediate latent variables to condition on the high-level features and facilitate the pixel-level decoder to generate detailed image structure. These intermediate latent variables can capture additional information learned from the teacher AR model, and help the model to generate a more coherent image. We also introduce a new loss function to better align the intermediate latent variables with the teacher AR model's predictions.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the hierarchy depth, the design of the high-level feature predictor, and the intermediate latent variables.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: If the modified hierarchical design effectively captures the high-level features and utilizes the intermediate latent variables, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Optimization of Teacher and Student Models for One-Step Sampling
PROPOSAL: We propose a joint optimization approach that learns both the teacher AR model and the one-step generator (student model) simultaneously. The teacher model is used to generate the target images and the student model is trained to match the teacher's output distribution. We introduce a novel loss function that combines the reconstruction error and a term that encourages the student model to output a probability distribution that is close to the teacher's output distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the joint optimization approach and the design of the novel loss function.
COST: 16200
PREDICTION: If the joint optimization approach effectively captures the complexities of the teacher AR model and the student model, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the initial teacher model, the design of the novel loss function, and the computational cost of joint optimization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Refine the Student Model's Output Distribution
PROPOSAL: We propose a technique to refine the output distribution of the student model, which is learned through the joint optimization approach. The refinement process involves generating additional samples from the student model and selecting the ones that have high likelihood under the teacher model's probability distribution. We use these selected samples to update the student model's output distribution, effectively refining it to match the teacher's output distribution more closely.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the refinement process and the selection of samples.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: If the refinement process successfully captures more details of the teacher model's output distribution, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the initial student model and the selection of samples, which could lead to overfitting or underutilization of the updated output distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving One-Step Sampling with Meta-Learning for Teacher AR Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach to improve the performance of teacher AR models. During meta-training, the teacher model is trained on a set of diverse datasets, and during adaptation, the teacher model is fine-tuned on a target dataset with few-shot learning. We also propose a new way to adapt the Meta-Teacher to a specific class of images using the largest n classes w.r.t the meta-training dataset. 
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR model and with DD1 on a set of real-world image synthesis tasks, evaluating metrics such as log likelihood, visual fidelity, and inference speed; ablate the meta-learning approach and the adaptation process.
COST: 32400
PREDICTION: If the meta-learning approach effectively adapts the teacher model to the target dataset, we can achieve better performance than the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality of the meta-training dataset, the adaptation process, and the number of shots used for few-shot learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Direct Mapping Training (DML)
PROPOSAL: Implement an autoencoder-based training pipeline where the generator is a one-step mapping model that predicts the entire sequence of tokens directly from a latent variable. The decoder part of the autoencoder is trained to reconstruct the sequence from the predicted tokens, encouraging the generator to produce tokens that are coherent and consistent with the teacher model's predictions. The training objective combines the reconstruction loss and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the generator's output distribution and the teacher model's predictions. During inference, the generator directly maps a latent variable to the output token sequence.
CONTROLS: Compare against DD1 in terms of performance drop from the original AR model and training speed, and against a single-step sampling approach that does not rely on the teacher model.
COST: 30,000
PREDICTION: DML achieves competitive performance with DD1 regarding the performance drop from the original AR model, but its training speed might be slower due to the need to reconstruct the entire sequence, potentially leading to a error in retaining the correlation with the teacher model's predictions for longer sequences, where these correlations, though implicit in the one-step prediction process of the teacher, get more subtle.

PROPOSAL: Improve the stability and efficiency of training the one-step generator by incorporating early stopping with latent space encoding. The generator is trained for a limited number of iterations, and at each iteration, the latent space encoding of the generator's output is compared to the latent space encoding of the teacher model's predictions. If the difference between the two encodings is below a specified threshold, the generator is stopped, and the weights at that iteration are retained as the optimal weights. TITLE: Triviality of Single-Step Generation

This model can theoretically generate images in a single step but will necessarily ignore all conditioning information from the teacher AR model, effectively rewriting it.

PREDICTION: The trivial baseline should achieve a poor match with the teacher AR model, likely quantifiably worse than Distilled Decoding 1, but it will serve as an important lower bound on performance for future experiments. It might fail to correctly capture simple shapes or patterns that the mean embedding would predict incorrectly (e.g., circling a center pixel).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information Maximizing Latent Variable
PROPOSAL: Design a latent space where the information gain of additional dimensions, as measured by the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the prior and the conditional distribution of the next token given the embeddings, is maximized for each position. This is essentially asking which additional dimensions the teacher AR model relies on the most when generating subsequent tokens.
CONTROLS: Compute the KL divergence for different subsets of dimensions and visualize the values to understand how they relate to the conditional entropy of each token.
COST: 16.56 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment should provide insight into the structure of the latent space, which may be informative for designing more efficient one-step generative models. It might fail to generalize well to different codebooks or images, as the information gain could be heavily task-dependent.

TITLE: Triviality of Single-Step Generation
PROPOSAL: Establish a trivial baseline for single-step generation by training a model that simply outputs the mean embedding vector from the codebook for all positions. This model can theoretically generate images in a single step but will necessarily ignore all conditioning information from the teacher AR model, effectively rewriting it.

COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The trivial baseline should achieve a poor match with the teacher AR model, likely quantifiably worse than Distilled Decoding 1, but it will serve as an important lower bound on performance for future experiments. It might fail to correctly capture simple shapes or patterns that the mean embedding would predict incorrectly (e.g., circling a center pixel).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information Maximizing Latent Variable
PROPOSAL: Design a latent space where the information gain of additional dimensions, as measured by the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the prior and the conditional distribution of the next token given the embeddings, is maximized for each position. This is essentially asking which additional dimensions the teacher AR model relies on the most when generating subsequent tokens.
CONTROLS: Compute the KL divergence for different subsets of dimensions and visualize the values to understand how they relate to the conditional entropy of each token.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment should provide insight into the structure of the latent space, which may be informative for designing more efficient one-step generative models. It might fail to generalize well to different codebooks or images, as the information gain could be heavily task-dependent.

PREDICTION: Knowledge distillation might improve the performance of the one-step generator by enabling it to leverage the expertise of the teacher AR model, but it might fail to achieve state-of-the-art performance due to the difficulty of matching the internal embeddings and output sequences between the two models.

TITLE: Specialization via Orthogonal Router Regularization
PROPOSAL: Experimentally analyze and compare two variants ofusal orthogonal weight matrix regularizers: one based on the spectral norm, and another on the nuclear norm. We hypothesize that encouraging expert weights to be orthogonal, using the nuclear norm is more effective in guiding the expert router to specialize. Specifically, we add a term to the load-balancing loss that computationally penalizes the nuclear norm of the router's weight matrix. To train our MoE models, we will use the Penn Treebank (PTB) and WikiText-103 (WT103) datasets, along with the widely used Generative Preptraining (GPT)3-and 4 model as baselines.
CONTROLS: [1] Baseline: standard MoE model with only load-balancing loss; [2] un-regularized MoE model; [3] addition of the spectral norm regularizer variant
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: This experiment provides evidence that, compared to standard MoE models, our novel orthogonal regularizer (nuclear norm) improves the specialization of experts especially in longer sequences where uniform expert usage is more detrimental. In our predicted outcomes, we expect PTB results to show only moderate improvements while WT103 exhibits the most significant gains in terms of specialisation in the interest of keeping costs of the added dimension minimised, this *may* cause a suplus in lack of supervision solution that could degrade ensemble performace in longer sequences.

PROPOSAL: Explore different routing diversity strategies that encourage functional specialization among experts, including: 1) batchSize-dependent routing (where the number of experts used depends on the batch size), 2) pseudo-label based routing (where each token assigns a confidence score to its assigned expert, making it less likely for tokens belonging to the same class to be routed to the same expert), 3) and permutation-based load balancing (the model assigns each token to an expert based on a set of permutations of the experts, making it less likely for tokens to be consistently routed to the same expert). CONTROLS: Baseline (standard load-balancing and language modeling objectives), mutually exclusive experiments (each routing diversity strategy is used in isolation)
COST: 576
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating routing diversity strategies will lead to improved expert specialization and functional diversity among experts, with some potentially leading to improved performances on downstream tasks, while potentially causing decreased performances if too much diversity is encouraged.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Latent Gaussian Routing: Balancing Expert Usage and Functionality with Bayesian Mixture Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a new Gaussian routing mechanism, where each expert is associated with a latent Gaussian component, and the routing logits are modeled as a Bayesian mixture of these components. This approach encourages diverse expert usage by enforcing a global Gaussian cluster structure, while promoting organized collaboration and specialization among experts by allowing each Gaussian component to capture unique data distributions.
CONTROLS: Ablations of this routing mechanism and separate experiments using existing MoE models (e.g. MoE-T5; Molinet et al., 2022) on standardized benchmarks (e.g. GLUE; Wang et al., 2019).
COST: 429.5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in expert specialization and a 10% gain in downstream performance for mathematical reasoning tasks, while showing competitive performance in other domains due to the Gaussian mixture's ability to adapt to diverse text distributions.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-theoretic Regularization for Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: We design an information-theoretic regularization term based on the mutual information between the input, the learned representations, and the expert indicators. By penalizing zero mutual information, we enforce experts to capture unique aspects of the input data, thereby promoting specialization and reducing redundant functionalities.
CONTROLS: We compare the proposed regularization with other recently introduced regularization methods (e.g., projector loss; Frieder et al., 2023) and analyze its impact on MoE's parameter space and representative capacity using dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, UMAP).
COST: 768 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this regularization to significantly alleviate expert homogenization and efficiently allocate representations to each expert, outperforming existing regulation methods in expert specialization and downstream performance on reading comprehension tasks. It may lead to a performance plateau for dense representations when there's too many experts since global mutual information could be saturated in extensive dimensions.

TITLE: Adaptive Expert Training with Dynamic Routing Inheritance
PROPOSAL: We introduce a dynamic inheritance mechanism, where experts learn to inherit routing patterns from their parent experts in a hierarchical way. This allows for adaptive and context-dependent routing, enabling experts to focus on the task at hand and adapt to the specific input data distribution.
CONTROLS: Comparison with static routing mechanisms (e.g., permutation routing; Gu et al., 2020) and analysis of the inheritance mechanism's impact on expert specialization and downstream performance using techniques such as proto-type analysis.
COST: 1130 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this adaptive approach to enable the model to quickly adapt to changing task requirements and data distributions, leading to improved performance on exam-style knowledge question answering tasks and potentially influencing performance in English reading comprehension benchmarks, although adaptation might be over-fit to the val or test set.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Latent Gaussian Routing: Balancing Expert Usage and Functionality with Bayesian Mixture Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a new Gaussian routing mechanism, where each expert is associated with a latent Gaussian component, and the routing logits are modeled as a Bayesian mixture of these components. This approach encourages diverse expert usage by enforcing a global Gaussian cluster structure, while promoting organized collaboration and specialization among experts by allowing each Gaussian component to capture unique data distributions.
CONTROLS: Ablations of this routing mechanism and separate experiments using existing MoE models (e.g. MoE-T5; Molinet et al., 2022) on standardized benchmarks (e.g. GLUE; Wang et al., 2019).
COST: 1286 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in expert specialization and a 10% gain in downstream performance for mathematical reasoning tasks, while showing competitive performance in other domains due to the Gaussian mixture's ability to adapt to diverse text distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-theoretic Regularization for Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: We design an information-theoretic regularization term based on the mutual information between the input, the learned representations, and the expert indicators. By penalizing zero mutual information, we enforce experts to capture unique aspects of the input data, thereby promoting specialization and reducing redundant functionalities.
CONTROLS: We compare the proposed regularization with other recently introduced regularization methods (e.g., projector loss; Frieder et al., 2023) and analyze its impact on MoE's parameter space and representative capacity using dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, UMAP).
COST: 2294 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this regularization to significantly alleviate expert homogenization and efficiently allocate representations to each expert, outperforming existing regulation methods in expert specialization and downstream performance on reading comprehension tasks. It may lead to a performance plateau for dense representations when there's too many experts since global mutual information could be saturated in extensive dimensions.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Latent Gaussian Routing: Balancing Expert Usage and Functionality with Hierarchical Bayesian Mixture Models
PROPOSAL: We extend the latent Gaussian routing mechanism to incorporate hierarchical Bayesian mixture models, where each expert is associated with a multilevel Gaussian component. This modification encourages not only diverse expert usage but also organized collaboration and specialization among experts at multiple granularity levels, enabling the model to capture complex data structures and relationships.
CONTROLS: Same as before, with an additional ablation study on the number of hierarchical levels in the Gaussian mixture.
COST: 1916 GPU-hours (competitive costs are relatively easy with minimal changes needed)
PREDICTION: We expect a further improvement in expert specialization, enabling the model to capture subtler nuances in text data and leading to a 2% boost in mathematical reasoning performance and a competitive performance on other tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Expert Training with Dynamic Routing Inheritance
PROPOSAL: We introduce a dynamic inheritance mechanism, where experts learn to inherit routing patterns from their parent experts in a hierarchical way. This allows for adaptive and context-dependent routing, enabling experts to focus on the task at hand and adapt to the specific input data distribution.
CONTROLS: Comparison with static routing mechanisms (e.g., permutation routing; Gu et al., 2020) and analysis of the inheritance mechanism's impact on expert specialization and downstream performance using techniques such as proto-type analysis.
COST: 3368 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this adaptive approach to enable the model to quickly adapt to changing task requirements and data distributions, leading to improved performance on exam-style knowledge question answering tasks and potentially influencing performance in English reading comprehension benchmarks, although adaptation might be over-fit to the val or test set.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Information-theoretic Regularization for Expert Specialization with Causal Learning
PROPOSAL: We extend the information-theoretic regularization term to incorporate causal learning principles, where the mutual information is computed between the input, the expert indicators, and the counterfactual expert representations. This design encourages experts to develop causal relationships with the input data and each other, promoting more structured and interpretable representations.
CONTROLS: Comparative analysis with traditional information-theoretic regularization and ablation study on the causal learning module's impact on expert specialization and downstream performance.
COST: 2510 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: We expect this novel regularization to lead to better-structured expert representations, directly improving reading comprehension tasks and isolating the information contributed by each expert, albeit with potential increase of VRAM usage.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Expert Learning and Transfer with Cross-Task Knowledge Graph
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical expert learning framework, where experts learn to specialize in tasks at different levels of a domain hierarchy (e.g., arithmetic operations, numerical reasoning, and inference). We also introduce a cross-task knowledge graph to facilitate knowledge transfer across tasks and enable experts to leverage knowledge from related domains to improve performance on novel tasks.
CONTROLS: Comparative analysis with traditional hierarchical learning frameworks and evaluation of the cross-task knowledge graph's impact on expert specialization, downstream performance, and transfer learning.
COST: 5134 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this framework to significantly improve knowledge transfer performance, outperforming existing knowledge transfer methods on mathematical reasoning and Chinese reading comprehension tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Adaptive Expert Training with Dynamic Routing and Uncertainty-Incorporating Feedback Loops
PROPOSAL: We enhance the adaptive expert training framework with uncertainty-incorporating feedback loops, where experts receive feedback on their uncertainty estimates and adjust their routing patterns accordingly. This interactive process enables experts to adapt more effectively to the task at hand and improve their performance in situations with high uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Comparative analysis with traditional adaptive expert training and analysis of the impact of uncertainty incorporating feedback loops on expert specialization and downstream performance using techniques such as model interpretability.
COST: 3828 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this revised framework to lead to expert representations with enhanced uncertainty-awareness and promote confidence-aware routing decisions that mitigate uncertainty explosions, potentially improving performance by a moderate margin on exam-style question answering tasks, and inherited efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Multi-Label Training via Meta-Learned Component Coordination
PROPOSAL: We will adopt a meta-learning approach to develop a dynamic multi-label training framework. We'll train a meta-model on a set of simulations of different training scenarios, each characterized by a distinct augmentation strategy, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function. During meta-training, the meta-model learns to predict the optimal configuration for a given training episode. At the start of the actual multi-label training process, we'll leverage this meta-model to adapt the training components dynamically, seamlessly adjusting the augmentation strategy, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function as the training state evolves. This will allow us to coordinate the components adaptively to the emerging patterns in the data.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our framework to the traditional static configuration paradigm, as well as to existing adaptive techniques that tune components one by one (e.g., learned augmentation policies, adaptive optimizers, cyclical learning-rate schedules). For ablation, we'll also experiment with a variant of our framework that doesn't use the meta-model, and instead applies a fixed set of pre-trained configurations.
COST: 672
PREDICTION: Our adaptive framework can significantly outperform static configurations and conventional adaptive techniques, achieving better performance on rare labels, more stable training dynamics, and faster convergence. It might struggle with interpreting complex interactions among components, and potential over-adaptation might lead to oscillations or divergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dataset-Driven Exploration of Configuration Space for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an exhaustive offline search on a subset of the PASCAL-Part dataset to understand the landscape of configuration choices for multi-label image classification. We'll divide the configuration space into smaller blocks, and for each block, we'll sample a small set of augmentations, optimizers, learning-rate schedules, and loss functions. We'll then train our model on each of these combinations and measure its performance on a validation set. This will allow us to build a heatmap or a Pareto front that highlights the regions of the configuration space that are more promising for multi-label image classification. We'll also analyze the results to identify patterns and correlations between different components.
CONTROLS: We'll hold fixed the most tries or epochs to keep the search manageable, and use these as a baseline to compare with the adaptive strategy from proposal 1.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: This offline search may highlight a non-trivial correlation between the choice of augmentations and the use of auxiliary tasks in multi-label image classification, potentially informing our adaptive framework in novel ways. However, it's likely that we'll discover that certain regions of the configuration space are more challenging to navigate due to the high dimensionality and local optima.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Loss Function vs. Standard Cross-Entropy for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of using a multi-task loss function on multi-label image classification performance. Specifically, we'll compare the standard cross-entropy loss to a multi-task loss function that penalizes the model for predicted label pairs that are known to co-occur in the training data. We'll train our model using both loss functions on the CIFAR-100 dataset, and analyze the results to see if the multi-task loss function leads to improved performance on rare labels and better overall multi-label accuracy.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the results to a version of our adaptive framework from proposal 1 that uses a standard cross-entropy loss, and also explore the effect of varying the weight assigned to the multi-task loss term.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: Our results may show that the multi-task loss function leads to improved performance on rare labels and better overall multi-label accuracy, particularly on datasets characterized by complex co-occurrence patterns. However, we may also find that its benefits come at the cost of increased training instability or poor generalization to unseen data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Fast and Efficient Inference Method for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We will propose a new inference method for multi-label image classification that efficiently handles the simultaneous prediction of multiple labels. Our method, called "_label tree search_", uses a hierarchical structure to prune the possible label assignments, significantly reducing the computational cost of inference. We'll evaluate the performance and efficiency of _label tree search_ on a variety of multi-label image classification datasets.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the results to existing state-of-the-art methods for multi-label image classification, as well as to an ablated version of our method that does not use the hierarchical pruning strategy.
COST: 3325
PREDICTION: Our results may show that _label tree search_ significantly reduces the computational cost of inference for multi-label image classification while maintaining comparable performance to existing methods. However, we may also find that our method struggles with certain types of datasets or has high computational costs for very high-numbered classification tasks.
